blocks.x: Hearing tech startup Legato announced that its AI-based hearing glasses, Legato Frames, are now available. They build its patented hearing-assistance tech into the arms of eyewear frames. Starting at $999, they are designed for adults with up to moderate hearing loss, aiming to address the cost, comfort, and stigma of traditional hearing aids.

Rather than directional microphones, Legato's AI-powered system distinguishes voices from background noise, amplifying voices while reducing unwanted sounds. A dual-speaker system directs sound to the wearer and cancels escaping sound, reducing it by 99% a few inches from the ear.

All processing happens on the glasses, with no cameras or recording. They weigh 34 grams with lenses, get 10-12 hours of battery life, come in three styles, and support prescription lenses and Bluetooth streaming.

Legato, founded in 2024 by Bose veterans Mehul Trivedi and Steve Romine, recently emerged from stealth with $12 million in funding. The frames are sold online and through select U.S. eye care providers, eligible for vision insurance coverage.

Guided Vision is launching in Gemini Live on compatible Android devices today to use AI to give real-time audio descriptions of anything you point your phone’s camera at. By sharing your camera in Gemini Live, you can have Google’s AI help with things like reading small text, describing your surroundings, finding or identifying objects around you, and describing details on specific objects.

Like the VoiceOver Live Recognition feature Apple has added to the iPhone and Vision Pro, it’s designed for people who are blind, have low vision, or want assistance in specific situations. In addition to the Gemini app, Guided Vision is also available in Google TalkBack, or users can set up an accessibility shortcut for it in the Settings app on devices running Android 9 and above, after it was announced in a recent set of Pixel updates.

You can also ask follow-up questions about whatever you’re looking at, like asking Gemini to read off the expiration date on an item it helped you find. Google says Gemini will give you audio cues to help line up your camera if you ask about something that’s not in the shot. However, Google cautions users not to rely on Guided Vision for things like “navigation, safe-travel guidance, or obstacle detection,” or as a replacement for a cane or mobility aid.

blocks.cap: Oura Ring 5

blocks.x: Oura has partnered with Xella Health, a women's precision health platform that combines lab testing with telehealth care. Oura ring owners in the US who subscribe to Xella can share sleep, HRV, resting heart rate, temperature trends, recovery, activity, and menstrual cycle insights.

Xella then runs what it calls "multi-omic" diagnostics, using custom AI to analyze Oura's physiologic data alongside hormones, metabolism, inflammation, nutrition, reproductive health, and cardiometabolic risk to spot patterns that may indicate a change in health. Xella's AI then creates a care plan with a doctor, which can include treatment for more than 130 conditions that impact women, such as endometriosis.
"Wearables have transformed our ability to detect physiologic change," said Xella Health CEO and co-founder Kelly Lacob.
Xella is a separate membership costing $499 a year, available in all U.S. states except New York and New Jersey. The Oura Ring 5 starts at $399 plus $5.99 a month, and is not a medical device.

Google Home is getting its third update this September. Google says it has enhanced how Gemini for Home filters out background conversation when you give it a command in a loud room, so requests register more often, and it replies faster across common smart home, media, alarm, and timer commands.

Gemini for Home should also be more reliable in multilingual households, and it no longer gets stuck repeating "I didn't understand" after an error. Asking it to find your phone is now a lot more reliable.

In the Home app, sliding brightness to 0% now sends a proper power-off command, online camera and doorbell tiles appear as filled icons, and Nest setup on Android and iOS is smoother, with the app able to securely cache network credentials for back-to-back setups.
The update also fixes Matter switch offline status, Favorites tiles, camera playback and buffering, Walmart Onn camera history, and Automations device names.

blocks.cap: Apple (Aqara), Ring, and Google Nest video doorbells

blocks.x: A few years ago, The Verge's Jennifer Pattison Tuohy was hunting Easter eggs with her kids on the beach. Her phone kept buzzing in her pocket, but every alert just said motion detected. When she got home, the chicken coop she hadn't locked properly was open, and her border terrier had already killed four chickens.

If the first alert had said a small dog is chasing the chickens, she would have run home right away. That kind of alert is possible now. A vision-language model writes a one-sentence description of what the camera sees and sends it before the video even loads. Ring, Google Nest, Blink, Wyze, and Arlo already offer this, and Apple added Apple Intelligence for Home to HomeKit Secure Video this month with iOS 27.

Apple is the most expensive. Tied to iCloud+ plans, one camera costs 9.99 dollars a month, two cameras cost 29.99 dollars, and up to five cameras cost 59.99 dollars. Google and Ring charge 20 dollars a month for unlimited cameras with AI descriptions, video search, and facial recognition.

Tuohy compared the Ring Wired Doorbell Pro, the Google Nest Doorbell 2K, and the Aqara Doorbell Camera G400 for Apple. Google and Ring gave the most specific descriptions. Apple often went no further than someone is walking in the yard. Google even specified which cat, as in a black and white cat is crossing the porch.

blocks.cap: She stood at the door wearing a Ghostface mask. Nest sent the most useful alert.

blocks.x: Ring was the most accurate at facial recognition. Apple often hedged with phrases like a person who might be Jennifer Pattison Tuohy, and Google mistook the author for her daughter's friend about half the time. Apple does have features of its own: clip stitching, which recognizes the same subject across multiple cameras and splices the footage into one video, and a feature that surfaces events that look important above the search bar.

Ring's Unusual Activity solved alert fatigue best. Each camera learns its normal scene and only alerts on what breaks from it. Alerts that used to run about 40 a day dropped to two or three. It stays quiet when her son comes home from school, but alerts her if he comes in at 2am.

The next step is automation that acts on what the camera sees, like turning on the sprinklers when a raccoon shows up in the backyard. Google Home added a feature that runs automations from camera alerts, but a setting meant to feed only one specific cat triggered every time any cat appeared. Recognition accuracy is what matters.

blocks.cap: Because Google Home couldn't tell the cats apart, all of them got extra food.

blocks.x: Privacy remains an issue. Ring processes all video in the cloud by default. With Apple Intelligence turned on, video summaries are decrypted and processed on Private Cloud Compute (PCC), and Apple says it permanently deletes the data once processing is done. Tuohy believes local AI processing is the right answer.

Right now, Apple's premium buys less. Paying 10 dollars a month for one camera is fine, but paying 60 dollars a month for five cameras just to get a notification that a cat sat on the porch doesn't add up. AI has made cameras able to say what happened. What's left is telling people what actually matters.

blocks.cap: The C2PA Verify app screen

blocks.x: Generative AI's biggest headache is how hard it is to tell the real from the fabricated. As models get better, even sharp-eyed people struggle to tell the difference. Given how fast the technology is improving, it's unlikely to get easier.

A new app called C2PA Verify aims to help with this problem. It's an Android app that reads the C2PA (Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity) credentials embedded in an image to show where it came from and how it was edited.
The app summarizes the long, complex record. Users can see the signer, the creator, and the image's timeline, and open the raw data if they want.
There are limits. C2PA credentials can be stripped out. If an image has had this data removed, the app can't tell whether it's AI-generated or a real photo either.
Still, Android Authority called it a tool worth keeping on your phone. It's open-source and free, built by Dark Rock Studios, the maker of the privacy app SnapSafe.

The same article also featured two more AI apps. Retirement Planner is a web app vibe-coded with Claude Opus 4.5. Based on user inputs, it calculates and displays projected net worth, post-retirement withdrawal rates, and taxes, and it's built for users in the US and Canada.

blocks.cap: The gallery app Memoria

blocks.x: Memoria is an Android gallery app that supports natural-language search using offline AI. It uses Apple's MobileCLIP-S0 model, so both the search and the data stay on the device. The trade-off is an install size well over 250MB. Users can search by text or by similar images, and it's also open-source and free.

blocks.cap: The PixelMob portable AI workstation

blocks.x: TechRadar reviewed the PixelMob portable AI workstation from UniDrive. It's aimed at photographers, video creators, and other creators. A small box with a 7-inch OLED touchscreen packs in file backup and management, editing, monitoring, and tethered shooting, and it launched through Kickstarter.

It runs a custom version of Android with 12GB of LPDDR5 RAM and 256GB of storage. Three M.2 slots let it expand up to 24TB using 8TB modules. It supports CFexpress Type B (up to 800MB/s), SD, microSD, USB-A and USB-C, HDMI input and output, and a LAN port, and weighs 550g. The built-in 11,600mAh battery lasts two to three hours under heavy load, and a Sony NP-F battery can be attached on the back for longer use.

blocks.cap: A body sized somewhere between a phone and a tablet

blocks.x: AI pulls its weight in file organization. Moving files from a card into the Lightbox folder lets the built-in AI automatically tag them, group similar burst shots, recognize faces, and flag over- or underexposed photos. People and bird recognition, as well as empty-scene detection, can also be turned on. Thumbnails loaded faster than in Adobe Bridge.

Photo editing happens in the Cones app. Star trails and focus or exposure stacking are also handled there. There's a video editor called Framebox too, but the reviewer downloaded CapCut instead. Approved third-party apps, such as Lightroom or the DJI app, can also be installed.

blocks.cap: Tethered mode for use with a camera

blocks.x: Connected to a Sony A7 IV, it lets you control shooting while watching a live feed. Its long-exposure simulation, which composites 30 shots taken in succession, produced long-exposure photos without an ND filter. In Deck mode, it monitors the camera's feed over HDMI while recording at up to 50Mbps and applying LUTs.

There are drawbacks too. The casing feels distinctly plastic, like a prototype, and the NP-F battery doesn't sit perfectly secure. Some 1TB and 2TB CFexpress Type B cards weren't recognized. It's also not obvious at first that you need to create a Lightbox folder before anything else.

Even so, the reviewer called it one of the most feature-packed creator devices they've seen. It combines portable storage, AI-powered organization, tethering, editing, and video monitoring in a single device, and they said they plan to keep using it.

blocks.cap: Magic Pointer on the Acer Googlebook 14

blocks.x: Google looked at the mouse cursor, one of the oldest elements on a desktop, and decided that with Gemini, it could do more than just clicking. That is how Magic Pointer came about. It understands what you highlight on a Googlebook screen and helps you do something with it.
It sounds convenient, but it raises an important question: exactly when does what is on screen leave the laptop for Google's cloud? Google explained where that line sits.
Alexander Kusher, Google's senior director for laptop and tablet products, appeared on Android Faithful to explain how Magic Pointer works behind the scenes.

According to Kusher, at the 1 hour 6 minute 37 second mark, the first step is handled inside the Googlebook. Turning on Magic Pointer makes the laptop find and highlight things on screen you can interact with, such as an email, an image, or a block of text.

The cloud comes in only after the user picks something and hands the task to Gemini. Kusher gave the example of checking whether an email is spam: recognizing that it is an email is handled on the device, and asking Gemini to analyze it sends the selected content to the cloud model.
So the line is fairly simple. Just having the cursor on does not mean screen content is sent to Gemini every time. Google says the AI cursor does not act until the user calls on it directly.

Google appears to have studied the ordinary cursor for quite a while. Kusher said internal testing found some employees moved the cursor about a mile over a single workday. The team took this as confirmation that the pointer is a useful signal of where a user's attention is.

Before launch, Android Authority dug into Magic Pointer and found several Gemini features Google was testing, and hands-on time with the Googlebook confirmed the feature sits at the center of the platform. Now it is also clear where local processing stops and the cloud takes over.

blocks.cap: Siri AI in iOS 27

blocks.x: I did not expect to say this, but in iOS 27, Siri has become more useful than ever. It launched with the iPhone 4S and was a punchline for a long time, trailing Amazon's Alexa and Google's assistant before falling further behind LLMs like ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini.

Now Apple's AI has finally caught up, with a little help from Google Gemini. Apple Intelligence, mocked as vaporware after a demo years ago, now runs properly across almost all of Apple's '27' operating systems.

It can still answer things like how many milliliters are in a teaspoon, but the real strength of Siri AI is that it knows your personal context. The iPhone knows your contacts, reads your messages and email, and checks your calendar to surface the right information at the right moment.

There is something to check before you start. Siri AI is not available in every region, and it is not coming to the EU for now. You need to turn the feature on in Settings and let it index your app data, which can take more than a few hours, so be patient.

One, find a recommended song. My friends and I have similar music taste, so our group chat is always full of Spotify links. Asking, 'What song did Phil recommend last week?' lets Siri dig the link out of the conversation. At the time of writing, though, WhatsApp does not yet support Siri AI.

Two, plan your day. Saying, 'Show me this week's meetings' pulls together your upcoming schedule. You have to turn on each calendar individually in Settings. Leave out a work calendar and you could miss an important meeting.

blocks.cap: Visual Intelligence also finds nutrition information on a menu

blocks.x: Three, pick a restaurant. Thanks to the new screen recognition feature, Siri understands what is currently on your iPhone's screen. Pull up a few restaurants and ask Siri to recommend one based on user reviews, or to narrow it down by cuisine. Visual Intelligence can also translate a menu on the spot or look up nutrition information for a dish.

Four, find and expand photos. Saying, 'All the photos I took at Altea beach' pulls them from your photo library. Saying, 'Expand this image' runs the generative-AI tool that fills in the edges and reframes the shot.

blocks.cap: Finding photos in the Photos app with natural language

blocks.x: Five, manage files. As a small-business owner, the author saved a fair amount of time by having Siri track down lost files. Finding a specific screenshot or the latest version of a file works not only on the iPhone but also on the iPad and Mac. Asking, 'Siri, where's my Tom's Guide presentation?' gives you the location and pulls out key data from inside the file.
A lot of this has been possible on Gemini devices for a while. Still, if this is your first AI assistant, there is plenty to learn. The one piece of advice is to just try different things.

At Qualcomm's Snapdragon Summit in Maui, it was Microsoft's Surface booth that stole the attention. Spec talk took a back seat. The focus was on what the new Snapdragon devices could actually do, offering a glimpse of where local AI on Windows PCs is headed — from small interface touches to fairly heavy creative work.

The first demo was haptics. Tactile feedback built into the Surface touchpad and pen responds with small vibrations when aligning objects or scrubbing a timeline in Affinity, DaVinci Resolve, or PowerPoint. It sounds minor, but it feels different in use. The laptop doesn't get faster, yet in creative apps full of constant nudging and aligning, that extra layer turns out to be quite useful.

blocks.cap: Copilot CLI picking out phone photos and moving them into a Surface folder

blocks.x: There was also a demo combining Phone Link, an Android phone, and the Copilot CLI. Asking in plain language for photos suited to an SNS post, pulled from a connected Nothing phone's gallery, had the AI analyze the images, pick the right ones, and copy them into a new folder on the Surface. The phone just supplied the data; the heavy processing ran locally on the Surface.

blocks.cap: Sketching a football on the Surface Pro

blocks.x: The most striking demo was the creative workflow. A Microsoft 3D artist hand-drew a football in Photoshop, brought it into Blender, and had AI turn it into a 3D asset. After resizing the model and adding elements, they went back to Photoshop to refine the lighting and shadows, then added animation and camera movement. The Surface ran on battery power the entire time without stuttering.

blocks.cap: Generating a football 3D asset with AI inside Blender

blocks.x: The finished asset then moved into image generation, becoming a stadium scene complete with lighting and environmental effects, and that fed into a short video. None of the individual technologies are new. What's interesting is stringing them together, one after another, on a portable 2-in-1. The new X2 Plus model's NPU puts out up to 80 TOPS, but what mattered to onlookers was less the number than whether it actually got the job done. The answer leaned toward yes.

blocks.cap: Ink Canvas demo

blocks.x: For usability, Ink Canvas was the most interesting part. Instead of describing an idea to a chatbot in words, you start from a blank canvas. You build a mood board by dropping in images, scribbling notes with the pen, and adding highlights, then lasso part of it to generate an image from that context or get a summary. It cuts down the effort of translating a visual idea into an elaborate text prompt. Ink Canvas comes built into touch-enabled Surface devices, though its generative features require an internet connection and a Microsoft 365 subscription.

Asked to compare it with Nvidia's RTX Spark, a Microsoft designer gave a grounded answer. Nvidia still leads on raw compute and memory. Snapdragon is aiming to deliver enough local AI on thin, battery-powered devices. Professional creators can still get real work done on an X2 Elite Surface, the designer said — the difference comes down to the ceiling.

Meta's AI glasses are getting a feature for wearers with hearing loss. At Meta Connect, Meta announced it will roll out a 'Hearing Enhancement' feature to supported devices before the end of the year. At least initially, Ray-Ban models are excluded.
It's included with a Meta One subscription, or a one-time $149 payment if you don't subscribe. A 30-day free trial is available before you pay.

The software has FDA clearance and qualifies for HSA/FSA reimbursement, though reimbursement must be confirmed separately with each insurer. It can be set up at home without a prescription. Turning it on or off takes just one voice command (“Hey Meta, start Hearing Enhancement”).

Meta already offers a 'Conversation Focus' mode that sharpens speech in noisy places. The new feature targets users with mild to moderate hearing loss who would otherwise wear a hearing aid. It arrives alongside a 'Detailed Responses' feature refined with input from the blind and low-vision community, plus new audio and control customization settings.

Samsung has halted the rollout of a SmartThings software update for refrigerators. The reason is that some units that installed the update stopped working entirely. The trouble broke out in the afternoon of September 22, Korea time, just days before the Chuseok holiday.

According to StarNews and SBS News, dozens of posts appeared on Samsung's official community, Samsung Members. They described refrigerators freezing the moment users tapped the update notification in SmartThings. One post said that on returning home, the interior light was off, the touch panel was unresponsive and there was no cooling at all. Another said the screen stayed stuck on 'Updating' even after unplugging and replugging the power. Complaints about having to throw out Chuseok food followed one after another.

Most of the affected units are from the Bespoke AI 4-Door series released since 2024. ZDNet Korea reported the cause was internal test software that reached customers due to a system error. Samsung told the outlet it halted distribution as soon as it identified the deployment error.

Samsung also issued a public apology. It advised customers to book a visit so a technician could inspect the product directly, and recommended moving food into a cooler in the meantime. Some users said even the booking system struggled under the surge of traffic.

The repair schedule triggered further complaints. Some customers said service centers told them they could only get a visit after the holiday. Samsung Electronics Service said it would keep engineers and call center staff on hand during the holiday to respond to urgent cooling failures, and SBS reported those dates as September 26 and 27.
Samsung has not yet disclosed how many units were affected or whether it will compensate for spoiled food. In the meantime, users are getting by packing their refrigerators with dry ice.

blocks.cap: Asus GB300 workstation (image: StorageReview)

blocks.x: Asus has released a workstation built around Nvidia's GB300 Grace Blackwell Ultra Superchip, the 'ExpertCenter Pro ET900N G3.' It packs 72 Arm cores, a Blackwell Ultra GPU and 748GB of coherent memory into a single chassis. At 27kg and 584×232×565mm, it was never meant to be portable.

The exterior is brushed silver with a dark mesh front, topped with two thick metal handles designed so several people can move it without having to grip the side panels. Inside, a sealed liquid-cooling loop with copper cold plates cools the superchip, memory and network cards. A dedicated fan sends separate airflow to the optical transceivers that the liquid cooling doesn't reach.
Power comes from an 80 PLUS Titanium-certified 1,600W supply. The default storage is two 2TB NVMe drives mirrored together, with three empty PCIe slots and two empty expansion bays.

In testing, it ran 128 concurrent streams on the MiniMax M2.7 benchmark, producing 4,793 output tokens per second. For a large model like GLM-5.2, 215GB of expert weights were pushed directly into coherent memory. On GPT-OSS-120B, output reached 9,280 tokens per second, with total throughput exceeding 45,000 tokens per second.

Reviewers agreed it looks like Apple's boxy Mac Pro, but the performance is in an entirely different class. Brian Beeler of StorageReview said, “The GB300 DGX Station is the most powerful machine we've ever put on a desk.” Running dozens of coding agents at once didn't noticeably slow down any individual agent, and scaling from one agent up to 128 caused no stalling or lag.

Linking two 400-gigabit network ports to another GB300 station at up to 800Gb/s creates a 1,496GB memory pool. YouTuber Alex Ziskind showed in a video that power draw climbed to nearly 1,000W while running dozens of coding, research and writing agents at once. Asus hasn't disclosed pricing, with estimates ranging from $100,000 to $120,000.

These days, phones can't escape AI features. Launches are increasingly built around AI, and every brand pushes its own AI assistant. Nowhere is that clearer than in the dedicated AI button. For Android Authority's Megan Ellis, the AI button had been the least welcome part of her phone.

blocks.cap: A phone held in hand showing its side buttons

blocks.x: The AI button sits apart from the power and volume buttons, and pressing it opens an AI assistant or AI feature directly. The Motorola Razr Fold and Motorola Edge have it on the left side, and even the budget Nothing Phone 4a has a dedicated button. The HONOR 600 Pro, which Ellis recently switched to as her main phone, puts the AI button at the bottom right of the frame.

For someone who doesn't use AI daily, the button was something she pressed by accident and closed right away. Gemini tied to the power and home buttons wasn't welcome either. She finally went into settings looking for a way to turn the button off, and instead found a way to make it useful.

blocks.cap: The AI button settings menu on the HONOR 600 Pro

blocks.x: The HONOR 600 Pro lets you assign a function to a long press, a double press and a single press separately. You can pick functions unrelated to AI, like the flashlight, camera or sound-mode switching. The real find was 'Quick Services.' It can open not just an app, but a specific feature inside that app directly — things like creating a new event in Google Calendar, starting song recognition in Deezer, or opening Firefox's password manager.

blocks.cap: The Quick Services settings screen for the HONOR AI button

blocks.x: She settled on three, mixing fun, practicality and productivity. A long press opens Pokémon Go, which she plays daily; a double press brings up the notes app NotesNook; a single press turns on the flashlight, handy for crossing a dark room to bed after turning off the bedroom light at night. It's much faster than opening quick settings through a split notification panel she dislikes.

blocks.cap: AI button options on the Motorola Edge 70

blocks.x: Not every AI button works this way. The Motorola Edge 70 she's currently reviewing only lets you either use the AI feature or turn the button off — nothing in between. Ellis believes that if manufacturers open the button up as a free shortcut, it becomes far less of an annoying dead weight. For people who actually enjoy using AI, the original function still remains. She hopes other manufacturers stop locking the button down and follow HONOR's lead.
When Google launched the Pixel 11, it promised a major Pixel Buds update in September. The first results are now showing up: the latest Pixel Buds companion app adds Gemini audio controls.

Updating the app to version 1.0.981607934 adds @Pixel Buds to Gemini's list of connected apps. Settings like EQ presets, ANC modes, conversation detection and touch controls can now be changed through Gemini. Just say something like “Hey Google, turn up the bass” or “Hey Google, turn on noise cancellation.”

blocks.cap: The Gemini overlay that appears after a command

blocks.x: Giving a command brings up the Gemini overlay, which confirms it by voice along with a “Connecting to Pixel Buds” message. On devices without the update, the same command only opens the system Bluetooth settings screen. Version 1.0.981607934 is rolling out widely through the Play Store today.

The other three features Google announced alongside this appear to need a separate firmware update. Pixel Buds Pro 2 will get dynamic ANC that corrects for slight seal shifts when the earbuds move inside the ear. A feature linking Pixel Watch sleep tracking to pause music, turn off touch controls and silence notifications is also coming. Tapping the Pixel Buds will enable real-time interpretation as well.

blocks.cap: Photo: Liminal VR

blocks.x: Liminal, known for short VR experiences tailored to emotional states like calm, focus and energy, has brought that know-how to smart glasses. Its new app, Liminal: Walking Meditation, uses the Meta AI Glasses camera to photograph surroundings while you walk, then delivers a near-real-time voice meditation built around what you're currently looking at. The smartphone app launches in October for iOS and Android.

Pair the phone app with the glasses, pick a theme, voice and pace, then put the phone away in your pocket — that's it. At launch there are 12 meditation themes, 8 voices and 3 pace options. According to CTO Tin Nguyen, the pace setting determines not just the silence between lines but also how much narration there is and the overall length. The shortest walks run about 10 to 13 minutes.

blocks.cap: Photo: Liminal VR

blocks.x: The hard part is choosing what to say. Early versions brought up a trash can about eight times, and once spun an unexpectedly impassioned story about a neon sign in an adult store window. Instead of shooting continuously, the app looks at one frame at a time at intervals during the walk. A UploadVR reporter who tried it with Ray-Ban Meta found it felt close to real time — pointing out a tree right as they passed it — and the generous silences kept it from feeling overwhelming.

blocks.cap: Liminal: Walking Meditation iOS app screen

blocks.x: Images are processed through the phone by Google Gemini. With data retention turned off, images are discarded as soon as a response comes back. The app deliberately doesn't request microphone access. There's no navigation, either. CEO Damiano Moratti said it's hard to make hazard warnings reliable, so they decided to leave navigation out, at least for now.
It costs $9.99 a month or $99.99 a year, which includes 30 contextual walks a month and unlimited access to offline scripted versions for each theme.

blocks.cap: PrismML's smart glasses tried out at the Snapdragon Summit demo room (Photo: ZDNet Korea)

blocks.x: “This is a water bottle.” Wearing the glasses and looking at an object, asking “What is this?” brought an immediate answer near the ear. These are the smart glasses from U.S. AI startup PrismML. The entire process happened on-device, without any internet connection.
On the 24th (local time), at the demo room of 'Snapdragon Summit 2026' held in Maui, Hawaii, ZDNet Korea tried on three AR glasses from PrismML, SPECS and XREAL.

Pressing the physical button on the upper right of the PrismML glasses takes a photo, and asking about the subject gets a spoken answer from the AI. Asked about the color of a trading card handed out at the venue, it immediately answered “blue.” The key is Qualcomm's Snapdragon AR1 platform combined with PrismML's compression technology, which shrinks a heavy AI model that ran at 8-bit down to 1-bit to get past memory limits. Qualcomm senior vice president Ziad Asghar had emphasized in his keynote the day before that 1-bit models could give blind users real-time information about their surroundings and objects.

blocks.cap: SPECS' AR glasses (Photo: ZDNet Korea)

blocks.x: The SPECS glasses are operated entirely with palm and finger gestures, with no controller. Opening an empty palm brings up a menu in midair, and pinching the index finger and thumb together opens an app. In a Harry Potter demo, gesturing to call the owl Hedwig and extending an arm made it land gently on the arm.

blocks.cap: Trying out XREAL's AR glasses (Photo: ZDNet Korea)

blocks.x: The XREAL glasses offered a taste of spatial computing. Several huge virtual monitors appeared in empty space, and a web browser and video window could be pinned in place while moving between them just by turning the head. Even moving the head quickly produced no screen stutter or dizziness.

blocks.cap: GMKtec Evo-X5 Pro (이미지: GMKtec)

blocks.x: GMKtec이 에이전트형 AI 미니 PC 'Evo-X5 Pro'를 내놨다. AMD 플래그십 라이젠 AI 맥스+ 프로 495에 LPDDR5X-8533 메모리 192GB를 얹었다. 2TB PCIe 4.0 SSD 모델은 6,799달러, 4TB 모델은 7,099달러다.

이 칩은 코드명 '고르곤 헤일로'인 라이젠 AI 맥스+ 400 제품군의 최상위 모델이다. 공간 효율형 젠 5c 코어를 빼고 풀사이즈 젠 5 코어만 16개(32스레드) 담았다. 기본 3.1GHz, 부스트 5.2GHz에 L3 캐시는 64MB로, 사실상 라이젠 9 9950X의 모바일판이다. 에이스매직 F9A와 미니스포럼 MS-S1 Max-P495가 같은 칩으로 맞붙는다.
메모리 192GB는 엔비디아 GB10과 AMD 이전 세대 스트릭스 헤일로의 한도인 128GB를 넘는다. 24GB 칩 8개를 256비트 인터페이스로 묶어 대역폭은 약 273GB/s이고, 이 가운데 최대 160GB를 대형 LLM용 VRAM으로 돌릴 수 있다. 성능 모드에서는 지속 120W, 순간 최대 160W까지 쓴다.
슈퍼 얼리버드와 얼리버드 구매자는 각각 6%, 3% 할인을 받는다. 4TB 모델은 최저 6,699달러, 2TB 모델은 6,399달러까지 내려가고, 슈퍼 얼리버드가는 선착순 30대에만 적용된다. 2대·3대·5대 묶음 할인은 고작 10·20·40달러다. 톰스하드웨어는 하드웨어에 32,995달러를 쓰는데 0.12% 할인은 의미가 없다고 꼬집었다.

blocks.cap: Dyson CameraJet (© Dyson)

blocks.x: When Dyson unveiled an AI smart toothbrush at IFA 2026 earlier this month, the writer let out a deep sigh first. With AI being added to everything else, it was only a matter of time before it reached toothbrushes too.

The CameraJet combines a toothbrush with a water flosser. A camera on the brush head gauges the gaps between teeth and fires water at just the right moment. It also supports Wi-Fi and an app, and Dyson made a point of stating in its announcement that images aren't stored on the device or in the cloud.

This week, Philips added AI to its 'Next Generation DiamondClean 9900 Prestige.' There's no camera. Instead, an AI model automatically switches modes based on brushing habits and tooth sensitivity, and divides the mouth into 12 zones to show spots that weren't brushed well enough. The toothbrush even has a screen.

blocks.cap: Philips AI toothbrush (© Philips)

blocks.x: Counting startup products too, an entire market has already formed. Yet research shows that even electric toothbrushes don't clean noticeably better than a manual toothbrush you can buy for $5 at CVS. At best they help you brush with the right amount of pressure.

blocks.cap: Dyson CameraJet (© Dyson)

blocks.x: From its first week on sale, the CameraJet has had problems ranging from stopping working entirely to water getting into the battery compartment. Dyson told Wired that it had “identified a single component issue affecting some early batches,” but didn't say which component.

The more complex a device gets, the more complex its failures get too. Since electric toothbrushes aren't much better than manual ones, the writer concludes there's little chance adding AI will improve dental health. It's mostly window dressing, and it has already become a case of overengineering. If you want brushing tips, booking a dentist appointment is a better option — and cheaper too.

blocks.cap: Flourish 1 learns a new task from a phone demonstration

blocks.x: A humanoid for under $4,000 is hard to believe. Yet startup Flourish Robotics has priced the ready-to-ship 'Flourish 1' at $3,555. A CNET reporter called it the cheapest humanoid they had heard of.

Reservations for the first 50 units opened Tuesday, with shipping set for December. Cloud compute used for some AI features is sold separately as an optional subscription. CEO Antoine Marcel said this is a product launch, not a paid beta. He said what remains is no longer R&D but the supply chain, with the key being getting parts like batteries, which take about two months to procure, on time.

blocks.cap: Flourish 1 at work

blocks.x: It handles repetitive chores such as picking up and tidying objects, watering plants, and cleaning a cat's litter box. The company says any household task can be taught in 30 minutes using only a mobile app, with no coding. One example is demonstrating the motion by pushing a phone across a table to wipe it. After the demo, the robot spends about an hour learning the new task, then sends a notification that it is ready to work on its own.

Marcel says the robot isn't just recording and repeating a motion; AI helps it generalize within a certain range. If taught to put shoes in a shoe rack, it learns the task rather than fixed coordinates, so it can find the shoes even if they're in a different spot each day. He says no one remotely operates it during normal use.

Its limits are clear too. It must not enter water, cannot carry items over 1.5kg or anything fragile, and cannot climb stairs. It does not look after children. It stands 3 feet 7 inches tall, weighs 44 pounds, and runs for 12 hours. It stops if a person or animal enters its work radius, and users can turn off data sharing for model training in the app.

CNET called the price optimistic. 1X's Neo costs $20,000, and Weave's Isaac 1 costs $7,999. Marcel said a wheeled base and lightweight arms cut costs, and that the company is not selling at a loss. Still, the company acknowledges it must industrialize production to get beyond the first 50 units.

blocks.cap: 벽에 설치하는 유피 S4 비디오 초인종

blocks.x: 앤커가 스마트홈 라인업 ‘엣지 5.0’을 공개했다. 그중 유피 비디오 도어벨 S4는 문 앞에 누가 왔는지 VR로 볼 수 있다고 한다. 괴짜 기술 명예의 전당에 새로 오를 만하다.
차임 2와 함께 지금 예약 판매 중이고, 10월 말 출하 예정이다. 가격은 299.99달러로 꽤 비싸다. 그래도 테크레이더는 가격과 굳이 필요한지 의문인 간판 기능을 감안해도, 기능이 워낙 많아 최고의 비디오 도어벨 반열에 들 수 있다고 봤다.
구독료가 없고 4GB 저장 공간을 내장했다. 이 값이면 기대할 만한 부분이다. 필립스 7000 시리즈 같은 경쟁 제품과 갈리는 지점은 VR 보기다. 앤커는 이런 기능을 갖춘 비디오 도어벨이 세계 최초라고 주장한다.
초인종이 사람을 감지하면 앤커 유피 앱에서 영상통화 같은 알림이 온다. 열면 가로·세로 모두 180도 화각의 영상이 뜬다. 집 앞을 늘 초광각으로 보여 주니 보안 카메라를 따로 달 필요가 없다. 라이브 화면에서 스마트폰이나 VR 헤드셋을 움직이면 보는 방향도 따라 바뀐다.
영상은 3072×3072 해상도의 3K로 찍어 사람 전신이 다 담긴다. 유피의 AI 기반 옴니트랙이 화면 속 인물을 붙잡아 따라가고, 오토 프레이밍이 파노라마 화면을 잘라 그 사람을 늘 가운데에 둔다.

blocks.cap: 유피 S4의 시야 범위

blocks.x: 오경보도 줄였다. 먼 거리는 레이더로 잡고, 문 가까이에서는 듀얼 PIR 센서로 사람 움직임을 가려낸다.
알렉사, 구글 홈, 애플 홈킷과 연동된다. 다만 홈킷에서 쓰려면 유피 홈베이스 S380 허브가 필요하다. VR 보기와 옴니트랙은 앤커 유피 앱에서만 되고, 서드파티 플랫폼에서는 고정된 라이브 화면만 나온다.

blocks.cap: An Android phone screen

blocks.x: Google's Find Hub isn't just for locating Android phones, tags, and devices. Attaching a compatible tag is the surest way to avoid losing something important. But some items, like a birth certificate, passport, or Social Security card, are awkward to tag. For those, a feature that links Gemini and Find Hub lets you record where you put them.

First, check that Find Hub is turned on. You can download and set up the Find Hub app, or go to Settings > Google > All services > Find Hub. Next, set Gemini as your device assistant. Tap the profile icon in the top right of the Google app, then go to Gemini or Google Assistant > Google Digital Assistant and choose Gemini as the default.

Now it's time to register an item's location. Just tell Gemini something like, Hey Google, remember in Find Hub that I put my passport in the safe. Gemini will confirm it saved the location and show a Find Hub link.

Tapping the link shows the item saved in the hub. Attaching a photo of the storage spot makes it easier to recall. If you have multiple homes, a P.O. box, or a bank safe deposit box among your hiding spots, you can write the exact address and add a note for more detail. You can also add items directly in the Find Hub app: tap the plus icon in the Remembered items tab and choose manual entry.

blocks.cap: The Find Hub screen

blocks.x: That's it for recording. If you can't remember where you put a document, ask Gemini, Hey Google, where's my passport? It returns the last recorded location along with a Find Hub link. You can also open the Find Hub app and check the Remembered items tab. Tapping an item shows the photo you added, its most recent location, and any notes.

blocks.cap: Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studio

blocks.x: This spring, Apple made the Mac Pro's discontinuation official. Apple silicon's fast CPU, capable GPU, and unified memory suit running language models and agents locally. AI coders and designers are the core customers for the M5 Ultra Mac Studio. Demand for open-weight models combined with an AI-driven memory shortage has made these machines hard to buy for months.

Without an M4 Ultra, the processor skipped two generations. It has up to 12 super cores, 24 P-cores, and 80 GPU cores, with memory bandwidth just over 1.2TB/s, exactly double the M5 Max's key specs. In testing, the CPU was 80 to 90 percent faster than the M5 Max, and the GPU 50 to 80 percent faster.

blocks.cap: Same design as the Mac mini, just not as small

blocks.x: Prices jumped sharply. An AI-driven memory crunch pushed Apple to raise prices across the board. The base M5 Max rose $500 to $2,499, and the equivalent M5 Ultra rose $1,500 to $5,499. The 256GB RAM, 1TB configuration, which cost $5,599 eighteen months ago, is now $9,499.

For local AI, the numbers that matter most are GPU memory capacity and memory bandwidth. A 64GB Apple silicon Mac has more GPU memory than any single consumer GPU, with far better power efficiency. The M5 generation, thanks to a neural accelerator built into the GPU, also cut time to first token (TTFT) significantly.

blocks.cap: 'Bankee Doodle,' a bank-statement converter app the reviewer vibe-coded

blocks.x: The reviewer tried vibe coding for the first time with LM Studio Bionic and the Qwen 3.8 27B model. Despite disliking generative AI, he said it was the most fun he'd had with new tech in a long time. He had it write a Python script to turn bank statement PDFs into spreadsheets, then built a web app on top of that. The clincher was that financial data never left the house.

On the same prompt, the M5 Max hit about 31 tokens per second, and the M5 Ultra just over 50. The reviewed configuration costs $12,299. Local AI is fun and liberating, he wrote, but it's a shame to learn it just as Mac Studio prices across the line have risen more than 25%.

blocks.cap: Fitting a white earbud into an ear

blocks.x: Someday you might be able to talk freely with a Japanese person without knowing Japanese or having an interpreter. Communicating with the world through just one language is the promise most translation earbuds make. With AI advancing recently, that goal has never felt closer.

On the surface, it looks simple. With Apple AirPods Pro, you connect to an iPhone, pick a language in the translation app, and turn on real-time translation. When the other person speaks, you hear it in your language within seconds. Some products require handing one earbud to the other person.

Underneath, it's complicated. It broadly goes through three stages: voice recognition, machine translation (audio processing), and voice synthesis. First, a microphone picks up the voice. Premium products isolate the voice from background noise. The Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro uses eight microphones, two bone-conduction sensors, and a dedicated AI model. Some products achieve a similar effect with dual or beamforming microphones.

Next comes audio processing. It happens on the connected phone, in the cloud, or both, depending on the brand. With AirPods Pro, downloading a language pack lets the iPhone handle all the processing. Google Pixel Buds translate in the cloud, so they need an internet connection. At this stage, which converts speech to text and renders it in the target language, natural language processing (NLP) grasps the sentence's meaning and context. Some products use an LLM like ChatGPT to reinforce context.

Finally, the translated text is turned into synthesized speech and sent to the phone, which relays it to the earbuds over Bluetooth. Some products, like AirPods Pro and Galaxy Buds Pro, handle the entire process offline, so check before buying if that matters to you.

blocks.cap: White earbuds and case on a pink surface

blocks.x: Things have improved a lot since the early days. Still, the 95 and 99 percent accuracy figures touted in ads are, at least for now, marketing exaggeration. Ninety-nine percent isn't a lie, but it requires near-perfect conditions that are rarely met outside a manufacturer's lab.

Speed and accuracy are common stumbling blocks too. Even under good conditions it takes a few seconds, and longer under bad ones, which drags out conversation. Translation gets confused by unclear pronunciation, unfamiliar dialects, slang, homonyms, idioms, and heavy noise, and mistranslations are more frequent for less common language pairs.

Offline mode has limits too. Timekettle offers 14 offline language pairs, with the first two free and the rest $10 each. Media translation, phone calls, and advanced AI features require an internet connection. Many of these products also double as earbuds for calls or music, so checking which features you need can save you from buying two separate pairs.

blocks.cap: Alexa+ can now handle more complex questions

blocks.x: From November, US Fire TV users will get new Alexa+ features on the TV screen and in the mobile app. A dedicated AI assistant hub appears, along with prompt suggestions tailored to viewing history. Alexa+ now has reasoning, so it can answer more complex questions. It draws on the user's subscriptions and watch history, as well as real-world current events. For example, it can answer questions like “Alexa, find shows that were nominated for the recent Emmys but got snubbed” or “Alexa, show me MCU films based on their in-universe timeline order”.

Alexa+ also comes to the upgraded Fire TV mobile app. Hand it a link to an article about a show or movie, and it adds the titles mentioned to a watchlist. Upload a photo, and it recommends titles the image brings to mind. If a location, screenshot, or poster reminds you of something, show it to Alexa+. It makes suggestions based on what it recognizes in the photo. The mobile app also supports deep links straight into streaming services. Tap a streaming icon in the app to play instantly on the phone, or pick it up later from the TV's ‘Continue Watching’ row to move to the big screen.

Fire TV now pulls together live content from more than 40 apps, including YouTube TV, Peacock, Tubi, Sling, and DirecTV. A game hub lets users pick cloud games from Xbox, Luna, and NVIDIA GeForce NOW in one place. The update rolls out to US users this year and to other regions early next year. Amazon is also launching a new music app for Fire TV this fall, covering everything from music videos and podcasts to live concert and festival streams.

blocks.cap: Nanoleaf wall panels

blocks.x: If you've installed several smart lights at home, you're probably used to speaking set commands out loud. Phrases like “turn off the bedroom lights” or “dim the lights to 50%” are easy to memorize, but they're far from how people normally talk. Nanoleaf has set out to fix that.
The Toronto-based company announced today that it's launching an MCP server. Users can connect Nanoleaf smart lights to AI assistants like ChatGPT and Claude to control them.

blocks.cap: Nanoleaf MCP server

blocks.x: Nanoleaf MCP lets you control lights with natural language, so there's no need to open a separate smart home app. Say “make my room feel like sunset,” and Claude or ChatGPT picks the exact colors to match that mood and sends them to the lights.

The MCP server also opens the door for lights to respond to real-time information like weather, letting you shape a lighting environment that changes throughout the day — cozy during a thunderstorm, bright and lively on a clear one.

One-click integrations for AI assistants like ChatGPT and Claude arrive in October. Just add the integration to the assistant you use, and you can control Nanoleaf lights right away. Developer MCP tools and guides are already live on Nanoleaf's website as of today, for building custom routines, connecting APIs for real-time updates, and more.

It's nice to imagine clearing out multiple lighting apps and running your home's lights through ChatGPT or Claude instead. Here's hoping the integration can actually make sense of rambling descriptions of weather and mood and still land on the lighting you want.

blocks.cap: The Freckle Phone (Image: Freckle Phone)

blocks.x: Before cell phones, kids went to a friend's house alone and roamed the local creek. Researchers believe the loss of that kind of autonomy is a major reason anxiety and depression have risen among children. Sam Terris, who created the Freckle Phone, grew up that way too, and his answer, paradoxically, is yet another phone. Terris describes it by saying it's the first phone for kids that encourages real-world adventure.

The roughly 3x3-inch, 0.61-inch-thick square device is worn on the body. It is a 5G device running on the Freckle mobile network, so it has a phone number, and it texts and calls only numbers approved by parents. It also has two cameras, one with 12 million pixels and one with 5 million pixels, plus a microphone and a speaker. That is where the similarities end. The Android-based operating system has no app downloads and no internet access. In their place are outdoor-exploration tools and AI features such as Quest, Chat (ask the AI or send tough questions to parents), Map, Walkie-Talkie, and Characters.

blocks.cap: Image: Freckle Phone

blocks.x: The onboard AI blends Gemini with small local models. When a child asks a question or photographs a plant, animal, or object nearby, it explains it right away. Tapping two devices together over NFC turns on walkie-talkie mode, and tap payments work through a wallet that parents have topped up. By the end of the day, Artifacts pile up in the backpack of the on-screen character: things captured with the curiosity camera, places visited, stories made together, and badges earned, gathered like souvenirs.

blocks.cap: Image: Freckle Phone

blocks.x: Pricing starts at $199 for the 4GB RAM, 64GB storage model, with a $25 monthly service fee. It comes in green, blue, and burnt orange with a shoulder strap, and is IP54-rated, so it can handle rain. The TechRadar writer who covered it suggested the device could still end up being just another wearable AI gadget. Asked how it avoids the fate of Humane and the Rabbit R1, Terris said those earlier products lacked a clear need or an obvious use. Freckle, he argued, has the basic utility of staying in touch alongside the exploration experience.

blocks.cap: Image: Freckle Phone

blocks.x: The Freckle Phone launches in the US in December. Terris said he has about 1,000 new features stockpiled and plans to roll out new ones every few weeks. Olympia, the daughter of investor Alexis Ohanian, has been taking part as a beta tester.

blocks.cap: Peloton Tread Vision

blocks.x: Peloton is rolling out three treadmills starting October 1: the Tread Flex, Tread Vision, and Tread Vision Plus. The Tread Flex, at $2,195, is the cheapest Peloton product and the company's first foldable treadmill. It arrives outside the US in spring 2027. Chief Product Officer Nick Caldwell said it's very quiet and takes up 46% of the footprint of the base Tread Vision platform.

A new software feature called ‘ReRun’ extracts elevation changes from real-world routes and recreates them as treadmill inclines. A five-segment course based on the New York Marathon comes built in, and users can also upload a GPX file from an outdoor run to recreate it exactly.

The Tread Vision is Peloton's AI model, starting at $3,495. It has new cushioning and a jump button, but the core feature is its ‘Movement Tracking Camera.’ Caldwell said, “We've created a new form feedback system for runners.” The camera counts steps and cadence through vertical displacement, and tells you whether your form is correct and whether your running efficiency is at its peak. It combines metrics like vertical oscillation into a running efficiency score and gives personalized AI feedback. Caldwell suggested it's more accurate than similar metrics from wearables like Garmin.

blocks.cap: Running analysis on the Tread Vision

blocks.x: The $6,695 Tread+ Vision adds ‘Sled Mode,’ a Hyrox-style sled push workout. Every treadmill gets Peloton IQ features like ReRun and IQ Pace Target, which uses AI to calculate segment-by-segment target times, and these are also available on previous models. Chief Marketing Officer Megan Imbres said, “The only thing that is gated is the Run Analysis because it uses that Computer Vision camera.”

blocks.cap: Peloton treadmill

blocks.x: A TechRadar reporter ran on the Tread Vision for 10 minutes at the company's London headquarters. Entering height and setting up the camera to capture an upright posture took no time at all. The result was a running efficiency score of 66, along with fairly useful advice to fix vertical oscillation. The reporter thought accuracy would improve with a longer run.

blocks.cap: A robot that mimics emotion, between comfort and unease

blocks.x: Humanoids can now hold conversations, dance, and mimic human expressions with eerie precision. Now Yanxin-X2 adds something else — something no consumer device has done before: a robot that cries on request. In a video from the 2026 Inclusion Conference in Shanghai, a demonstrator asked, “Can you shed tears for me?” A few seconds later, a single tear ran down the robot's face.

It's not just a spectacle. Behind that tear duct is affective computing, an active research area in robotics — the field of making machines recognize, interpret, and respond to human emotion. The goal isn't to make people believe the robot is actually sad, but to make human-robot interaction feel more natural. Still, a machine welling up with tears sits squarely in the uncanny valley.

blocks.cap: A crying robot engineered for emotion

blocks.x: Yanxin-X2 was built by Yanxi Technology, a Chinese robotics company based in Ningbo. According to the company, it works in three stages. First, an AI algorithm analyzes the context and tone of a conversation to identify moments that call for an emotional response. When sad or empathetic language is detected, it signals biomimetic components beneath a medical-grade silicone face to shift the expression to sadness. Finally, a separate microfluidic device releases ‘tears’ near the eyes.

The current version is a stationary model that can't walk. Instead, it turns its head, tracks people with its gaze, and gestures with its arms. The company plans to eventually replace servo motors with biomimetic muscles for smoother, more varied expressions. A 2023 study in Frontiers found that robots whose expressions matched the emotion of a conversation were rated more likable, trustworthy, and human-like than robots with no expression or mismatched ones.

blocks.cap: The fast-growing robotics landscape

blocks.x: Yanxin-X2 isn't the only standout. CES 2026 featured LG's laundry-folding CLOiD and SwitchBot's Onero H1, which loads laundry into a washing machine. At the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing, Tiangong Ultra ran 100 meters in 9.39 seconds. 1X's $20,000 NEO is setting out to learn household chores. The industry is pushing forward on speed, dexterity, usefulness, and now, emotional believability.

Samsung's long-awaited smart glasses have cleared FCC testing, suggesting their release is right around the corner. Two distinct models, SM-O200P and SM-O200J, have appeared in FCC filings, typically one of the last steps before commercialization.

The two product codes indicate Warby Parker and Gentle Monster frames, respectively, as seen on pre-production models. Multiple frame styles will use those codes: three from Warby Parker and two (so far) from Gentle Monster.

Built with Samsung and Google, the glasses are set to be the first to run Android XR, with onboard cameras, microphones and off-ear speakers for calls, podcasts and interacting with Google Gemini. They are said to use a Snapdragon AR1 Gen 1 chipset, a single 12MP camera with indicator LED, and up to 9 hours of use per charge. No pricing or launch date has been announced outside the Fall 2026 window.
Road to VR notes Samsung will face Meta's multi-year lead, and the same public scrutiny over camera-clad glasses that Meta has drawn.
Code left in iOS 27 beta 5 points to a new feature. It's a mechanism that confirms whether a photo was taken on an iPhone, that is, whether that camera is really the source.

blocks.cap: iPhone Camera app

blocks.x: Composite images that pass themselves off as real aren't a new problem. But the flood of generative AI images has made it urgent. Work that used to take a skilled editor hours or days can now come out in seconds from a single half-formed idea.

So several companies rolled out ways to flag AI-made content first. Google built SynthID, which embeds invisible watermarks in images and other media, and the technology spread beyond Google, with OpenAI using it on generated images. Meta also added AI-generation labels on Facebook, Instagram, and Threads. But these systems showed a limit: they failed to catch manipulated media properly, missing even content made by their own AI models.

Apple appears to be addressing this too, going further than just tagging the metadata of images made with Image Playground. New code in iOS 27 beta 5 references something called Apple Reference Image. It's a feature that proves a photo's origin using unique data tied to the iPhone camera hardware that took it.

The approach Apple has kept for handling sensitive user data in the cloud applies here too. It's designed so Apple can't view the original photo itself. The image is sent to Private Cloud Compute for verification, and only some sensor information and photo metadata come back to Apple. If a sensor is judged to have been tampered with, Apple can revoke prior certifications issued through that sensor.

The feature is off by default. It's turned on later in Settings > Camera > Reference Image, and used by tapping Reference Mode. What matters is the moment of capture: the photo has to be taken in the camera's new “Reference” mode. A photo taken normally leaves no basis for certifying it later.

blocks.cap: The privacy notice screen shown when turning on Apple Reference Image

blocks.x: Reference mode doesn't automatically certify a photo. The user chooses to certify it later, and at that point the original image and provenance data go to Private Cloud Compute. Once verification is complete, Apple attaches a unique ID to the photo.
A certified photo can also be sent to someone else. The recipient's Apple device checks on-device whether the certification still holds. Apple doesn't know which photo that person is viewing.

What information travels along with it depends on the transfer method (AirDrop, Messages, etc.) and the photo's state—whether it's the original, an edited version, or a certified one. Apple writes that choosing to send “All Photos Data” can carry over a unique hardware identifier and even uncropped footage.

USB transfers get a “Transfer with Provenance” option. If it's turned on, Reference Image data travels along with certified photos moved to a Mac or PC. Even uncertified photos can retain provenance information like a unique hardware identifier or uncropped footage.

When I first built automations in Home Assistant, some of them worked, but I had no idea why they kept working after updates. I promised myself I wouldn't touch them unless they broke. They were patchworks stitched together from forum posts and guesses about sensor states. Once I had them running through trial and error, I just left them alone, afraid the magic that made them work would stop.

blocks.cap: The screen for adding a device to the Home Assistant dashboard

blocks.x: Home Assistant 2026.7 eased that fear. Intent-based triggers and conditions, which had sat in Labs for months, are now a default option when building automations. Instead of fitting your idea to Home Assistant's logic, you start from what you actually want. It's not a small change. I realized that after rewriting my messiest automation.

Building an automation the old way meant answering questions that had little to do with what you actually wanted to do. Was it a state trigger, a numeric state trigger, or a device trigger? The hardest part was figuring out whether a sensor reports 'on' or 'detected' when it's triggered. Would a lock say 'locked,' or would it say something different depending on the integration behind it?

That made even something as simple as turning on the AC when a room gets hot harder than it needed to be. You had to know exactly what value a sensor reported, and guess whether it might briefly show 'unavailable.' Once an automation like that barely started working, you never opened it again, afraid of disturbing logic that was holding together by a thread.

blocks.cap: The automation template for turning on the AC

blocks.x: With intent-based triggers, picking 'Battery low' and specifying the sensor was all it took. Home Assistant sets the threshold itself using logic appropriate to that sensor. It only works if the sensor properly identifies itself as a battery sensor, though—if it's a node you built yourself, you have to get the configuration right first. Temperature was the same. Swapping a numeric state trigger for a 'Temperature threshold crossed' trigger gave the same result.

blocks.cap: The battery-low trigger in the automation

blocks.x: My living room lighting automation was tied to a single PIR motion sensor by entity name. It was fine until I added another sensor to cover a blind spot. I had to go back into the automation and manually add the sensor to the trigger list. The thought of repeating that every time I swapped or added a sensor was dreadful.

The new trigger targets a whole area instead of a single device. The living room automation now watches for motion in the room. It doesn't matter how many sensors there are. Because the automation records intent rather than a specific device, adding, removing, or swapping out a misbehaving sensor is easy.

blocks.cap: The screen for creating a motion-detection automation

blocks.x: On weekends I built a movie-night automation that senses a late evening homecoming and sets the mood: warm, dim lights and the TV turning on. I used the phone's location tracker switching from not_home to home as the basis, but if the signal dropped for a few seconds while walking in, the tracker would show 'unavailable' before finally settling on home.

When that happened, the automation either missed the transition or jumped to the old value first. I added conditions to get it working and never touched it again after that. Intent-based triggers don't have this problem. The automation's building blocks handle 'unknown' and 'unavailable' on their own. After I switched to the new arrival trigger and removed the old conditions, it hasn't misfired once since.

Automations you haven't touched still run exactly as before. For people who write YAML instead of using the interface, intent-based triggers translate cleanly too. This isn't just an interface-only release, and existing trigger types haven't gone away.

What's changed is the starting point. The next automation you write starts from what you want to do, not from which trigger type fits. When an old automation breaks, you're now more likely to go in and fix it instead of just leaving it alone. If you've been avoiding a few automations, now's an excuse to rebuild them.

HoverAir, which has built autonomous-flying selfie drones, has unveiled Versa. It pairs the flight tech the company has accumulated with the convenience of a pocket camera. At its core is a high-end stabilized pocket camera like DJI's Osmo, which turns into a cinematic selfie drone once a drone body is attached magnetically. By going after two product categories at once, it has a single goal: making it as easy as possible to film yourself, or someone else.

Versa is HoverAir's first pocket camera. It carries a 3-axis gimbal that handles tilt, yaw, and pitch all at once. Other pocket cameras on the market don't go beyond 2 axes. It has a rotating screen and camera controls, with RGB lighting that doubles as a status light. From the outside, it looks like a well-made, ordinary pocket camera.

blocks.cap: HoverAir Versa | Source: HoverAir on YouTube

blocks.x: Pulling out the wings changes things. A small foldable drone body attaches magnetically to pogo pins on the back of the device. After connecting it, you unfold the wings and give it a light tap on top, and it lifts off straight from your palm. There's no separate controller. AI follows the user on its own. There are more than 10 intelligent modes that use AI framing to shoot from any direction, plus a 360-degree feature.

blocks.cap: The drone body that attaches magnetically | Source: HoverAir on YouTube

blocks.x: In this mode, called 3D World, the drone circles the surroundings, takes photos from multiple angles, and stitches them into a single 360-degree scene to look through and share later. In effect, it's also going after Insta360's user base. That said, Insta360 records 360-degree video in real time, leaving much more room for post-production, so it's not quite the same thing. Still, it's a fun trick, and it remains to be seen how well HoverAir pulls it off.

blocks.cap: 3D World mode | Source: HoverAir on YouTube

blocks.x: There's no price or release date yet. With only a teaser video promising it's coming soon, specs are also unconfirmed. The company is pushing the widest dynamic range in this class. In promotional material, the lens looks large and the drone body very small. Going by HoverAir's earlier selfie drones, it seems plausible it could shoot 8K video in 10-bit Log or HLG and fly up to 45 km/h.

The test footage on HoverAir's website, and the video embedded above, are quite impressive. The idea invites both excitement and skepticism. Still, it's hard to deny that Versa feels like magic. Nothing like it exists on the market right now. HoverAir has already made selfie drones like the X1 series well, and a pocket camera isn't especially hard technology, so what's left is simply weaving the two into one body.

Bill Swearingen repeated roughly the same test for about a year. He had a computer generate patterns that surveillance cameras blanketing American streets couldn't detect. After running it around 31 million times, he says he can now produce such a pattern whenever he wants.

Put this pattern on clothing or an object, and the most widely deployed license plate readers and surveillance cameras can't pick out what's underneath it—whether it's a person or a vehicle. The project, named noRecognition, lets people slip past automated detection and algorithmic surveillance running in the US and elsewhere.

blocks.cap: A pattern made by Swearingen | Source: Bill Swearingen

blocks.x: The pattern doesn't stop filming itself. It disrupts a camera's ability to identify objects, people, and faces, so no detection alert goes off. In front of a camera that used to pick a needle out of a haystack, that person becomes a needle in a haystack again—until someone who knows where to look shows up.
“Privacy is a basic right,” he told TechCrunch this week on a call. He described his pattern as a way to “opt out of being tracked.”

A Kansas City resident, he's a security professional who co-founded the security meetup SecKC. He said cameras stand just a few steps apart in his neighborhood, and no one ever consented to being watched. It started last year when he was heading to a rally and felt uneasy at the thought of all those cameras tracking people exercising free speech.

He set up a proof-of-concept lab and took down open-source video detection algorithms one by one. People who showed up with compute resources helped him scale it, and the proof of concept grew into a reinforcement learning model—one that learns on its own which patterns work and which don't. He described it as teaching his own model “how to draw.”

blocks.cap: A pattern that defeats detection | Source: Bill Swearingen

blocks.x: Every time a pattern got caught, the model tried again, and it eventually broke through several algorithms at once. He arrived at a combination that defeats all 11 open-source detection algorithms he tested. That includes the software behind Flock license plate readers, Axon body cameras, and cameras running Clearview AI. The model now generates a new pattern every minute, he said, and each batch is mathematically ahead of the last.

The first real-world test came Friday at DEF CON in Las Vegas. With help from Donut Media, he wrapped a 2009 Toyota Yaris in his latest pattern and checked whether a Flock camera would catch it. “It proved it works,” he said. The wheels, though, were tricky. The demo video will come out within a few weeks.

blocks.cap: The 2009 Toyota Yaris wrapped in the pattern | Source: Bill Swearingen / Donut Media

blocks.x: The next step is putting the pattern into the hands of anyone who wants it. noRecognition is lining up early merchandise like T-shirts and hoodies through crowdfunding, and is even looking ahead to vehicle wraps. The goal is resolution good enough to work from a distance while still looking decent. He hasn't posted the strongest pattern online, so camera makers can't crack it. “Every time it fails, the model gets better, so the pattern keeps improving,” he said.

Pulling together several reports, including Bloomberg's Mark Gurman and Macworld's Filipe Espósito, Apple plans to release as many as three new products carrying the “Ultra” name between late 2026 and early 2027.

blocks.cap: Apple's foldable iPhone.

blocks.x: The long-rumored foldable iPhone looks set to be named “iPhone Ultra.” Reports point to a 7.7-inch internal display and a 5.3-inch external display, two rear cameras and one front camera, and a Touch ID power button in place of Face ID. The wide internal screen suits video watching and multitasking.
The “iPhone Ultra” is expected to launch alongside the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max this September. Its US starting price is estimated to fall between $1,999 and $2,499.
The “AirPods Ultra” could arrive as early as this year. It would line up if revealed alongside the “iPhone Ultra” in September.

blocks.cap: A mockup of AirPods Ultra.

blocks.x: The “AirPods Ultra” is essentially AirPods Pro with a small infrared camera attached to act as Siri's eyes. According to Gurman's reporting, the camera enhances the Visual Intelligence feature on iPhone 15 Pro and later models, and a small LED on the earbud signals whether the camera is active.
In iOS 27, Visual Intelligence moves into a new “Siri” mode in the Camera app. With the “AirPods Ultra,” you can do the same thing hands-free.
“The idea is to let users ask about whatever they're looking at right away,” he said. For instance, you could look at the ingredients on a kitchen counter and ask Siri what to make for dinner.
Last month, traces of camera-equipped AirPods were found in the code of the second iOS 27 developer beta, a sign that release is getting close.

blocks.cap: MacBook Pro.

blocks.x: Last is the “MacBook Ultra.” It's said to carry an OLED display that doubles as a touchscreen. Also mentioned are M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, a Dynamic Island, a design thinner than the latest MacBook Pro, and even Apple's own in-house C2 modem for 5G/LTE connectivity. Gurman reported that Apple plans to release this MacBook by early 2027.
That would put the iPhone Ultra, AirPods Ultra, and MacBook Ultra arriving one after another over the next six or seven months.

Smart glasses have been getting attention for the wrong reasons, and I've written several times that major regulation was likely to follow. As expected, bans and restrictions are starting to take shape. No country has moved to an outright ban yet. Instead, some places have blocked use in specific situations, and others are considering tougher measures. Private companies like event organizers are also barring them from their own venues.

blocks.cap: Magic Leap's Android XR smart glasses (Image credit: Magic Leap)

blocks.x: The US is mostly free to use them, but New York State has banned them in every courtroom in the state. Glasses that can record could be seen as an attempt to intimidate people involved in a case, and unauthorized recording carries real risk in trials where sensitive information comes up. Philadelphia, Hawaii, and North Carolina have put similar bans in place for courtrooms. The US Air Force wrote into its service regulations that “smart glasses or mirrored lenses with photo, video, or AI capability are prohibited while in uniform.” Some events, like the hacker conference DEF CON 34, have banned bringing them in at all.

The UK is in a similar spot. Courts haven't banned the glasses outright, but after someone was found getting coached by a glasses' AI during a trial, the mood has turned toward discouraging their use. UK courtrooms already restrict recording, so taking photos or video with the glasses breaks the rules the same way a phone or ordinary camera would. Monopoly Events banned camera glasses at its own Comic Con after repeated reports of covert filming, and there's also a petition calling for their sale and promotion to be banned.

blocks.cap: Memomind One smart glasses (Image credit: Future / Hamish Hector)

blocks.x: In the EU, the European Data Protection Board is writing a report on smart glasses, expected within a few months. Member states are moving first. Germany's data protection supervisor warned that existing law banning recording devices hidden in everyday objects could already be used against camera glasses. Digital rights activists in the Netherlands have flagged the problem of being filmed without knowing it, and France's CNIL has also pointed to the privacy risks of camera glasses.

Korea's ban comes from a different angle. After cases surfaced of people caught trying to cheat with smart glasses, the country specifically restricted bringing them into exam rooms. Given the weight of the College Scholastic Ability Test, the rule simply spells out, with no room for confusion, whether the glasses can even be carried in.

blocks.cap: Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses (Image credit: Meta)

blocks.x: Not many bans have actually taken effect yet. That will grow if the hardware doesn't change. The biggest worry is the privacy of people who get caught in someone else's camera by chance, especially when they have no idea they're being filmed. The fix is obvious: make it far more obvious that recording is happening. Think brighter capture indicator lights, a loud shutter sound when a photo is taken, or a sound that plays while video is rolling. On the user side, people want control over what the manufacturer can access, and want to know for certain which photos and videos get passed on to outside parties or contractors. It's unclear how much longer smart glasses can hold out before serious regulation arrives.

Chinese projector maker XGIMI opened crowdfunding in June for its first smart glasses, Memomind One. The bet was that consumers would respond to display glasses without a camera, and the funding has now passed $1 million. The category has earned another round of early confidence.

blocks.cap: Memomind One | Source: XGIMI

blocks.x: As soon as the Kickstarter launched on June 28, it easily cleared its HK$80,000 (about $10,000) goal, and raised $500,000 within a week. Now, with 20 days left before the August 28 deadline, it has passed $1 million.

The product was first unveiled in January at CES 2026 in Las Vegas. It leaves out a camera entirely, and instead packs in a 2,000-nit dual green micro-LED display and audio, plus AI features like real-time translation, note-taking, context-aware assistance, and navigation.

The price is on the low end even among display smart glasses. All three styles—Nomad, Gotham, and Archive—start at $400 for the Standard Edition. Adding prescription lenses brings it to $500, and the Custom Edition, which offers a choice of colors, starts at $450. Shipping is set for August 2026.

blocks.cap: Memomind One Nomad | Source: XGIMI

blocks.x: XGIMI didn't set a separate stretch goal. The campaign looks, in practice, closer to a pre-order.

If Memomind One's numbers say anything, it's that skipping the camera is a much stronger marketing card than expected. The backlash Meta is currently facing over its camera-only glasses, which lack a display, is part of that too.

Until recently, Meta hasn't managed to properly stop people from disabling the recording indicator LED or otherwise defeating the system by other means. It's too early to be certain since there's no real competitor yet, but there's a sense in which Meta has poisoned the well.
Memomind isn't the first to push display glasses without a camera. But it's cheaper than its main rival, Even Realities' G2, which costs $600 even without prescription lenses.

That said, I'm not convinced that “display-only” glasses are really about to take off in a big way. Given today's power and compute constraints, running a camera and a display together is hard, so this looks more like a temporary split being smoothed into its own market segment. I plan to test that assumption by living with Memomind One for a while.

Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reported in the Power On newsletter that Apple is reexamining the Apple Watch lineup from the ground up. He compared the shift to the “revolutionary design change” represented by the foldable iPhone, writing that it would be “a transformation of the product for a new era.”

blocks.cap: Complications on the Apple Watch Ultra 2.

blocks.x: The industrial design team has floated several directions. Under consideration are a screenless fitness tracker, Apple Watch models with different display types and sizes, and even a round-screen model. Gurman, however, thinks a round model is unlikely to actually ship.

Price points would also spread further apart, with talk of a higher tier sitting above Ultra and Hermès, and a cheaper option below the SE. Apple isn't taking lightly the renewed sales momentum of screenless fitness bands and smart rings either.

No direction has been settled yet. But as competition intensifies, the resolve to rebuild the lineup is said to be firm. The goal is to revive the slow-growing wearables, home, and accessories segment, with plans that stretch out to weaving in AI features and overhauling the Health app.

Google rolled out an August 5 update to Gemini for Home (early access) and the Google Home app. The standout is Storytime, where AI makes up stories on the fly, while the app side focused on making everyday controls more reliable.

blocks.cap: Google Home app | Source: Edgar Cervantes / Android Authority

blocks.x: Interactive Storytime makes up stories by voice and lets you change them midway. You can ask for a new story or make a child the main character. You can swap the wolf in The Three Little Pigs for a Tyrannosaurus, or have the main character suddenly pick up a treasure map.

Everyday use got attention too. Alarms and timers set with natural language are understood better, and the system now respects 12-hour or 24-hour format preferences. It answers questions about how much time is left on a timer more accurately, and catches requests like a timer for soft-boiled eggs.

There are small speaker fixes as well. The confirmation sound for turning off lights or dimming them has changed, and a bug where the light ring stayed on after a routine finished has been fixed. Google also said it resolved a brief Spotify outage from late July.

The Google Home app update is bigger on the camera side. You can now add more third-party security cameras—Eufy, Tapo, Wyze, Reolink, Nanit—to see more feeds in one app. Recording storage is faster, and live-streaming stability and panning have improved. Home Premium Advanced subscribers get AI camera event summaries, so they know what happened without watching the full recording.
