Automations are available in more countries and languages, and smart lock integration has better notifications and error handling.

The $700 SwitchBot Kata Friends is a bear-shaped AI robot with LCD eyes. It nods, twitches its ears, waves its arms, and roams the house on three wheels. A camera tucked into its nose spot recognizes people and responds to simple gestures. The author lived with this robot for two weeks.

blocks.cap: SwitchBot Kata Friends © Wes Davis / Gizmodo

blocks.x: It roams for about three hours on a 3,200mAh battery and heads back to its dock on its own once it runs low. There's no way to turn off the eye screen, so at night the author simply pressed the power button. While connected to Wi-Fi, you can switch between Normal, Standby, and Sleep modes in the app, and like a robot vacuum, it draws no-go zones on the map it builds for itself.

blocks.cap: Maps and the diary piling up in the app © Screenshots by Wes Davis / Gizmodo

blocks.x: The app also has a diary. Every morning, AI posts a summary of the previous day. A photo album the robot has taken also opens up, and the author's was full of close-ups of a child's face and awkward-angle selfies of itself. With a SwitchBot hub, it can also command devices around the house, like a HomePod or Echo—though it often failed to understand on the first try and needed to be told twice.

The problem is the pricing. Setting it up for the first time starts a 15-day free trial of the Companion Care Plan. The $400-a-year Premium plan bundles turning the robot on with free repairs, an annual checkup, and fur grooming. The $15-a-month ($150-a-year) Essential plan only keeps the device and app features alive. Without a subscription, even the device's internal functions that don't need the internet stop entirely. The robot just sits there, with no sound and no movement.

blocks.cap: When the subscription ends, a dollar sign appears in its eyes © Wes Davis / Gizmodo

blocks.x: Two days before the trial ended, the author told the child the robot would soon stop, and the child cried. The author had to hold the child and talk about death, the healing that time brings, and the losses and new connections one encounters in life. The author wrote that they were angry at SwitchBot for blocking even basic functions that need neither the app nor the cloud.

Asked whether SwitchBot plans to change its subscription policy, the company said it would make it so the robot can open its eyes and roam around before returning to its charger even without a subscription. There was no mention of restoring interaction. It's hard to recommend a product that costs $700 and still requires a subscription on top. It recalls the backlash BMW faced for trying to turn heated seats into a subscription—except back then, at least the car still drove.

AMD released two Gorgon Point notebook chips on August 9: the Ryzen 5 439 and the Ryzen 7 449. Neither has the NPU that defined the Ryzen AI 400 series. AMD's own spec pages leave the NPU field blank. That's where they part ways with their closest siblings, the Ryzen AI 5 Pro 440 and the Ryzen AI 7 Pro 450.

blocks.cap: The Ryzen 400 series | Source: AMD

blocks.x: The 439 uses the same Zen 5/Zen 5c 3+3 configuration as the Pro 440. Instead, boost clock drops from 4.8GHz to 4.6GHz, and the Zen 5c cluster drops from 3.5GHz to 3.3GHz. L3 cache is also cut in half, from 16MB to 8MB. The up to 50 TOPS XDNA NPU figure the Pro 440 touts has disappeared entirely from the 439's page.

The 449 is closer to the Pro 450. The 4+4 core configuration and Radeon 860M integrated graphics stay the same. Only the boost clock, down slightly from 5.1GHz to 5.0GHz, and the Zen 5c, from 3.6GHz to 3.4GHz, are lower. The up to 50 TOPS NPU and the platform-wide 66 TOPS figure attached to the Pro 450 are absent from the 449's listing.

Everything else is the same. A default TDP of 28W with a 15-54W configurable range, the TSMC 4nm process, and the FP8 socket all match the Ryzen AI siblings. Pricing hasn't been announced, and neither have any laptops built around these chips.

AMD's product finder also has what looks like a labeling error. Both chips sit under the “Ryzen 400” tab, but the header above the comparison table reads “AMD Ryzen 6000 Series Processors.” It has the look of something posted in a hurry.

Wacom is a Japanese company founded in 1983, and one of the longest-running makers of graphics tablets. In recent years it has put its weight behind the Movinkpad, an Android tablet built for drawing directly with a stylus.

blocks.cap: Wacom Movinkpad 11 | Source: Wacom

blocks.x: What TechCrunch borrowed and tried out is the first model in the series, the Movinkpad 11. The latest entry is the Movinkpad Pro 14, released last fall, which adds a 3K-resolution OLED screen and a wider color gamut for $899. Starting with the first model was a deliberate choice, to see where the series began.

The short version: it's easy to set up and worth the money. $500 is expensive for someone with little interest in drawing. But for those who like digital drawing but don't have much money to spare, it sits in a middle zone—somewhere between the $30-something Huion Inspiroy H640P, the $3,500 Wacom Cintiq Pro 27, and iPads that run up to $1,100.

blocks.cap: A drawing made with the Movinkpad 11 | Source: Lucas Ropek/TechCrunch

blocks.x: The specs: an 11.45-inch screen, 8GB of memory, and 128GB of storage. It weighs 1.3 pounds, so carrying it around isn't a burden. The included Pro Pen 3 is a 6.3-inch stylus with three side buttons you can assign as you like, and the nib can be swapped using a $15 replacement pack. In hand, it feels close to a thin felt-tip pen.

Being Android, it's tied to a Google account. The free Wacom Canvas comes preinstalled, and if you need more features, you buy the paid Clip Studio Paint. The character of the tip—pen, brush, pencil—gets changed inside the software.

There's plenty of competition, starting with iPads that use the Apple Pencil. Even so, the Movinkpad is a device built around one thing, drawing, and the company behind it has stuck around in this space for a long time. Over a weekend, spending a few hours and drawing a handful of silly pictures, it turned out to be a pretty fun way to spend an afternoon.

Abbott has partnered with Google Health in a multi-year collaboration to connect its continuous glucose monitor, Lingo, to the Google Health app. Lingo users will see their own metabolic data in Google Health and receive lifestyle and diet advice flagged by AI through the Google Health coach.

blocks.cap: Abbott headquarters sign | Source: Engadget

blocks.x: Lingo is a device aimed at adults who don't use insulin. Engadget reported back in 2023 that continuous glucose monitors were trending among people without diabetes. But it found little research backing up any benefit that group gets from scrutinizing their blood sugar so closely.

A piece published by the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health in 2026 struck a similar tone. Whether continuous glucose monitors are a health benefit for people without diabetes still isn't clear. They do make people more conscious of what they eat, but a body without diabetes corrects for blood sugar spikes on its own. Fixating too much on the numbers can even end up disrupting eating habits.

Dr. Idris Mugal said that even trained physicians need other indicators to read continuous glucose monitor results. For someone without training, he said, “they don't even know how to interpret it. So it's completely useless.”

The two companies will also run what they call “the largest real-world metabolic health study yet” as part of this partnership, looking at how activity, sleep, and metabolic health are intertwined. Still, there's a chance the results end up steering people toward buying yet another device. It's better to talk with your own doctor before changing any health habits.

Over the past decade, making physical objects at home has mostly meant 3D printers. Lately, computer-numerical-control equipment, or CNC, has been encroaching on that territory. Prices have dropped compared with industrial machines, and the CAM software used to plan tool paths has become approachable for hobbyists too. That's driven a rise in desktop milling machines that can handle metal, wood, and various thermoplastics.

blocks.cap: InfiMaker K1 | Source: InfiMaker

blocks.x: InfiMaker K1's pitch is that it skips CAD entirely. It turns a single flat image into a 3D model that AI can carve. On desktop CNC machines, commercial software supporting 4- and 5-axis machining has always been a barrier, and this is meant to lower that barrier. It also accepts standard 3D files like STL, STEP, and OBJ as is.

Machining runs on 5 axes. Beyond the basic 3 axes, it carves while tilting or rotating the target. Tilt ranges from -30° to +110°. It also has an automatic tool changer that swaps between five tools, plus a ruby centering probe.

blocks.cap: A model carved by the K1 | Source: InfiMaker

blocks.x: The spindle runs at 1.5kW with a top speed of 20,000 rpm. The company cites 0.01mm repeat accuracy. Materials it can carve include acrylic, aluminum, brass, composites, copper, engineering plastics, jade, resin, steel, titanium, wax, and wood.
The Kickstarter launches today. The early-bird price is $5,199, 40% below the planned retail price of $8,599. Higher-tier backers get a water-cooling unit, vise jaws, and a wireless jog handwheel.
iOS 27's fifth beta widened how much you can tweak Siri's AI voices. Before this, speed and expression controls only worked on two American voices.

blocks.cap: Speed and expression controls for Siri voices | Source: MacRumors

blocks.x: Now the same controls apply to 11 voices: seven American and four British. Speed sets how fast it talks, and expression sets how strongly it emphasizes words. All of the adjustment happens on-device.

There's a hardware catch, though. On iPhone, it only works on the 17 Pro, 17 Pro Max, and iPhone Air. On Mac, it needs an M3 chip or later with at least 12GB of RAM, and on iPad, an M4 iPad Pro or later model with at least 12GB of RAM.

Microsoft released the August cumulative update KB5121003. It targets Windows 11 24H2 and 25H2, raising builds to 26100.9165 and 26200.9165 respectively. Improvements previewed in July's optional update are now included in this security patch.

blocks.cap: Windows 11 August Patch Tuesday | Source: Notebookcheck

blocks.x: On Copilot+ PCs, users can now remove just the image-generation AI component on its own. This is done under Settings > System > AI components. It opens a path to removing local AI features one at a time instead of all at once.

Windows Hello's enhanced sign-in security now extends beyond built-in fingerprint readers. It supports compatible external fingerprint readers too, bringing hardware-isolated authentication to desktops without sensors and to Copilot+ devices. It's found under Settings > Accounts > Sign-in options.

File Explorer's Details view no longer lists every size in KB. It now shows KB, MB, or GB as appropriate. Middle-clicking a folder in the address bar or on Home opens it in a new tab. Search now tolerates typos in installed app names better, starts matching from two characters, and ranks Settings results higher.
Voice Access gained a voice isolation mode that filters out nearby speech and noise. Precision touchpad settings let users adjust scroll and zoom speed, and turn on accelerated scrolling.

The rollout happens automatically through Windows Update. Enterprises follow their usual steps via WSUS or Intune. Deployment of updated Secure Boot certificates also continues ahead of their existing expiration dates. Support for Windows 11 24H2 Home and Pro ends on October 13, 2026.
Reuters reported that Apple trained its own large language model for the Chinese market. The choice means Apple Intelligence features on devices sold in China will not rely on an outside model.

blocks.cap: Apple Intelligence. In China, a different model runs this feature.

blocks.x: Sources in the report say the LLM was developed with help from Alibaba. It marks a shift from Apple's earlier strategy of relying on local models to bring generative AI to China.

The AI features are expected to launch in China within the next few months. The report calls this a “dual-track strategy” for deploying AI in China. It lets Apple clear the regulatory hurdles that have tripped up other US tech companies.
This makes Apple the first foreign company approved by the Chinese government to offer its own AI model.

Apple had earlier agreed with Chinese regulators to add Alibaba's Qwen model to Apple Intelligence features, similar to the ChatGPT extension used in other regions. Apple briefly posted a support document in China explaining how Mac users could connect Alibaba's Qwen AI to Siri and its writing tools, then pulled it entirely within a day.
Legacy hardware companies are adding humanoids to their roadmaps one by one. This time it's LG's turn, though the timeline is still being handled carefully.
LG's bipedal humanoid runs on Nvidia's robotics stack, with a target date of early 2027. It sits within a broader plan that extends into AI factories and autonomous vehicle platforms.

blocks.cap: LG CLOiD, unveiled earlier this year. This wheeled robot will enter factories first.

blocks.x: Earlier this week, LG and Nvidia signed a memorandum of understanding at Nvidia's Santa Clara headquarters. LG Chairman Kwang Mo Koo and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang were both present.

At the center of it is the bipedal humanoid LG plans to unveil in time for CES 2027 in early 2027. Reportedly it will include the Nvidia Jetson Thor chip for inference and the Isaac GR00T foundation model for processing. It will also carry Nvidia Halos, described as the industry's first full-stack safety framework built for robots.
Parts will be sourced in-house. Actuators, sensors and batteries will come from LG Electronics, LG Innotek and LG Energy Solution — convenient, and it keeps costs down.

LG isn't waiting idly until 2027. This year it will test the wheeled robot LG CLOiD in factories — an industrial version of the home robot unveiled earlier this year. The partnership also includes building a “robot data factory” using LG CNS's PhysicalWorks platform to feed it large volumes of training data.

Beyond robots, LG will build two factories over the next two years. By mid-2027 it will build an AI factory reference site using Nvidia's Vera Rubin platform, and by mid-2028 it will raise an 80-megawatt LG AI Factory in Cheonan, South Korea.

This reads less like a shift in internal priorities than preparation for a product to bundle and sell alongside another giant company. Worth watching is Nvidia's Halos safety framework. Liability for humanoids sharing floor space with people has been one of the industry's biggest unresolved problems for years.

For months, word has circulated that OpenAI's first piece of hardware would be a screenless smart speaker. It was already known that it would sense its surroundings, be portable anywhere in the home, and proactively offer help. A new report from Bloomberg gives the first clear picture of what the device actually looks like.

According to the report, the device is donut-shaped and about the size of a hockey puck. It can be carried from room to room or simply left within reach. The price won't be cheap: OpenAI is reportedly considering a $300 to $400 range, with a launch targeted for 2027.

Earlier reports mentioned controlling smart home devices, playing media, answering questions, replying to messages, and calling on ChatGPT to help throughout the day. Voice is the main input, but the device also includes a camera and environmental sensors, letting it read what's happening nearby without being told. Apple is sketching a similar picture with next-generation AirPods that add a camera.

blocks.cap: An Apple HomePod 2023 sitting on a desk at home. Photo: Zeke Jones / Digital Trends

blocks.x: Another goal is for the device to get to know its user over time. What it says will shift based on daily rhythms, preferences and past conversations, and it will offer to help before the user even picks up a phone or types a prompt. An advanced, human-like conversational model is of course part of the package. OpenAI has already shown considerable progress on this with the recently unveiled ChatGPT Live.

Conversation is handled by a microphone and speaker, with lights signaling whether the device is listening or responding. Part of the device actually moves during interactions, a design meant to evoke the sense of a small robot rather than a speaker sitting still in a corner. It brings to mind WALL-E or R2-D2 — both feel alive, attentive and emotionally present through movement and response alone. OpenAI appears to be chasing the same effect by giving ChatGPT a physical form and an expressive personality.

blocks.cap: WALL-E holding a Rubik's Cube. Image: Walt Disney Studios Motion Pictures

blocks.x: How it will actually play out remains an open question. A moving, donut-shaped AI companion can easily look like a cheap toy if the design or motion is even slightly off. But OpenAI is building the device with former Apple design chief Jony Ive and his studio, LoveFrom, which gives reason to expect a polished object rather than a toy.
OpenAI President Greg Brockman has already confirmed the company is preparing a lineup of devices. This small companion could be the first object to give ChatGPT a place of its own in the home.
Rogbid has released the $69.99 VisionW 3-in-1 AI smart glasses. The headline feature is swappable frames, shown off through three styles that cover both outdoor and everyday use.

blocks.cap: The Rogbid VisionW. It comes with three interchangeable frames.

blocks.x: The first is a thick black wayfarer with dark tinted lenses: 145.7mm front width, 48.8mm lens height, 18mm bridge. The second uses a wider double bridge with dark lenses at 147.4mm width and 48.4mm height. The third is a browline half-rim with clear lenses, the widest of the three at 151mm, with a 44mm lens height.

One thing is worth noting: nowhere in Rogbid's product information does it clearly state that all three frames are included in the $69.99 package. The “3-in-1” name and the side-by-side presentation of the three designs suggest that they are, but the company hasn't published a parts list.

blocks.cap: A VisionW spec graphic published by Rogbid.

blocks.x: Connectivity runs on Bluetooth, with a 200mAh battery and magnetic charging. One of the product graphics carries the phrase “long battery” alongside the number 39 days, but with no explanation of whether that's standby or actual use time, it's too early to take that as real usage time. It supports 3D surround sound, and the AI voice assistant uses large language models including ChatGPT and Grok. The lenses include blue light and UV blocking.

Rogbid says the frames use skin-friendly TR90 material, but the spec images show that two of the three designs have metal fronts. There's no camera anywhere in the published specs. This is a device focused on audio and AI features rather than photo or video.

Right as Google rolled out the Pixel Watch 5, its freshly overhauled Google Health app came under fire. The AI coach built into the app has been inventing workouts and numbers that don't match reality.
The strongest backlash has come from longtime Fitbit users.
This case stands out as a sharp example of what happens when you layer generative AI on top of a health-data screen people trusted.

Since I reviewed the squared-off Matic robot vacuum last year, I've written more than once that I like this thing. It can't get under a couch, but everywhere else its design and performance are good enough that it became the yardstick I measure other floor-cleaning robots against. Matic, which has been steadily filling in small features, just shipped a big update that adds voice and gesture control.

blocks.cap: When it hears the wake phrase, the screen turns blue to signal that it's listening.

blocks.x: The bundle of new input methods is called 'Matic Cues.' Starting August 13, users who get the new firmware wake the robot with 'Hey Matic' and give it commands in natural language. The commands are interpreted by Google Gemini on a cloud server. It takes anything from a simple phrase like 'start cleaning' to a compound command like 'vacuum the dining room rug, then mop the bedroom floor.' You can also tell it to follow you, or point at a spot on the floor and say 'clean here.'

I used it for a few days. Say the wake phrase and the robot turns to face me, with the screen switching to a blue background reading 'Listening…' The letdown was the follow feature. It routinely lost track of me around corners or past chairs, and it would sometimes chase a chair leg instead of my leg.

blocks.cap: The Matic Cues screen, which bundles voice and gesture control.

blocks.x: Everything else worked well. I scattered cornmeal on the kitchen floor and bits of paper on the living room rug, then pointed at each and told it to clean. The robot backed up to get a better view of me, or, if there was no room to back up, displayed text on screen asking me to step back a bit, then cleaned the spot.

It also handled compound commands properly. Being able to tell it to vacuum one room and mop another in a single instruction was convenient. The Matic app has no feature for setting different cleaning modes per room, so voice commands effectively unlocked that capability for the first time.

Co-founder Mehul Nariyawala said they'd held off adding that because they didn't want to complicate the app. "Of course we want to. But going forward, we're trying to approach everything voice-first."

blocks.cap: Matic navigating to a spot a hand pointed at and cleaning it.

blocks.x: There's a catch, too. This is the first Matic feature that requires an internet connection. Working entirely over Bluetooth used to be one of this robot's selling points. Nariyawala said the goal is to shrink the model so voice runs within the 4GB of RAM on the robot's Nvidia Jetson Orin chip, and added that staying local-only still gets you "80% of the benefit."
Prices are climbing. The robot vacuum that cost $1,095 at review time rose to $1,245 because of tariffs that pushed up component costs, and it rises again to $1,495 on September 9, 2026.

Looking at the hardware changes in the new Pixel 11 series, the standout is Tensor G6's new TPU. Google says compute performance is up 50%, with some tasks up to 3.5x faster. The numbers sound good, but the question is what this actually means for someone holding a Pixel 11.

blocks.cap: The DevCheck app showing Tensor G6 information on the Pixel 11 Pro XL.

blocks.x: Start with what a TPU actually does. If the CPU handles apps and the GPU mainly handles games, the TPU is dedicated to machine-learning computation. It has its own dot-product matrix units and high-speed memory access. It's effectively the AI processor inside the Pixel, handling tasks that don't need the cloud, like speech recognition, dictation, and sentence suggestions.

The TPU doesn't just run Gemini Nano. It's deeply tied into Tensor's image-processing pipeline and is also used for computational-photography features like Night Sight, super-res zoom, subject separation, and video processing. This upgrade is also behind the telephoto zoom growing from 100x last year to 120x this year. A stronger TPU means headroom to run heavier AI tools without the cost, latency, and privacy issues that come with the cloud.

New features also arrive with the Pixel 11. Google says Gemini Nano's responses are more accurate and faster. When turning speech into text, it automatically strips out filler words like 'um,' and the Pixel Camera app can transcribe sign language into text. Magic Capture takes up to 500 photos and lets Gemini pick five photos and one video. Live Translate converts video, podcasts, and voice messages into the language you want as you watch or listen.

blocks.cap: The Proactive Assistance screen on the Pixel 11.

blocks.x: Proactive Assistance surfaces information scattered across contacts or messages right when you need it. It's aimed at helping you not miss appointments and reply to messages and emails faster. Since this processing finishes on the device, the data stays in an encrypted space.

Starting mid-2026, outside developers will also be able to target Tensor's TPU directly through LiteRT and the Google Tensor SDK beta. But since the SDK is still in beta, it's too early to expect a flood of products right away. A 50% boost in compute doesn't mean every app gets 50% faster; it's closer to having the headroom to run bigger, heavier models locally.

blocks.cap: Google Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro, Pixel 11 Pro XL.

blocks.x: The limits are clear. Gemini Intelligence still handles some processing in the cloud, and the 'Banana' image generator and Video Boost remain cloud-only. A 50% faster TPU doesn't let the phone replace a high-performance cloud. Even so, in the broader shift of moving AI computation out of data centers and into your hand, Tensor G6's TPU marks another step forward.

Meta is handing over 15,000 Ray-Ban Meta glasses to Vision Ireland, an organization for blind and visually impaired people in Ireland. To receive one, you have to apply through the Vision Ireland website, but the glasses themselves are free. Meta said the 15,000 units are enough to cover every adult blind or visually impaired person the organization supports.

blocks.cap: Ray-Ban Meta glasses set against a white background.

blocks.x: Meta's AI glasses have drawn plenty of criticism. There's room for them to be used to secretly record someone without consent. The outlook got worse once a service surfaced offering to disable the LED that signals recording is underway. Meta responded that it would disable the camera on any glasses whose LED has been tampered with or broken. On top of that, Wired found code suggesting Meta had been considering adding facial recognition to the Meta AI app.

Even so, glasses like these help blind people a great deal. They read text aloud and identify nearby objects. Having the surroundings described lets someone finish tasks faster and more safely. You can also ask it to read a message aloud and then have Meta AI dictate a reply. Meta has also partnered with the Be My Eyes network, letting people call volunteers through the glasses. Volunteers help with things like picking out clothes or finding the right carton of milk at the grocery store.

Anyone who wants a free pair of Ray-Ban Meta glasses can apply through the Vision Ireland website or by calling the dedicated line, +353 1 882 1910. Vision Ireland handles selecting recipients, in-person training, and follow-up support.

Agentic AI tools have moved into ordinary people's workflows faster than expected. A tool that directly touches and handles files is as useful as it is costly when it gets something wrong. A chatbot that makes things up is merely annoying; an agent that handles files and goes off the rails does so inside your actual files and folders.

So this time, instead of looking at generative ability, I looked at how a tool handles what already exists. I gave the two tools I reach for most, Antigravity and a local LLM, the same office task and watched whether they followed my rules.

Most comparisons judge output quality. That's the wrong yardstick for a tool that holds file access and is about to touch important documents. Just as important as benchmarks is whether a tool understands the structure it's walking into, or sees everything as a blank canvas to paint however it likes. My Obsidian vault made a good test bed. Small mistakes, like wikilinks that point nowhere, or frontmatter fields invented from scratch without checking the existing schema, pile up without being very visible. The folder doesn't visibly collapse, and the tool reports success, but over time the folder turns into a junk heap nobody can touch.

blocks.cap: A screen showing Antigravity restructuring a messy meeting note.

blocks.x: The basic task was to restructure a single file. I asked it to give a messy meeting note a title, add a summary at the top, and organize action items at the bottom. Antigravity split the content by topic in a way you'd miss at a glance. The local model also imposed structure, but a bit more mechanically (for reference, the temperature was 0.6). Both got the frontmatter right.

Next was a multi-step task. I gave it the same five notes and asked it to pull out a common thread and build a synthesis note linking back to each source with wikilinks. Antigravity found four themes running across the five notes and placed each note's position along a single axis. The local model also found four, and its wikilinks were accurate too, but they read more like one-line summaries than themes. Both finished. But Antigravity read what the five pieces were saying together, while Qwen read them one by one and reported them one by one.

blocks.cap: Qwen finishing a synthesis note with four themes in LM Studio.

blocks.x: The gap opened up over where to put the new note. Antigravity scanned the folder set, recognized this was a piece about conceptual principles, and chose the 'notes/ux' folder. The filename followed the sentence-case convention I use, it copied the frontmatter schema exactly, and it wikilinked to existing notes in the same folder, slotting the new piece in among its neighbors. The local model also read the config file and eventually found the right folder, but it skipped several reasoning steps along the way. It first classified the notes as 'orphan documents' before correcting itself, and it had a habit of wanting to write to the vault's top level whenever it wasn't sure.

Both finished what was asked. That's the bare minimum you expect from an agent. What differed was attentiveness. Antigravity read before writing on every single task. Qwen also showed flashes of that same instinct, in the moments it recognized a change that didn't need to be made. Still, if I were handing over a folder full of files that matter, I'd hand it to Antigravity. That's not to say the local LLM wrecks folders, only that Antigravity is a bit more careful.

MacRumors found a short clip in a macOS Tahoe 26.7 release candidate — the first moving footage of the long-rumored camera-equipped AirPods. In the video, a man wearing the new AirPods lifts up a book cover, a gesture meant to let Visual Intelligence read the title.

blocks.cap: A frame from the camera AirPods demo video found in a macOS beta.

blocks.x: Siri's voice plays over the clip: “with Visual Intelligence, your world becomes savable. See something you like? Just ask me to save it for later.” The idea is to save what catches your eye for later.

Bloomberg's Mark Gurman previously reported that these AirPods are designed to take in “visual information in low resolution” and serve as the eyes for Apple's AI features — the picture being Siri reading turn-by-turn directions or answering questions about your surroundings.

The AirPods in the video look like a slightly thicker AirPods Pro 3, matching what Gurman had predicted. There have also been reports that the stems are longer to fit the camera, with an LED that lights up while data uploads to the cloud. The video only shows them from behind, though, so the light isn't visible at that angle.

Add Visual Intelligence, and the competition becomes camera-equipped AI devices like Meta's Ray-Ban smart glasses. Apple is also reported to be working on its own smart glasses separately. The camera isn't meant for taking photos or videos, but a design that doesn't look like a camera only raises more concern — the backlash Meta faced over being called “pervert glasses” is the precedent sitting right there.

That's all the information there is for now. If a demo video has already made it into a beta, these AirPods could surface alongside the new Siri expected to arrive in September with the next-generation iPhone.

For The Verge's smart-home reviewer, the most useful thing a security camera can do is watch the animals in and out of the house. The trouble is that the flood of alerts buries the ones that actually matter. That's why there was reason to hope when Google added Pet Memory to Gemini for Home.

blocks.cap: Boone leans in close to the Google Nest Cam. Photo by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

blocks.x: Pet Memory is a feature meant to teach Google Home who the pets in your house are. A Nest camera moves from “an animal was seen” to “which animal was seen,” and the house responds accordingly. The plan was to tell three cats apart so a feeder would run automatically. After two weeks, Gemini still couldn't tell the three apart.

Cameras moving from motion alerts to describing what they saw is a recent development. Nest separated people from animals back in 2017 with the Nest Cam IQ, then later added animal detection and AI descriptions. Ring, Wyze, and Apple Home have added AI descriptions too. Google Home is the first to try calling individuals by name.

The mechanism is simple. It matches the description a user writes into Gemini against the description Gemini generates from camera footage. Google Home product manager Rudra Bhatt explained it this way: “If these are the same, we will replace the pets with the name in the caption.”

blocks.cap: Smokey, the only cat Google Home remembered. Every cat caught by the Nest Cam becomes Smokey.

blocks.x: The conditions and the cost aren't light either. It requires the $20-a-month Google Home Advanced Plan, and in testing it only worked with Nest cameras. Since it's indoor-camera only, it couldn't be used on the cat that comes and goes through the front door. Above all, unlike Familiar Faces, it doesn't build a visual profile for each individual. There's no training process, no way to upload photos, no way to correct a mistake. You enter a name and breed, and it's supposed to figure out the rest on its own.

There's Boone, a white-pawed tuxedo cat; Osa, a tabby kitten; and Smokey, a large gray-and-white cat. Writing more detailed descriptions only got a response that the system couldn't process the extra information — and then it called every cat Smokey. Bhatt admitted it does fine with one pet and can tell a dog from a cat, but struggles with multiple animals of the same species.

blocks.cap: Not Smokey. But it does show how much more detailed Gemini for Home's descriptions have gotten.

blocks.x: Feeder automation went wrong too. The setup was for the Aqara feeder to run only when the Nest Cam saw a specific cat, but since it couldn't tell Boone and Smokey apart, food came out whenever either one walked up. The Google Home app has no setting to cap how many times an automation can run. By the end of the day, the bowl was overflowing.

The most troubling part was misidentification. One day, Home Brief reported that Smokey was eating something in the garage. A cat eating in the garage isn't a good sign. Pulling up the clip showed it was actually Boone eating his own food in the laundry room, and rewinding a full day of the garage camera showed no cat at all. At that point, it's worse than doing nothing.

Recognizing individuals is a much harder problem than recognizing that an animal is present at all. It's possible to see where AI cameras are headed, but this isn't a feature to lean on today. Continuous recording, which comes with the same $20 a month, is still more useful for now.
Robots can dance, do backflips, and run faster than people. None of that counts for much when the task is putting out a fire without putting a person in danger.

blocks.cap: A humanoid firefighting and rescue event staged inside an actual fire station.

blocks.x: The second World Humanoid Robot Games held the first outdoor firefighting and rescue event for humanoids — a step beyond last year's controlled indoor setting. The 2026 task took place inside an actual fire station, putting the robots in conditions close to a real scene.

Each robot had 30 minutes. It had to find and report randomly placed hazardous materials using image recognition, locate and shut three randomly assigned valves, then find a fire extinguisher and put out an actual fire. Active firefighters judged whether the fire was lit and the extinguisher used correctly.

The results showed just how fragile robot perception and motor control still are. The moment teams stepped outside sandbox demos or remote VR-assisted operation was where things got hard. Rain, constantly shifting outdoor lighting, and clutter scattered around the fire station all threw off vision systems and mechanical precision. Of the 23 teams registered for the event, 12 competed on August 16, and three completed every stage.

UniX AI's robot stood out, finishing the task within the time limit at the required precision. Still, its overall speed fell well short of a human firefighter, and it had to retry aligning its hand with the extinguisher handle twice.

The conclusion that human firefighters are far better still stands. Even so, competitions like this earn their keep by generating failure data. Using what they learned from the August 16 outdoor firefighting event, each team is working to refine perception, motion planning, and balance control, aiming to properly grip the extinguisher and valves at the next competition.
Meta has spent all year trying to ease worries that facial recognition is coming to its smart glasses. A newly surfaced patent application shows the idea was never shelved.

The application, first reported by Patentlyze, was filed by Meta in February. It describes using AI facial recognition alongside smart glasses to identify people and pull in information tied to that person when creating media.

blocks.cap: A diagram from the published Meta patent application. Image: US Patent and Trademark Office

blocks.x: Filing a patent doesn't make something a product. Still, this document arrives after months of reports piling up that Meta kept examining facial recognition for wearables.

In February, an internal feature called Name Tag came to light — one meant to let smart glasses recognize people in real time. In June, things got stranger. Researchers found a dormant facial-recognition component inside the Meta AI app, including a system that detected faces and converted them into biometric data. Meta deleted the code and said it had never shipped a facial-recognition feature.

Around the same time, it emerged that Meta had licensed facial-recognition technology from Rank One Computing, a company whose clients include the US military and law enforcement agencies. That software was also found dormant inside the Meta AI app.

blocks.cap: Meta Ray-Ban Gen 2 smart glasses. Image: Meta

blocks.x: There's no longer any doubt that Meta has been digging into facial recognition for glasses. The question left is whether that work ends up in something you can actually buy.

The patent is already drawing criticism. In a statement reported by CNET, the Center for Democracy and Technology warned that vulnerable people, including stalking and domestic-violence survivors, could be exposed to this technology.

It's the same worry that trailed Name Tag. Facial recognition tucked inside a photo library is different from a camera worn on someone's face moving through public spaces. Meta's glasses already don't look much different from regular glasses. Add facial recognition, and the person standing nearby has no way of knowing whether they're simply being seen or quietly being identified.

Pixel Watch 5 shipped with a feature nobody really asked for: generative AI that creates watch faces from a voice or text prompt. Gemini powers it under the hood. Whether it's worth using mostly comes down to how creative you're feeling and what you like that day.

blocks.cap: The Create Watch Face app on the Pixel Watch 5. Photo by Dan Bracaglia / Tom's Guide

blocks.x: The process is surprisingly simple. Open the Create Watch Face app, tap to create your own, then enter a text or voice prompt. A cellular or Wi-Fi connection is required. After submitting a prompt, it takes about 10 to 30 seconds. About one in five times, the app refused — usually when the prompt was hard to parse, overly complex, or the connection was weak.

blocks.cap: The screen that appears while a prompt is processing. Photo by Dan Bracaglia / Tom's Guide

blocks.x: The first prompt was “Teddy bears and laser beams.” What came out looked less like the phrase itself and more like Pink Floyd-style cereal art. There was also a noticeable habit of over-weighting the first word or two when setting the texture.
Once generation finishes, six options show up. You can generate more with the same prompt or start over from scratch. Right now, there's not much difference among the six.

blocks.cap: The result of the “A raging river with jumping orange salmon” prompt. Photo by Dan Bracaglia / Tom's Guide

blocks.x: The second prompt was “A raging river with jumping orange salmon.” It came out a bit better, though it reads more like clip-art carp than salmon. The third prompt, “Deli meats,” produced the piece that led the article.

blocks.cap: No matter what prompt goes in, the generated watch face comes out as a still image. Photo by John Velasco / Tom's Guide

blocks.x: Anyone hoping for motion — fish slowly swimming, say — should set that expectation aside. Whatever the prompt, the result is a completely static face.

The watch faces Google already gives away for free are more feature-rich than anything this app produces. It's worth trying for fun on a special occasion. Just maybe skip “teddy bears and laser beams.”

The NIH counts 73.1% of US adults as overweight or obese. But getting a real picture of body composition takes more than stepping on a scale — accurately measuring where fat sits and how much of it there is usually requires a demanding X-ray analysis. Google researchers are exploring a way to get similar information with nothing but a phone camera.

PhotoScan is a Google Research system that analyzes several 2D photos of a person's body with AI to estimate body composition. It trained on dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) scan data, measuring not just total body fat but also the android-to-gynoid (A/G) fat ratio and the visceral-to-subcutaneous (V/S) fat ratio.

blocks.cap: google photoscan body fat

blocks.x: The researchers also added MRI scan data, and fine-tuned the model with real photos taken on smartphone cameras. The resulting model estimated body fat more accurately than bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA) sensors found in wearables, and it was also more accurate on A/G and V/S ratio estimates — something BIA can't even attempt.

Google Research also looked at whether PhotoScan results could predict conditions like insulin resistance, an area where the company has visibly leaned in recently, as seen in the insulin resistance trends feature coming to Pixel Watch's Health Guardian.

The research itself looks solid, but another problem remains. Convincing users to upload several photos of their body that they may not love looking at is not easy, no matter how airtight the privacy policy is. The bigger hurdle comes after showing the data: actually getting people to change their diet and habits. Google hasn't announced any plan to turn PhotoScan into a product, but it wouldn't be surprising if it eventually surfaces from Google Health.

Google's wrist-based safety features don't stop at fall and crash detection. Pixel Watch 5 adds breathing emergency detection and blood pressure trends, while the pulse loss detection introduced in 2024 still hasn't been matched by any other brand. Tom's Guide spoke with Google product manager Pramod Rudrapatna and researcher Jake Sunshine, who helped build breathing emergency detection.

Sunshine said he wants to shift the assumptions about what these devices can do — moving beyond fitness and wellness to include the ability to save lives. The phrase he used for the Pixel Watch was “conceptually, an airbag for the wrist.” As with a car airbag, it's best if you never actually need it.

Rudrapatna called breathing emergencies a population-level problem. Hundreds of thousands of people experience them from causes like drug overdoses, severe pneumonia, or airway obstruction. These emergencies arrive without warning, usually when no one else is around.

The detection algorithm looks for a combination that shouldn't occur in a healthy person: blood oxygen that was normal until recently suddenly dropping, paired with no movement and no responsiveness. Testing is done in specialized labs that can rapidly lower oxygen levels in a controlled setting. The design also works to reduce false alarms. Once detected, a 30-second countdown appears, and if it isn't canceled in that window, the watch contacts emergency services on its own.

They were clear about the limits. There's no guarantee the feature will catch every cardiac arrest or breathing emergency, and the blood pressure and insulin resistance trends don't replace a blood pressure cuff or a blood sugar test either. Rudrapatna drew a clear line: the feature isn't meant to screen or diagnose hypertension or diabetes, or to guide medication changes — it's aimed at invisible problems that happen without the person even knowing.

Asked about the rollout plan, Rudrapatna said the goal is to put it on as many devices as possible, but for now the focus is on the premium Pixel Watch line. It's also coming to Pixel Watch 4. There's no word yet on whether Fitbit Ace will support breathing emergency detection, but blood pressure and insulin resistance trends are coming even to the $99 screenless tracker. As of this writing, breathing emergency detection is still awaiting approval from the US FDA.

blocks.cap: XREAL AURA | Courtesy XREAL

blocks.x: Xreal said on August 20 that global pre-orders for Aura passed 10,000 units. It's the first AR glasses to launch running Google's Android XR.

The company read the number as a sign of strong early demand across consumers, developers, and enterprise customers. The $99 reservation, which converts into a $199 credit at launch, has already sold out, while the refundable $199 deposit is still open.
There's still no final price. Some of the roughly 10,000 refundable reservations could drop out once the price is set. The only line Xreal has drawn is that it won't exceed $1,500 before tax.

blocks.cap: XREAL AURA | Courtesy XREAL

blocks.x: The optics use the same birdbath design as Xreal's previous products. The field of view is 70 degrees, and the weight on the head is under 95 grams. That weight is offset by a pocket-sized compute unit connected by cable. Aura splits computing in two: Qualcomm's Snapdragon Reality Elite handles XR processing and AI tasks, while an in-house X1S spatial co-processor handles the display and sensor processing.

Unlike other birdbath glasses that just project existing content onto a virtual screen, 6DoF tracking, hand tracking, and multimodal AI experiences all run on top of Android XR. It uses Android apps from the Play Store and a growing list of XR apps as-is. Launch is set for fall 2026, with more on pricing and sales timing to come in the next few weeks.

blocks.cap: Amazon Alexa+

blocks.x: Amazon has made Alexa+ free for anyone using a Fire TV device in the US. Using this AI assistant on its own used to cost $20 a month. It had always been free for Prime subscribers, but now nobody has to pay.

The eligible devices are the current-generation Amazon Fire TV Stick, Fire TV Cube, and the Amazon Ember Smart TV. It also covers smart TVs from other makers with Alexa+ built in, like Hisense or Panasonic.

After years of development, Amazon unveiled the new Alexa experience this past February. The old Alexa only responded to memorized wake words or specific phrases for voice commands. Alexa+ understands natural language.

Instead of naming a specific show to play, you can also ask for recommendations. Say "show me a period drama with a strong female lead," then narrow it down with "recommend something more recent." You can even ask contextual questions about what's on screen right now, like asking it to explain an actor's other roles.

If you have smart home devices, you talk to Alexa+ to control them. Ask it to show the front door, and footage from the camera outside connects to the TV; if you have a smart lock, you can tell it to lock the door.
According to Amazon, the volume of back-and-forth users have with Alexa+ is nearly double what it was with the old Alexa, because it understands conversational questions and requests.

The company said it could expand free Alexa+ to more devices and regions going forward. Free access is currently limited to US customers, but Alexa+ itself is also available in the UK, Canada, Mexico, Italy, Spain, Germany, Austria, Brazil and France. Amazon plans to expand to more countries this year, and add 10 more regions in 2027.

blocks.cap: Photo: Jonathan Weiss (Shutterstock)

blocks.x: Comcast's Xfinity is pushing its WiFi routers toward becoming home security devices. Millions of subscribers can now opt into expanded monitoring features. The company has rolled out Xfinity Shield, a cyber and home protection platform offered to customers nationwide at no extra cost. On top of security features and parental controls, it adds WiFi Motion, which turns existing WiFi equipment into a motion-sensing device.

According to Comcast, WiFi Motion is opt-in. It detects movement in the home using the WiFi signal the Xfinity gateway puts out, without using a camera or recording device. It works by reading changes in the wireless signal traveling between the router and connected WiFi devices.

WiFi Motion itself first launched in 2025. With this expansion, Comcast is positioning it as a core pillar of the Xfinity Shield ecosystem. Jon Giesselman, Chief Growth Officer for Connectivity and Platforms, said the network needs to go beyond simple connectivity to protect residents and their information.

You get an alert when movement is detected near a connected device like a TV or printer. Settings adjust separately for when you're home, asleep, or away. The Xfinity app shows live motion alongside past history.

Comcast has acknowledged that performance varies with home size, layout, building materials, router placement and device arrangement, and it hasn't guaranteed consistent performance. Privacy groups and users have already raised concerns about the surveillance potential of this technology and its unsettling nature.

A recent study out of Germany showed that WiFi signals can be used for more than motion detection. Researchers used beamforming data and AI to identify individuals with 99.5% accuracy, warning that an ordinary router could turn into a surveillance tool.

The heaviest point sits in Comcast's own support documentation. It states that information generated by WiFi Motion can be shared with third parties. The company retains the right to share this data with law enforcement during investigations, in disputes involving Comcast, or under court orders or subpoenas.
Comcast did not respond to a request for comment on these concerns.

blocks.cap: Comu Action Pro

blocks.x: I talk to several people every day. Some conversations happen over video, some face to face. I kept hunting for a recording method that worked in both situations, and every option I tried turned up a different problem. I started with meeting-note tools like Otter and Fireflies, but vague policies and data privacy issues made me hesitant to keep using them. Clients weren't especially comfortable with these tools either.

For video calls, I settled on Notion. It's good at transcribing conversations and pulling out action items. For in-person meetings, I recorded on my phone and uploaded the audio to OpenAI's Whisper to transcribe. The results were fine, but moving and processing files every time got annoying. Recently I replaced the phone with a dedicated AI voice recorder.

blocks.cap: The phone already has a lot to do

blocks.x: Recording a meeting on your phone is actually quite convenient. The problem is that the phone is already busy with other things. Recording for two or three hours a day, sometimes four, puts a strain on the battery. I don't want to keep the phone plugged in all the time, and I don't want to worry about other apps, notifications, or calls interrupting the recording. Apple's Voice Memos app stops recording if another app plays sound. You have to set the phone on the table near whoever's talking, and sometimes that's exactly when you need the phone for something else.

blocks.cap: A recording device with just one job

blocks.x: So I started using the Comu Action Pro. It's a recording device that captures conversations without the ritual of pulling out your phone, opening an app, and checking whether recording actually started. This category gained popularity because devices like Plaud handle phone calls, online meetings, and in-person conversations with a single piece of hardware. Recording phone calls on a phone has always been inconsistent, since laws vary by state in the US. Some states allow one-party consent, but about 11 states require consent from everyone involved. Apple now supports call recording on iPhone, but it plays an announcement to everyone on the call, and it's still restricted in some regions and languages. A dedicated recorder is a more consistent option, but getting consent is still the user's responsibility.

The Comu Action Pro comes with a magnetic mount, so if you stick it on the back of your phone, you never have to wonder where it is. With six adaptive microphones and a pickup range of about 7 meters, it holds up no matter where you sit in a room. The battery lasts about two weeks on a single charge. The company advertises up to 70 hours of recording, so if you don't record often, it lasts close to a month. There are also two physical buttons: one for recording, and another for handing the device tasks the app would normally do, like transcribing or summarizing. A small OLED screen shows recording status.

blocks.cap: In the end, software is what separates this category

blocks.x: Like other AI voice recorders, this device comes with an app that automatically transfers and transcribes recordings. The most tedious step — recording an in-person meeting on your phone, hunting down the file, uploading it to Whisper, and waiting for a transcript — is gone. I didn't find much use for it in video calls, though; Notion is still better for that. English transcription was excellent even with multiple speakers, but accuracy drops when you mix two languages. Comu advertises support for 113 languages. It keeps the original audio next to the transcript, so if the text looks off, you can go back to that spot.

An AI recorder only survives if its software is very good. Hardware alone isn't a reason to buy another device. The phone already has a decent microphone and everything needed to record meetings, calls, and voice memos. A dedicated recorder's strength comes from how tightly its hardware and software fit together. Press one button, the conversation gets recorded, and from there the audio should move, get transcribed, summarized, and organized without you ever having to shuttle files between apps.

blocks.cap: Ray-Ban Meta first-generation smart glasses

blocks.x: Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has officially joined the list of organizations banning smart glasses.

According to the New York Times, ICE circulated a memo on Tuesday banning employees from using smart glasses. The ban covers field agents as well as office staff. The reason given is the potential for privacy violations.

The New York Times quoted a memo from Acting Director David Venturella that read: "...the use of Meta Glasses or similar devices may unintentionally capture, record, or transmit sensitive information, potentially compromising privacy and legal protections."

The phrase 'unintentionally capture' is the sharp part. It's not aimed at video and photos that an employee or agent deliberately shoots, but at information that smart glasses pick up on the side. That worry has grounds.

Earlier this year, whistleblowers who worked as Meta subcontractors raised concerns about footage used in the company's AI training program. They said they were instructed to review private footage involving sex scenes, nudity, and bathroom use. They said some of it appeared to have been recorded by accident. Given Meta's terms of service, video and photos shot with Meta's smart glasses aren't as safe as they look.

For reference, Department of Homeland Security (DHS) agents have already been seen using smart glasses, particularly Meta's products, so this ban isn't exactly preemptive. There have also been reports that DHS is developing its own smart glasses for use in US border surveillance, along with talk of interest in combining facial recognition with smart glasses to automatically match people's faces against a database.

ICE's ban isn't a matter of philosophy. Surveillance is this agency's everyday business. There's a different concern here, though, and it has more to do with the murky user data policies surrounding smart glasses than with the devices themselves.

blocks.cap: The Siri app in macOS 27

blocks.x: With beta testing entering its final stretch, Apple is expected to officially release macOS 27 Golden Gate sometime next month. The biggest change in this year's update is a newly built Siri app for the Mac.
Upgrading to macOS 27 adds a new Siri app icon to the Mac Dock. This is the first time Apple has shipped a dedicated Siri app for Mac.

The headline feature of macOS 27 Golden Gate this year is Siri AI. Apple rebuilt Siri from the ground up. Capabilities like understanding personal context, world knowledge, screen awareness, and taking actions inside apps are all built on top of the new architecture.

The Siri app is the core of this system. Inside the app, you can browse through all past conversations or start a new one. Conversations also sync between Apple devices through iCloud. That means you can start a Siri conversation on your iPhone and pick it up again sitting in front of your Mac.

blocks.cap: List view and card-style grid view

blocks.x: The Mac's Siri app offers two interface options. One is a list view similar to the Messages app; the other is a grid view where each conversation becomes a floating card.

System Settings controls how long the Siri app keeps conversations. You can choose forever, 30 days, or one year, and if you pick either of the latter two, conversations past that limit get permanently deleted.

System Settings also lets you set whether opening the Siri app goes to your most recent conversation or starts a new one. You can also adjust how many lines appear in conversation previews, from 0 to 5 lines.

blocks.cap: Siri app options in System Settings

blocks.x: The Siri app runs on the MacBook Neo (A18 Pro) and Macs with M1 or later.

9to5Mac's take is this: the app itself is fairly basic, but it's welcome that Apple decided to include a chatbot-style Siri app in macOS 27. In an interview last year, Apple executives described the company's AI strategy as building "not a bolted-on chatbot, but an experience integrated into everything you do." At the time, that read as a signal Apple had no intention of shipping a Siri chatbot app, but at WWDC this year, Apple explained that it had decided a dedicated app was the best way to revisit past conversations.

The real question is whether Mac users will reach for the Siri app instead of Claude or ChatGPT. In the end, it comes down to the quality of the output. The Siri app was good for questions about world knowledge or personal context, but for more complex queries, Claude still gets the call. If Apple keeps refining Siri AI and Apple Intelligence, that calculation could change.

The new HiLight notification LED on the Pixel 11 Pro is nearly useless out of the box. By default, it lights up in only two situations: when you're using Gemini with the phone face down, and when someone on your favorites list calls. The color choices are limited to just five.

With a feature that was beloved on older Android phones shipping this locked down, developers moved first. HiLight Studio, built by X user Dhananjay_Tech, lets you control this LED array pretty much however you want. You can set it so a Slack notification containing a specific word makes it pulse rainbow colors, or a text message makes green light ripple across it. You can even adjust the timing, brightness, intensity, and saturation per cycle.

blocks.cap: Default screen

blocks.x: Unlike Google's official feature, colors come from eight preset options, or you can set them directly with a color slider. There's also an export/import function for presets, so you can share them with friends.

It's not on the Play Store yet. You have to download it from GitHub and sideload a few apps, unlock developer settings, and tweak a handful of phone settings to get it running. Reviewer David Imel's take is that it's not as simple as a regular app, but it's worth it if you're willing to deal with that.

Signs have emerged that Apple Watch-style “faces” are coming to Apple's new smart home hub, commonly called the “HomePad,” expected this fall. 9to5Mac's reaction is that this is one more reason to want one in every room in the house.

It's been nearly two years since Mark Gurman covered this product in detail. Apple had it slated for an early-2025 launch but pushed it back because of delays to Siri AI, and now a debut as early as next month is being predicted.

The author lists four things to look forward to: Siri AI, now far more usable than the old Siri; Apple Photos slideshows and Memories; security camera features; and Apple Music showing lyrics and artwork on screen. If the price is right, the author says, they'd put one in nearly every room.

Now add the “faces” and “face gallery” found in code this week. It looks like you pick widgets to include and can even add a Smart Stack, so it seems set up to show different widgets depending on the time of day.

If faces can be freely changed, the HomePad takes on a different character depending on the room it's in. That means setting different widgets and layouts for the kitchen, the living room, and the bedroom, which gives people a reason to buy more than one. The author wrote that they hope this is the last HomePad delay.

blocks.cap: The AI shopping assistant open in the Apple Store app.

blocks.x: A small group of users has gotten an “early preview” of a new AI shopping assistant in the iPhone's Apple Store app.

If your account has it, tapping the speech bubble with two sparkles in the lower right corner of the app brings up the chatbot. You can ask about Apple products, an in-progress Apple Store order, trade-in prices, or payment methods, or start by tapping one of the frequently asked topics shown on screen.

MacRumors was first to report that an AI shopping assistant was coming to the Apple Store app, based on a newly posted privacy policy on Apple's website. The policy states that Apple uses personal data to personalize the chat experience and give relevant answers, and, with user consent, to improve the assistant as well.

Apple hasn't officially announced this feature yet. It appears to be in a quiet testing phase with a small number of users for now. Many on the MacRumors staff haven't seen the chatbot either, so there's nothing odd about not seeing it.

blocks.cap: Two budget AR glasses side by side.

blocks.x: For years, RayNeo owned the virtual-screen glasses segment starting at $299. This year's Air 4 Pro shows that position well. But in recent months, Xreal and Viture have both released products aimed at thinner wallets: X by Xreal a01+ and Viture Pro 2, both starting at $299.

Both companies make the best stuff at the high end of smart glasses. The trouble comes once the price gets cut, where the specs are nearly indistinguishable. Both screens are 1080p micro-OLED with up to 1,600 nits and 120Hz. The field of view is also the same at 50 degrees. Weight is 2.2 ounces for the Pro 2 and 2.1 ounces for the a01+.

blocks.cap: X by Xreal a01+ with its yellow USB-C cable and blue lenses.

blocks.x: The reason to pick the a01+ is looks. Most AR glasses settle for a thick black wayfarer, but this one dresses up with a yellow USB-C cable, blue lenses, a large logo set inside, and swappable faceplates. Xreal doesn't sell faceplates separately, but it recommends 3D printing them. It's also lighter and more comfortable than RayNeo's product. It's one of the few glasses that support HDR through AI SDR-to-HDR conversion, so Apple TV+ watching works too. The flaw is cheap-feeling plastic finishing and no IPD adjustment. The interpupillary distance is fixed from 54.5mm to 74.5mm.

blocks.cap: Viture Pro 2 finely adjusting its nose pads and arms.

blocks.x: Straight out of the box, the Xreal side is lighter and more comfortable, even though the difference is just 0.1 ounces. But the Pro 2 has a lot more room to tweak. Nose pad sizes come in three options, same as Xreal, but can move to seven positions. The temple arms also slide up and down independently on each side, and each lens has its own diopter wheel, a feature neither the a01+ nor RayNeo has. Brightness, refresh rate, and resolution numbers are the same, but the screen looked sharper on the Pro 2. There are up to nine adjustment steps, plus four filters: true color, blue light, cinematic, and warm.

The conclusion leans toward the Viture Pro 2. The combination of the diopter wheel, nose pad, and arm adjustments makes it comfortable for long use, and the screen is brighter with more room to fine-tune. If you want style and fun, it's the a01+. For gaming or binge-watching, either choice works out fine. Viture fits well, Xreal does HDR. RayNeo still packs a lot into $299, but there's real competition now.

blocks.cap: The Pixel 11 Pro with the Gemini overlay open.

blocks.x: A new tool called “Device help” has started showing up in the Gemini app on the Pixel 11 Pro. It's a feature that helps with using your phone through a personalized conversation.
Opening the Gemini app's plus menu or overlay puts this tool at the bottom of the list, right above Personal Intelligence.

blocks.cap: Device help, newly added near the bottom of the Gemini tools list.

blocks.x: It carries a “Labs” badge, and the description reads “Get help with your device.” The icon is the same one used for Proactive Assistance. This “Device Help Agent” adjusts settings, diagnoses problems, and explains features.

On the settings side, it covers display items like dark theme, brightness, and screen timeout, through to sound and vibration mode, Do Not Disturb, and Digital Wellbeing. Troubleshooting touches Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, mobile data, battery drain, audio, and app performance. Under battery and storage, it checks usage, turns on battery saver, and finds ways to free up space. Under apps and permissions, it reviews location, camera, and microphone access, and cleans up notifications and app timers. It walks through Pixel features, gestures, camera, and privacy settings step by step.
It doesn't look like something built from scratch, though. It appears to simply use the existing “Device Assistance” connected app, formerly called “Utilities.”

blocks.cap: A conversation screen with the device help agent.

blocks.x: As of this morning, the only device where this tool has shown up is a Pixel 11 Pro updated to Google app beta 17.52. It wasn't on the base Pixel 11 or any older phones checked.

blocks.cap: Apps like Zuckoff pick up nearby smart glasses through their Bluetooth signal. Photo Paweł Szydłowski/Zuckoff

blocks.x: A pair of black rims can no longer just be assumed to be regular glasses. As Meta's AI smart glasses have spread and other wearables followed, pushback has grown over filming that isn't visible. Smart glasses record, stream, and process video without announcing it to the people around them, unless a small recording light is considered enough.

So it's turned into a technology standoff. On one side, modders disable the LED indicator to make the camera even harder to notice; on the other, developers release counter-technology that flags hidden cameras.

One of them is the free iOS app Zuckoff. It's a detection tool that finds nearby Ray-Ban Meta glasses or Snap Spectacles, and its name is a pun aimed at Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg. Apps like Antizuck Smart Glasses Scanner or Nearby Glasses form a small ecosystem of their own. They scan the surrounding Bluetooth band to catch the vendor ID, system identifier, and hardware signature tied to smart glasses, and estimate a rough distance. They can't tell, though, whether recording is happening right now.

The Zuckoff website explains it this way: “Glasses broadcast loudest when they power on, pair, or come out of the case. Once paired to the owner's phone, they can go quiet, so quiet doesn't prove no one is recording, and being detected doesn't prove someone is recording either. Signal strength only gives a rough sense of distance, and no sense of direction at all.”

blocks.cap: Paweł Szydłowski, the developer behind Zuckoff. Photo Pawel Szydlowski

blocks.x: Developer Paweł Szydłowski was working on finding nearby devices via Bluetooth when he realized the same technique worked on smart glasses too. “It's the same technology with the paper just swapped,” he said on a video call with CNET. What pushed him to act were social media videos: clips of someone wearing smart glasses filming a prank or hitting on a woman, where the person filmed had no idea their likeness would end up posted.

Since launching in early August, signups have topped 2,000, and an Android version is in beta. The paid tier, $10 a year, keeps detecting in the background even without the app open. Tech reporter Joanna Stern was paid $100 and showed, on video, the process of removing the LED from a pair of Ray-Ban Meta glasses.

The trouble comes after detection. Once the app tells you smart glasses are nearby, about all you can do is leave the area or ask someone to take theirs off. Utkarsh Anantkrishnan, an assistant professor of information systems at Carnegie Mellon, believes the norms around wearables still haven't settled. Unlike a smartphone, she says, “smart glasses shift the entire privacy burden onto the person being filmed.”

blocks.cap: The Even G2 smart glasses, which drop the camera entirely. Photo Scott Stein/CNET

blocks.x: Some makers skip the camera altogether. Even Realities' G2 has no front-facing camera. Released in late 2025, the product leans more toward a personal assistant that feeds the wearer information. “We dropped the assumption from the start that smart glasses need a camera to be useful,” Even Realities CEO Will Wang told CNET by email.

Smart glasses keep getting cheaper, and models and companies keep multiplying. Demand for detectors is growing right along with it. Szydłowski says he hopes Zuckoff eventually becomes unnecessary. Just as AirTag detection ended up built into iOS and Android by default, he said that if consumers push manufacturers and governments until smart glasses are easy to detect, that would be “the perfect solution.”

blocks.cap: Two AirPods resting on a table.

blocks.x: Apple accidentally leaked footage of camera-equipped AirPods this week in a macOS Tahoe 26.7 test build. Code buried in the same build revealed more details about these unusual earbuds.

Putting a camera on earbuds is strange enough on its own, but how it works is even stranger. Each bud has one camera, and Visual Intelligence software merges the two images into one. What gets captured is an RGB still image of up to 1 megapixel.

Head movement is factored in too, which isn't surprising given that Apple's earbuds already carry several accelerometers. Shots that are too shaky or have an obstructed view get filtered out by the software. The code's use of the phrase “peripheral inference” suggests some of the processing happens on the earbud itself, closer to on-device sensing.
It doesn't shoot video. Instead, it captures images at set intervals, which is apparently enough for Visual Intelligence to understand the situation.

There are two modes, active and passive, with resolution that changes between them, so active mode produces better image quality. Each bud will likely carry a capture indicator light too, a cue meant to let people nearby know the camera is on.

The light is a welcome move for privacy, but this product has a different character from Meta's glasses. It isn't built for users to capture and keep the world around them; it's closer to a way of gathering images to feed the Visual Intelligence that Apple is building.
Visual Intelligence is one part of the Siri overhaul Apple has long put off. The idea is for a multimodal assistant to analyze images coming from the earbuds and act on them.

In the leaked short video, the only use case Apple showed was this: a man asks Siri to remember the book he was looking at. The narration says, “With Visual Intelligence, your world becomes something you can save. See something you like? Just ask it to be saved for later.” Human brains do that too. It's a basic function called memory.
The question is how accurately Visual Intelligence can read images sent from a low-end camera. AI models get things wrong often enough even when fed clean data.

An answer may not be far off. Apple holds its iPhone 18 event next month. Since the demo footage was sitting in macOS 26.7, more could be revealed there. Still, Bloomberg's Mark Gurman thinks the launch won't come until 2027.

blocks.cap: A Google Home speaker.

blocks.x: Google Home is rolling out an update that fixes long-neglected pain points in its voice assistant. It refines broadcast commands, improves recognition of Spotify requests, and lets smart light color temperature be tuned down to the Kelvin. No need to be embarrassed about it; everyone has a favorite Kelvin value.

Google has been steadily shipping worthwhile Home updates lately. Most of them have focused on improving Gemini for Home and on the polish it still needs while in early access. This update touches problems that bothered even the most casual users.

The August 20 update includes three changes related to Gemini, Google Home's voice assistant. First, Spotify command recognition has been cleaned up. Google said it “improved how it recognizes songs, artists and playlists requested from Spotify.” Anyone who has used Google Home for a while knows a specific song request would sometimes work and sometimes wouldn't. A general command could get misread as a music request, blasting a random song at an uncomfortable volume. The hope is that this update cuts down on that.

A change to how broadcasts are handled is also in the changelog. Broadcasts will now split into two steps: ask Gemini for a broadcast, wait, then tell it what the message is. That beats the old way of cramming it all into one sentence, which often led to misunderstandings.

The last voice assistant change will please anyone particular about color temperature. Google Home now understands specific color temperature requests. Say “Hey Google, set the living room lights to 2700 Kelvin” and the color changes precisely. It was always possible in the app, but not easy by voice. Now there's a reason to memorize your color temperature values.
The changelog also lists several app-side fixes. Temperature units are now unified across every device, and support for European-style door locks is being added.

Google said the app crashes less on iOS devices, and offline camera controls stay consistent even when connectivity is unstable. The improvement comes after Google recently expanded support for third-party cameras.
On Android, a bug that locked camera streams at 360p is fixed. As long as the connection can handle it, those cameras will stream at their native resolution.

Finally, a clear notification will appear if a Google Home Premium payment fails, meant to prevent features or camera storage from suddenly cutting off one day. The August 20 update starts rolling out today.
A new patent filed by Meta includes a ‘hardware lock’ that physically blocks the camera on smart glasses, according to Android Central.
The target is the fierce backlash against always-on AI glasses. The distrust over not knowing when a camera is active hasn't been settled by software settings alone.

The approach the patent proposes moves privacy from a settings-screen problem to an industrial design problem. Whether recording happens is decided by a physical mechanism you touch, not a toggle switch.

Putting consent in the hands of a mechanical device is a matter of product design, not privacy policy. A patent is just a patent, though, and it isn't yet known whether this lock will make it into an actual pair of glasses.

blocks.cap: The Oura Ring. Image credit: Oura/ZDNET

blocks.x: Can a smart ring that measures biometric signals like heart rate, body temperature and respiratory rate pinpoint sleep stages from that data alone? That question sits at the center of this lawsuit involving Oura.

The class action filed against Oura claims the wearable company engaged in unlawful marketing that misled consumers about the sleep-tracking accuracy of its smart ring. In the plaintiffs' view, the Oura Ring lacks the sensors and signals needed to properly measure the neural activity that defines sleep stages, namely brain waves, eye movement, cardiac activity, muscle movement and finger PPG.

The complaint states, “Oura's AI model merely guesses at what is happening based on the wrong inputs, and sells flawed AI inference as credible science, exploiting consumers who are desperate about sleep or worried about their health.”

The lawsuit targets Oura, but the fallout could spread to other wearables that detect sleep stages with similar sensors. The question remains whether signals taken from the wrist or finger really translate into accurate diagnostic measures.

Madison Server, the plaintiff named in the complaint, paid $503 for an Oura ring last year, believing it would track her sleep accurately. She claims she paid an “unjustified premium” for a device that fell short of its marketing promises. The complaint cites a Nature study finding the smart ring achieved only “limited accuracy” in determining sleep stages, correctly identifying each stage 53% of the time.

“Sleep happens in the brain, not in the finger.” If that single line from the complaint is accepted as fact in court, it would shake the multi-billion-dollar health wearable industry, because its entire value proposition rests on that premise. Smart rings and smartwatches read heart rate, heart rate variability, body temperature, blood oxygen saturation and respiratory rate from the finger or wrist to judge activity, sleep and even stress. The market's success and growth hinge on this translation of biometric signals.

Oura told ZDNET that it “stands behind our science, research and accuracy claims.” The company's response is that “there is well-documented, independently peer-reviewed scientific evidence that sleep stages are linked to distinct, measurable and reproducible physiological changes, which is why we classify sleep stages using these signals.”

blocks.cap: RayNeo iO smart glasses.

blocks.x: RayNeo's new AR glasses span one extreme that's utterly ordinary and another that's openly loud.
