The RayNeo iO smart glasses look like regular glasses but hide a small display, a sophisticated voice-capture setup and AI features that assist through the day. On the other end sits the GT series, which the company describes as built for “cinema-grade spatial viewing.” It looks like oversized sunglasses with thick arms, the kind that draws stares when you wear them out.

The two product lines serve different purposes from the start. The 33-gram iO smart glasses are meant to be worn all day, replacing the ordinary glasses you wear now. A small green monochrome display with a 23.5-degree field of view shows a simple interface and short text, things like real-time translation or a prompter for a speech. The GT series is dedicated-use display glasses for watching movies, gaming and working on a large virtual screen. One device might someday do both jobs, but that's a stretch with today's technology.

Going by the released product images and specs alone, the iO smart glasses are an interesting option for anyone who wants to add a bit of intelligence to the glasses they already wear. But RayNeo gave up some things to get a look far more “normal” than Meta's bulky Ray-Ban display glasses. A monochrome display is one of them, and, surprisingly, there's no speaker.

RayNeo instead put its weight behind capturing voice well. It arranged four microphones and added a bone conduction sensor that, per the company, “isolates vocal cord vibrations for perfect transcription even in noisy environments.” That's useful for real-time translation and voice commands, and it also feeds RayNeo's ambient AI productivity suite, which listens to conversations to “extract action items” and suggest schedule changes.

RayNeo said the iO smart glasses use Timekettle BabelOS 3.0 translation software to translate 55 languages and 109 accents in real time with roughly a one-second delay. The battery is said to last two days, about 18 hours of continuous recording, or 6.2 hours of translation.

As with the Xgimi MemoMind One, there's something unsettling about an AI feature that's constantly recording you. RayNeo said an indicator light turns on during recording and translation, but as we saw with Meta's Ray-Ban hardware, that's easy enough to cover up. These glasses have no camera, though, so they dodge the “creep glasses” mockery.

The new GT and GT Max go head to head with premium cinema displays like the Xreal One Pro. At 68 grams and 78 grams, roughly double the iO, they have room for a much larger display. The GT projects a virtual screen up to 231 inches with a 46-degree field of view, and the GT Max goes up to 307 inches with a 59-degree field of view. The wider the field of view, the more screen you see without turning your head.

Per the company, the GT is weighted toward AR gaming and video viewing, while the GT Max leans into a “cinema-grade AR display.” Both GT models carry four speakers tuned with Bang & Olufsen and use a 3DoF AR chip to anchor the screen in space. Connected to the separate RayNeo Pocket TV Pro, a Google TV-based streaming device, they also play back Dolby Vision HDR.
Pricing hasn't been announced yet. It will likely be revealed before the September 4 retail launch. RayNeo will show off all the new glasses at IFA in early September.
Apple unveiled the M6 chip. It's the first chip built on a 2-nanometer process, and it comes with a Dual 16-core Neural Engine.

blocks.cap: Apple M6 chip

blocks.x: The CPU gains two cores over M5, bringing the total to 12: two super cores, four performance cores, and six efficiency cores. Apple says single-thread performance is the fastest in the world, and multithreaded performance is up to 1.2 times faster than M5 and up to 2.4 times faster than M1.

The GPU also gains two cores, for 12 total, each with a Neural Accelerator. Peak GPU performance on AI workloads rises nearly 30% over M5 and more than 8 times over M1, speeding up prompt processing for on-device LLMs.
Apple also reworked the shader core architecture, Dynamic Caching, and hardware-accelerated ray tracing. Geometry throughput is up 50%, handling more complex graphics.

The Dual 16-core Neural Engine that M6 introduces delivers up to twice the peak compute of the previous generation. Because the system frameworks automatically use both engines at once, apps run AI models faster.
Unified memory tops out at 32GB, with bandwidth up to 170GB/s, 10% wider than M5 and 2.5 times wider than M1.
M6 debuts in the new Mac mini, launching Tuesday, September 22.
Here's another case showing how AI can turn into a threat to our devices. An Amazon security engineer demonstrated just how capable Claude Opus is at reverse-engineering PC peripherals.

blocks.cap: Webcams and microphones became the test subjects (Image credit: Shutterstock / LightField Studios)

blocks.x: Chaz Schlarp, a senior security engineer at Amazon, wrote up an experiment he ran on peripherals like webcams and microphones. He wanted to find out how easily AI could rewrite firmware to pull off useful tricks. The dark side is just as clear: the same approach, used maliciously, turns these devices into a way into a system.
The targets were an Insta360 webcam, a Shure microphone, an Asus monitor, an Elgato video capture stick, and an Elgato mini light for streaming. He used Claude Opus 5 for the work.

Here's how Schlarp describes it: “The process was nearly identical for each device. I'd pull the firmware and update tools from the manufacturer, drop them into my reverse-engineering setup, tell Claude Opus 5 the goal, and let it run.”
One thing became clear quickly: none of these devices had any meaningful firmware integrity protection. Only the Elgato light had any defenses at all, and even those weren't hard to bypass.

There were useful examples too. On the Asus ROG Swift PG42UQ monitor, he found a way to get rid of the annoying pop-up that periodically nags you to run “pixel cleaning.” He hasn't applied it to the firmware yet. He also found a way to run the Windows utility DisplayWidget's features on Linux, binding a hardware crosshair or an FPS counter to a shortcut via a shell script.

Most of what he did, though, was meant to show how easily firmware flips once you hand the hard work to AI. Turning off a webcam's recording indicator light was one example. Like surveillance malware, the camera can film secretly while the user has no idea. The same goes for the microphone: he produced a plain-text command shell that leaves the mute LED lit while the mic isn't actually muted.

Schlarp wrote: “Peripherals turned out to be an ideal target for agentic reverse engineering. They're small computers attached to my computer, connected to the host via data, and usually have a firmware update path, which gives an agent something to keep trying against. The result is that I now have better control over, and understanding of, my machines.”

blocks.cap: The microphone's mute indicator was also disabled (Image credit: Shure)

blocks.x: The key point is speed. Taking over all five devices took the AI 13 hours of self-directed work, with fewer than 100 prompts from a human.

In Schlarp's words: “Hardware is now essentially wide open with a couple of hours per device, and that's mostly hands-off labor handed to the machine.” He said he's looking forward to a near future where adding features to webcam firmware feels as routine as patching software on Linux.

He raised the flip side of the story himself, too. “As a security professional, this is scary for several reasons. I'll be operating under the assumption that any device plugged into a computer could have a malicious firmware implant. This used to be work that required real investment per model and was considered the domain of ‘nation-state actors.’”

The thing that's held back these kinds of attacks has always been labor and time, which kept them limited to going after valuable targets one at a time. If an AI agent takes over that grunt work, the same attack becomes far more common.

In other words, a peripheral plugged into a PC becomes a way into you and your system. Schlarp also said he got a root shell on a Dell commercial display, adding: “Letting untrusted clients touch these things was never great practice to begin with, but now the speed and scale have changed, and that makes the risk much bigger.”

A bigger threat remains, too. “It's a very small leap from here to imagining someone building self-replicating malware that scouts the environment, feeds reconnaissance data to a smart command-and-control system, and pushes itself into the accessories, IoT devices, and industrial equipment sitting next to an infected target.”

Garmin recently launched its first screen-free wearable, and leaks kept pointing to a new smartwatch waiting in the wings. That watch is here: the Garmin Fenix 9 and Fenix 9 Pro. The hardware is better than the Fenix 8, but as with rivals that lean less into sport, the real story is in the software.

blocks.cap: Garmin Fenix 9

blocks.x: The Fenix 9 comes in three sizes: 43mm, 47mm, and 51mm. All of them use a round AMOLED covered with a sapphire lens. Unlike the Fenix 8, where AMOLED was an optional upgrade, it's now standard across the lineup, and brightness is double the previous model's. It withstands diving down to 10 ATM, and the battery lasts up to 10 days on the smallest size. It packs 64GB of internal storage for offline maps and local music playback. It also includes a built-in flashlight with adjustable brightness, plus a mic and speaker for voice commands and calls. It works with Garmin's new stretch ComfortFit band as well.

blocks.cap: The Fenix 9 Pro has a full titanium body (© Garmin)

blocks.x: The Fenix 9 Pro comes in the same three sizes but with a full titanium body. Its AMOLED, protected by a sapphire lens, grows up to 1.5 inches on the 51mm model. A solar-charging display and an inReach satellite connection for receiving messages and weather off-grid are optional. The mic, speaker, and flashlight are the same as on the standard model, but the Pro's light adds red and green.

Both models support new stamina tracking, which shows how endurance has changed across your training history, and measurement for indoor rowing and rucking workouts has also improved. What stands out is Garmin Epic. Offered for free, this feature bundles multiple workouts and activities into one "epic" covering a specific trip, training period, or outdoor adventure. Garmin says it can combine up to 92 days of different activities, with photos and notes attached alongside the records. The summary is built as much for looking back on your own experience as for sharing it with others.

Pricing starts at $1,000 for the Garmin Fenix 9 and $1,100 for the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro — eye-widening numbers in a market now full of cheap fitness bands. Both models can be ordered from Garmin starting August 28, with pricing rising depending on size and, for the Pro, the solar and satellite options.

Nothing has officially unveiled Nothing OS 5.0. The goal it showed in a recent company update video comes down to one thing: making hardware and software, which had felt like two separately built pieces stuck together, feel like they came from the same mind.

Nothing's design lead said he's wanted hardware and software to feel like a single product since the Phone 1. The industrial design language that started with the Ear 1 carried over to the phones, but the software took much longer to catch up. OS 5.0 was introduced as the version that finally closes that gap.

The Geist font, previously used only in marketing and the Playground, now moves into the OS itself. Transparency gets pushed further too: widgets sit on the wallpaper with depth instead of lying flat. This design, spanning typography, icons, and color, is applied consistently across the camera, gallery, widgets, settings, and launcher.

There's also more room to customize. Two new lock screen clock styles are added, one sleek and simple, the other dense like a terminal. Initial setup has been simplified, and batch editing arrives too, letting you move home screen elements all at once instead of dragging them one by one.

blocks.cap: Two new clock designs added to the lock screen

blocks.x: Glyph gets a dedicated app. Nothing acknowledged that people like the feature but find it fiddly to configure, so it's shipping a separate app that makes the Glyph interface easier to adjust. Two widgets are added as well: a downtime tracker meant to encourage putting the phone down, and a collection widget that turns photos of things you treasure into home screen stickers.

blocks.cap: Two new widgets

blocks.x: The Essential Suite got attention too. Essential Voice, which lets you control the phone by speaking, keeps refining its model, latency, and dictation accuracy. Essential Space, where easily lost notes and files get collected, now has smart collections and MCP support, letting you connect the AI tools you already use directly to your own data.

blocks.cap: Smart collections added to Essential Space

blocks.x: The Essential Apps beta is also expanding. It lets you vibe-code widgets right on the phone, with examples shown including a custom-built metronome and a morning routine planner that pulls together your commute and first meeting.

blocks.cap: Example of a widget built and used directly on the phone

blocks.x: Nothing OS 5.0 runs on top of Android 17. Quick settings and notifications are now split instead of sharing one panel, screen recording has improved, and 3D emoji have arrived. Privacy, security, and Bluetooth performance have also improved.
The beta opens tomorrow at nothing.tech. The Nothing Phone 3 comes first, with other devices added gradually.

AI assistants usually have to send your questions, files, and data to someone else's servers to work. Perplexity's new Portable Computer flips that structure, running the entire AI system on hardware you own.
Unveiled on Tuesday, the product moves Perplexity's agent platform, Computer, onto an Nvidia DGX Spark, or onto a Linux machine with a compatible Nvidia graphics card.

According to the company, every task starts on your device. When the local model hits a step that needs deeper reasoning, it first asks whether that one step can be sent to a frontier model in the cloud. The answer comes back into the local workflow, and files and sensitive information stay on the device.

blocks.cap: An agent running on your own hardware (Image credit: Shutterstock)

blocks.x: It's an appealing picture for anyone who wants the convenience of an AI agent without automatically handing everything the agent touches to a cloud provider.
Downloading an open model and running it on your own computer is already possible. The hard part is turning that model into an agent that can handle files, use tools, and complete multi-step tasks.
Normally, you'd have to find and set up an inference engine, an agent harness, a sandbox, and connectors for outside apps yourself. Making all the pieces fit together was also on you.
Portable Computer bundles that whole stack together. A local model, an inference engine, agent tools, app connectors, and an isolated sandbox for running code and using tools all come packaged in.
It handles files stored on your computer, reads PDFs, and runs shell commands. It also does dictation and web search. It connects to services like Google Drive, Gmail, Slack, and GitHub.

Perplexity says code and tool use happen inside the local sandbox. That puts some kind of wall between the agent and the rest of the device, though exactly what it can access and how permissions are controlled is something worth learning more about.

blocks.cap: Hybrid routing is the core of this product (Image credit: Shutterstock)

blocks.x: Even a small local model is enough to find files, pull information out of a PDF, and handle a few simple steps. But it's hard to expect reasoning power on par with the largest models from OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google.
Perplexity's answer is simple. It keeps a task local until it hits a point the model clearly can't handle well, and at that moment, asks whether that step can be handed off to a cloud model.

Users never pick a privacy mode or write routing rules. The system makes the call mid-task, and a human approves the moment it hands something off. A "local" AI that quietly slips to the cloud every time things get hard wouldn't deserve the name.
Perplexity says work finished locally doesn't use billing credits. Only the portion that goes to the cloud counts as usage.

At launch, the models you can choose are a 27-billion-parameter Qwen and PPLX 27B, which Perplexity post-trained itself. Nvidia's Nemotron 3.5 Lightning is set to follow, and there's also a path to bring your own model and inference server and plug it in.

The catch is hardware. The software ships for Linux first and requires Nvidia hardware with at least 24GB of VRAM. It supports the desktop-sized Nvidia DGX Spark, as well as ARM and x64 computers running DGX OS or Ubuntu. Windows support is slated for September, and there's no macOS plan yet.

It's available to Perplexity Pro, Max, Enterprise Pro, and Enterprise Max subscribers. Even among people whose subscription qualifies, not many have that kind of equipment under their desk. So this first rollout is less about people weighing ChatGPT against Perplexity on a laptop, and more about enthusiasts, developers, and companies already running high-performance Nvidia systems.

The idea itself has room to spread much further. The information an AI assistant touches keeps moving into increasingly private territory: email, work documents, files on your computer. Pulling more of that work onto a local device gives users more say over what gets sent out, and when.
Portable Computer won't replace cloud chatbots anytime soon. But it offers an early look at what a more private AI assistant could look like once that kind of hardware becomes affordable.

Google is reportedly testing a new mode called “Listening area” in Google Live Translate on Android XR. It looks like the kind of thing that could become a signature feature of the Google smart glasses expected to arrive in a steady stream soon.

blocks.cap: Warby Parker glasses running Android XR

blocks.x: None of this is new, since Google has always said it would build real-time translation into Android XR. The promise was to handle it all through smart glasses: translated speech that preserves the speaker's tone and pitch, and text translation for things like menus and signs.

This time, Android Authority dug into version 10.32.66 of the Google Translate app and found two listening modes. One is “Front only,” which translates only speech coming from directly in front of the wearer, for one-on-one conversations. The other is “Surrounding area,” which uses the glasses' full microphone array to translate speech from everywhere around the wearer.

That said, since this feature comes from the apk code, there's no guarantee it will actually ship. Still, it fits well with the push to expand Android XR ahead of upcoming smart glasses launches. The frames revealed so far are ones from Gentle Monster and Warby Parker launching this fall, and frames from Kering, Gucci's parent company, are also reportedly in development.

Real-time translation has always been a strength of Google's. Since it has to go head-to-head with Meta's smart glasses, Google is likely to pack in every feature it can. Meta's glasses also include real-time translation.

Meta's approach is closer to the “Front only” mode mentioned above. The translated speech plays through the glasses' open-ear speakers, while the other person reads translated subtitles that appear on the user's smartphone.
Google has released Gemini 3.5 Transcribe. It is described as “the most accurate speech-to-text model yet,” and it is already running inside several of the company's own products.

“Unlike existing speech recognition models that struggle with background noise, complex jargon, and cleaning up stutters, Gemini 3.5 Transcribe turns raw audio directly into accurate, polished, formatted text.”

Google describes it as a model built to “capture natural speech patterns to better understand intent and recognize custom vocabulary.” As seen in Gboard's Rambler, it handles self-corrections like “let's meet Tuesday, no, Wednesday” and strips filler words such as “um” and “uh” from the output. It also handles formatting on its own, and users can edit sentences by voice.

blocks.cap: Gemini 3.5 Transcribe running in Gboard's Rambler

blocks.x: Google also cited the following figures. The word error rate (WER), as measured by Artificial Analysis, averages 4.0% for streaming and 2.6% for non-streaming. It accurately captures alphanumeric strings like zip codes and order numbers even in noisy real-world settings. Adding custom vocabulary lets it recognize jargon and unusual spellings. It automatically detects and transcribes more than 85 languages, and for pre-recorded audio it can distinguish up to three speakers with timestamps. Handling more than three speakers is still experimental.
Google calls the performance “a big step forward” compared with its 2025 Chirp 3 transcription model, with a lower word error rate and noticeably reduced latency.

“As measured by Artificial Analysis, time to final transcript is down 70%. It also outperforms Chirp 3 on the FLEURS benchmark covering major languages and locales, posting a word error rate of 5.50% for streaming and 5.04% for non-streaming.”

blocks.cap: Material Google released on Gemini 3.5 Transcribe

blocks.x: Another goal is “getting things done by voice.” With function calling attached, it hands off heavier tasks like image generation or file analysis to other Gemini models. Speak to Window in the macOS Gemini app is one example.

Beyond the macOS Gemini app and Android's Gboard Rambler, it is also available through the microphone in Google Antigravity's prompt window. There, with user permission, it reads screen context and conversation history together, accurately transcribing file names, the agent's reasoning, and open documents. Chrome is next. In any text field on the web, users will be able to speak to type replies or write text, and to enter prompts into Gemini inside Chrome.

Developers can use it in public preview through the Gemini API in Google AI Studio and Google Antigravity. Enterprises can access it in preview on the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, and it will soon come to Gemini Enterprise for Customer Experience.

LG and Nvidia are significantly expanding their robotics partnership in Seoul. A newly built data factory at LG's Yangjae research campus will produce 100,000 hours of training data before the end of 2026. LG blends data from manufacturing, logistics, and real-world robot deployments with synthetic data, while Nvidia contributes its Omniverse, Cosmos, and Isaac robotics platforms.

blocks.cap: LG's AI robot CLOiD greeting a visitor in Seoul

blocks.x: LG's CLOiD robot learns inside full-scale replicas of living spaces and simulated manufacturing and logistics workflows. One point where it diverges from Tesla's or BYD's approach is legs: CLOiD does not walk on two feet but moves on a wheeled base.

The data collected this way feeds into LG's Robot Foundation Model to expand what its humanoid robots can do. CLOiD already practices household tasks like taking milk out of the fridge, operating an oven, and folding and stacking clothes. It has two arms, each with seven degrees of freedom, and five fingers on each hand that each generate force independently. 1X NEO also targets the home, while Agility's Digit and Apptronik's Apollo are closer to logistics and industrial use.

blocks.cap: LG's robot data factory built in Yangjae

blocks.x: LG itself is growing its robotics business. In July, it established a center dedicated to robotics and plans to launch home robots in addition to industrial and service ones. Meanwhile, competition is heating up in China and the United States. Tesla is building the general-purpose humanoid Optimus, BYD is pushing Xiaodi for manufacturing tasks, Xpeng has Iron, and UBTech is promoting the industrial Walker S2. Unitree, maker of the G1 and H2, is also one of China's leading robotics companies.

The 100,000-hour target is meant to sustain an unbroken loop of real-world robot deployment, simulation, and AI training. LG aims to get robots ready for complex tasks faster and lay the groundwork for entering the home robot market. Still, this partnership does not by itself guarantee an imminent mass rollout of fully autonomous home robots.

James Park and Eric Friedman, co-founders who left after Google acquired Fitbit, shifted their focus from individual health to the health of the whole family. That vessel is a startup called Luffu, and an AI app that tracks medications and logs meals to ease the mental load on caregivers and parents. Their new release, Luffu Link, pushes that idea a step further, adding a few wrinkles to Fitbit Air-level health tracking so it doesn't stay just another fitness band.

blocks.cap: Luffu Link, a wearable with no screen

blocks.x: Luffu Link packs a button, sensors, an LED, a microphone, and a speaker into a square metal housing, strapped to the wrist with a silicone band. The first thing that sets it apart from other wearables is voice logging. Users hold the button and say what they just ate or which medication they took, and can also log intangible things like their mood or something they don't want to forget. That recorded speech moves to the Luffu app along with heart rate, sleep, and activity tracking data, and over time the AI returns patterns it has found.

blocks.cap: Logs piling up in the Luffu app © Luffu

blocks.x: The second point of difference is GPS and free LTE. Family members can see where the wearer has been, and pressing the button twice immediately shares the current location. Thanks to LTE, the wearer can call for help from a designated family member even without a phone nearby.

With no screen, Link joins a growing group of screenless wearables like the Oura Ring 5 or the Whoop 5.0. Luffu co-founder James Park told TechCrunch: “There's a trend in these new wearables toward removing the screen, and here it's very intentional. We want to be in the background. We designed Link to be a quiet guardian on the wrist all day, and we didn't want it to feel like an existing wearable at all—not a common fabric-brand item, not a wrist device with a screen, not a clunky pendant you wear around your neck for emergencies.”

Luffu Link can now be preordered for $250, $50 off its $300 list price, with shipping starting in early 2027. The LTE is “free,” but using it requires a Luffu Family Plan: up to four family members for $20 a month, or $200 a year. That's a steep entry fee for a healthy family, more so if each person buys their own. Whether Luffu's software is worth that price remains to be seen.

RAM prices are rising. Google didn't wait to see how bad things would get. It attached new memory rules to Android apps distributed through the Play Store, with a deadline set for developers to clean up their code. As prices rise, people are choosing lower-spec devices, and memory-hungry apps degrade the experience for everyone on those devices.

blocks.cap: Android apps now subject to memory rules

blocks.x: Starting in February 2027, apps will need to meet new memory standards in three areas. Dynamic memory usage measures the private data storage an app uses while running or sitting in the background. Bitmap memory covers what images and graphics take up — the standard is not to hold onto that memory while it's off-screen. DEX code optimization trims app code to make it run faster and use less memory.

blocks.cap: The three memory metrics the Play Store now measures

blocks.x: Google is adding new tools to Play Console so bloated code gets caught early. Apps that exceed the limits won't be removed. Instead, they'll see reduced store visibility and some distribution features blocked.

Buried in the same announcement is an item useful to anyone switching devices. Zero-tap sign-in requires apps to automatically restore logins when moving to a new Android device, so there's no need to re-enter passwords app by app after a device switch.

blocks.cap: Zero-tap sign-in restores logins even after switching devices

blocks.x: The rule takes effect in April 2027. Games are exempt for now, with separate guidance for game logins coming out sometime in 2027. Google has already cut the RAM in its Pixel 11 Pro lineup from 16GB to 12GB — a sign of how deeply the shortage has spread across the industry. Android 17 will also add a privacy feature that blocks internet carriers from tracking which sites and apps a device visits.

Meta is patching a hole in its AI smart glasses. The workaround let people keep recording while covering the front LED. Alex Himel, Meta's vice president of augmented reality, wrote on Threads that “covering the light while recording now stops the camera.”

blocks.cap: The recording light on the Ray-Ban Meta second generation

blocks.x: Meta smart glasses already turned off the built-in camera if you covered the recording light. The light blinks to tell people nearby that recording or capturing is underway. But some wearers found that covering the LED after recording had already started let them get around the restriction. This fix comes just over a month after Meta made physically touching the light turn the camera off.

blocks.cap: The outdoor ad Meta put up in Los Angeles

blocks.x: Himel said Meta will “keep shipping updates like this so the capture LED reliably tells people around you the moment something lands in someone's camera roll — photo or video.” “Very few people are trying to get around the safeguard, and the fact that they have to go to such lengths is itself proof that our effort is working.”

Meta's smart glasses have drawn privacy and harassment controversy. Some wearers filmed others without consent, or recorded social-media “prank” videos targeting strangers on the street. Combined with reports that Meta plans to add facial recognition, that fueled an opposition campaign against the glasses that spread worldwide.

Meta is now moving to publicize the recording LED instead. Meta spokesperson Albert Aydin told The Verge the company has launched its own “awareness” campaign in regions where the glasses have sold well. A billboard in Los Angeles shows the smart glasses alongside the line “The camera captures the moment. The light lets everyone around know it happened.” A video Meta released also says the recording LED “lets you know when the glasses are capturing photos and video” and that “no light, no capture.”

If you measure a robot's success by cuteness, Microduck is the best thing to come along in a while. Pollen Robotics unveiled it this week — a division of the AI company Hugging Face, yes, that Hugging Face. It's a 25-centimeter-tall educational robot that arrives with movement, balance, and personality already built in.

blocks.cap: Microduck, unveiled by Pollen Robotics

blocks.x: Preorders opened on August 27 at a price of $399 — an introductory rate. It's a fully assembled, duck-shaped robot weighing about 1.7 pounds, with a mouth that doubles as a gripper and a voice like a duck's quack. It has 15 degrees of freedom. Motors let it walk, waddle, and turn its head, and two IMUs help it keep from falling over when pushed.

blocks.cap: The 25-centimeter robot whose mouth doubles as a gripper

blocks.x: A single-eye camera paired with lidar scans its surroundings, and may even recognize its owner. Camera resolution hasn't been disclosed yet. It has a speaker for its voice and a microphone for listening. Its brain is a low-power Rockchip RK3566 ARM chip with 1GB of RAM and 32GB of storage. It has Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and NFC, and a small 2600mAh battery that runs for about an hour.

The specs aren't impressive. Even so, the robot in the teaser video is hard to look away from, especially the moments where it gets up on its own after falling or being pushed. Many of its movements are pre-loaded, but a good deal of the cuteness comes from the open-source platform and whatever users program themselves. The kit comes with a virtual training environment, learning scripts, tools, and an SDK with a “proven sim-to-real workflow.” It is, after all, an educational robot.

blocks.cap: A pose reminiscent of Disney's BDX droids

blocks.x: It resembles the BDX droids from Disney and Star Wars. Both stand on two legs, keep a low posture, and have a big head. That's where the resemblance ends. The BDX droids, which move via semi-autonomy and remote control, are much larger and far more expensive, and for now only roam inside Disney World. There are no plans for a consumer release.

The $399 price covers the basic package. Sold separately are a $39 charging pack, a $119 dev pack with spare motors, cables, and a battery, and an accessory pack with a laser pointer, roller skates Microduck can wear and ride on, and ten NFC tags. Microduck is Pollen Robotics' second educational robot. The first, Reachy Mini, was more of a desktop companion, and the company says it has sold 10,000 units.

The question is how much of that charm shows up the moment you open the box, and how much coding you'll have to do yourself. You can remote-control it with a game controller, so faking it at first is an option. The real fun starts once the robot begins responding in unexpected ways. What's left to see is how many people will pay close to $400 for a semi-autonomous plastic duck robot. Shipping is set for before Christmas, in four colors: cream, graphite, lavender, and sky.

Last year I made a flat statement: there's no reason to invent a new AI wearable, because the best wearable is something you already own. I mean headphones — the thing most of us have used for decades.

blocks.cap: Plaud's latest wearable, the Plaud One

blocks.x: Plaud, often called the biggest AI note-taking company in the world, seems to think the same way. It has packed what counts as industry-leading agentic AI into a pair of headphones. The reveal comes just before IFA 2026 in Berlin next week, where I'll see these headphones in person for the first time.
At a glance, it doesn't look different from any other earbuds — a sleek, unassuming design in off-white. How it fits and how it sounds are things I want to check alongside its AI performance.

blocks.cap: The Plaud One, which looks no different from any other earbuds

blocks.x: Plaud is known for a wallet-thin device that sticks discreetly to the back of a phone, and a pin you clip to clothing. Both are hardware gateways into the company's real weapon: its agentic AI and software platform. The Plaud One headphones carry the same software.

These headphones capture and upload conversations and calls happening nearby. They use 4G LTE through a built-in eSIM. It's good practice to tell others you're using a recording device, and in some U.S. states, recording a call without the consent of everyone involved can be illegal.

Plaud's software automatically transcribes meetings and turns that record into summaries, follow-up actions, or reports. The agent connects directly to tools you're likely already using, like Google, Gmail, Slack, and Notion.
Plaud co-founder and CEO Nathan Xu said, “AI agents only become useful once they understand the context in which human intent is formed.” “That context lives in conversation.”

The bonus with the Plaud One is two-way conversation. You can talk to the agent directly to ask something or give it instructions — something earlier Plaud devices couldn't do. To wake it, you either say “Hey Plaud” while wearing the earbuds, or press and hold the agent button on the case.
The Plaud One Explorer Edition is now available for preorder at £229 ($311). It comes with £150 ($204) worth of Plaud credits. Shipping begins later this fall.

Whoop's wearables are designed to scrape up as much data as possible — the company even built a separate battery that charges the device without taking it off. What held it back for a long time was how it looked. Even though it was less flashy than an Apple Watch, it still looked like a device, specifically a fitness device. Whoop's answer is the $149 Meridian band — a new body for its fifth-generation sensor, aiming for a look closer to jewelry.

blocks.cap: Whoop's new Meridian band

blocks.x: Meridian comes in four finishes: gold, silver, matte black, and rose gold. The material is titanium, prized by today's premium wearables for being tough and long-lasting. Like Whoop's fabric bands, it's adjustable in length, and the top carries the company's “W.” What catches the eye first is the Milanese mesh — the style Apple sells as its “Milanese Loop” for smartwatches, a weave known to wearable fans, made by interlacing metal threads one by one in an old watch-strap style. It's more flexible than a link bracelet while matching it in refinement.

blocks.cap: The Milanese mesh structure, woven from metal thread

blocks.x: The new band fits the Whoop 5.0 and Whoop MG, and can be added to an order when starting a new subscription. Meridian makes sense in that it lets you wear Whoop's sensor comfortably even outside the gym. It's also a way to raise the cost of wearing Whoop. Whoop sells its wearables only as a subscription — the device stops working the moment you stop paying. That tight subscription structure is what makes the $99 Fitbit Ace or the $200 Garmin Cirqa stand out. Both screen-free devices improve with a subscription, but they also work without one.

Whoop's plans come in several tiers. The cheapest is $199 a year. You can get a discount by trading in another company's wearable, or offset the cost with FSA or HSA funds. Even so, staying on long enough means spending more than you would on a competitor's product — though that may not matter much to someone who'd buy the Meridian band in the first place.
After the Pixel 11 series launched, Google updated its Gemini Nano 4 developer documentation.

blocks.cap: Gemini Intelligence.

blocks.x: 'Nano v4' devices first appeared from Google and Samsung in the past few weeks. On Google's side that's the Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro, Pixel 11 Pro XL, and Pixel 11 Pro Fold; on Samsung's side, the Galaxy Z Flip8, Galaxy Z Fold8, and Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra.
This list, updated yesterday, targets app developers, but there was movement on the consumer-facing Gemini Intelligence side too.
Google revised the requirements list on android.com, restoring the phrase 'Nano v3 or higher.' This line first appeared right after The Android Show: I/O Edition in May, then was quickly removed.

The document states: "Gemini Intelligence features are available only on Android devices meeting the most advanced performance and specification requirements." The conditions listed alongside it include on-device AI integrating AI Core and Nano v3 or higher, 12GB or more of RAM, a qualifying flagship chip, 5 OS upgrades, and quarterly security updates for 6 years.

Gemini Intelligence officially launched on Samsung's latest foldable last month and now supports task automation in more than 40 apps. The Pixel 11 series marks the first appearance of Rambler and Proactive Assistance (formerly Magic Cue).

It's still unclear whether the Pixel 10 or the Galaxy S26 series will officially get Gemini Intelligence. Create My Widget is also still pending. Google has said it is rolling out new features in multiple waves.

Google's Pixel 11 launched at $899. That's $100 more than its predecessor, but base storage has doubled. After weeks of use, an Android Central reviewer summed up this generation as the point where AI meets social media.

blocks.cap: Google Pixel 11. Priced from $899.

blocks.x: At 8.6mm thick, it's even chunkier than the Galaxy S26 Ultra. But the camera bump is smaller, so it sits flatter on a desk. Wired charging stays at 30W, but wireless has sped up to 25W, and turning on the hidden Extreme Charging option filled it from 0% to 50% in 30 minutes.

A new feature, Magic Capture, sits to the left of Photo mode in the camera app. Press the shutter and a video rolls while AI picks out a good moment in the background and saves it as a photo. The reviewer said it pulled a usable shot even at a poorly lit party.

blocks.cap: The Pixel 11's Pause Point. It makes you stop once before opening an app.

blocks.x: On the other side is Pause Point, a digital wellbeing feature that makes you take a breath, set a timer, or write down how you feel before opening a distracting app. The reviewer set it on Instagram and said the extra step was annoying enough that they stopped opening the app at all.

blocks.cap: Inside Google Messages, Gemini surfaces the schedule first.

blocks.x: Gemini is everywhere too. The Daily Brief scans the calendar and Gmail to lay out the morning schedule, and when a friend texted asking if they were free this weekend, Gemini prompted them to check the calendar first. The key point is that it all happens without ever leaving Google Messages.

Running all this is the Tensor G6, built with AI performance in mind. But without the Pixel 11 Pro's vapor chamber, it gets fairly hot during long gaming sessions. The camera setup is unchanged from the previous model, and colors come out a bit warmer than on the Pixel 10.

blocks.cap: A low-light indoor sample shot on the Pixel 11.

blocks.x: Pro-exclusive features like HiLight and Pro camera controls are missing. Still, it has the same 12GB of RAM as the Pro and most of the AI features, so the conclusion is that the Pixel 11 is worth buying if you don't specifically need the Pro.

Robot vacuums do the cleaning for you, but they don't let you fully let go. Hair wraps around the brush, mops need washing, and in a home that mixes hardwood and carpet, a wet mop can end up somewhere it shouldn't. Roborock's new Qrevo 2 Pro set out to cut down on that leftover fuss.

blocks.cap: The Roborock Qrevo 2 Pro cleaning a floor.

blocks.x: The starting point is suction power. At 25,000Pa, it easily handles crumbs under the dining table, dust under the sofa, pet hair on the floor, and dirt embedded in carpet.

The tangling problem falls to the dual anti-tangle system. The main brush and side brush steer hair toward the suction inlet instead of letting it wrap around the roller. Roborock said its own testing showed a 0% tangle rate and 100% hair removal rate, though that would need independent verification.

blocks.cap: The self-cleaning dock. It leaves the mops here before heading to carpet.

blocks.x: Moving onto carpet doesn't require hands either. Unlike products that only lift the mops, the Qrevo 2 Pro returns to the dock, detaches the mops entirely, and comes back out. On carpet, Carpet Boost+ raises suction, and turning on Deep Carpet Cleaning makes it cross the same spot once more in a crisscross pattern.

blocks.cap: The Qrevo 2 Pro making its way around the living room.

blocks.x: The rest wraps up at the dock. It washes the mops with 75-degree water, dries them with 45-degree warm air to prevent odor, and refills its own water tank. Roborock says the dust bin doesn't need emptying for up to 65 days.

blocks.cap: In the kitchen. It erases, one by one, the chores that would otherwise need a human hand.

blocks.x: The Qrevo 2 Pro goes on sale in the U.S. today, carrying a promotional price of $550, down from its $799 list price. The feature list is packed, but what matters most in the end is how long you can leave it alone.

Agentic AI has flooded the field over the past year, but the world that automated AI touches has mostly stayed inside the computer. It was all data and actions that ended on a screen, like text, images, and code. Anthropic is pushing that boundary outward. The driver specification the company calls the Model Hardware Standard (MHS) aims to let AI agents pick up and control almost any device.

blocks.cap: Anthropic's diagram showing MHS acting as a translation layer between AI agents and many kinds of devices. Image courtesy of Anthropic

blocks.x: What's out now is a research preview. Anthropic pitches MHS as cutting the work scientists used to face writing custom software every time they had to get lab equipment talking to each other. When devices share a common interface and common data format, they communicate over the network “without a separate translation program wedged in between.” The company writes that experiment setups that used to take weeks to months now shrink to “hours, minutes.”

In the video posted with the announcement, Anthropic technical staff member Alec Kemeny says the idea for MHS came from watching neuroscientist Arco Bast run memory-formation experiments on the brain at the HHMI Janelia Research Campus in Ashburn, Virginia. Bast had tied together all sorts of parts — a rotating laser beam, a microscope, a camera — into one shared interface. “With this approach, AI could run any science experiment in the world.” That's the thought Kemeny had at the time.

A shared machine interface language doesn't necessarily require an AI model. Anthropic also says MHS devices can be controlled in real time through command-line prompts and API code files. But attaching an AI model via the Model Context Protocol lets scientists operate equipment in natural language, and the model “reasons through each step of the experiment, changes parameters in real time, and in some cases recovers from hardware errors without human intervention,” the company explains.

Anthropic gives this example: a model like Claude adjusts a laser, checks the result with a separate camera, and repeats the process to auto-calibrate the whole system. It can also focus a microscope, analyze the results to decide where to look next, then move to that region and continue the experiment. In the video, Claude reasoned out on its own how to move a robot arm to pick up an aluminum can it had never been trained on. Instead of reasoning through every step each time, it can also write API scripts to sequence devices and adjust them as conditions change.

MHS also includes a standard tagging system that records the real-world constraints of hardware. For models trained mostly in virtual environments, it encodes physical traits like a robot arm's weight and range of motion, adjustable parameters, measurement options, and enforced safety limits. Bundling these tags into a reference file lets a model get the key information right away, even for a device it has never encountered before.
