Siri launched in 2011, and spent most of that time trailing the assistants from Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic. iOS 27 is Apple's attempt to close that gap. It rebuilds the assistant with new AI features and, for the first time, attaches a standalone app that works like a conversational chatbot.

blocks.cap: The new Siri app in iOS 27.

blocks.x: There's a catch, though. Even after updating to iOS 27, you need an iPhone 15 Pro or later to reach Apple Intelligence and the new Siri. Earlier models, including the base iPhone 15, remain stuck with the old, sluggish Siri. The language is still English only, and users in the EU and China are blocked by local regulations, with no setting to work around it.

blocks.cap: The screen for turning on the new Siri in Settings.

blocks.x: Turning it on is simple. If you skipped the prompt right after the update, go to Settings > Siri, tap Turn On Siri, and choose the new Siri. It sometimes opens right away, but sometimes you land on a waitlist. Beta testers reported wait times ranging from a few minutes to several days.

blocks.cap: The conversation screen in the new Siri app.

blocks.x: There are three ways to call it up. Swipe down from the Dynamic Island to bring up a search bar, or do the familiar long press on the side button. If you want something shaped like ChatGPT, there's a dedicated Siri app for that.

The app syncs and stores past conversations through iCloud. Answers don't come as a single line, but as a mix of text cards and images. You can tap the plus button to add photos or documents for context. The old command for checking the weather still works as before. What's different is that asking about a message or email now gets an actual answer instead of being told to go search for it.

blocks.cap: Conversation history shown as a card grid.

blocks.x: You can dig through history using the search button on the main screen. A toggle in the top right lets you switch between a list and a card grid, and a long press brings up pin, rename, and delete. You choose how long to keep history, 30 days, 1 year, or indefinitely, under Settings > Siri > Keep Conversations. Short commands like setting a timer or playing a song aren't saved to history.

iOS 27 is still a public beta, and the full release usually arrives in fall. If you don't want to wait, you can join early through the beta software program open to developers and testers. Just be sure to back up first.

Smartphone cameras pull out detail well even in tricky scenes. They're still weak against darkness, though. Once light disappears, even expensive phones pick up noise, shadows turn muddy, and fine texture gets flattened.

blocks.cap: A smartphone camera struggling in the dark. The research targets that exact spot.

blocks.x: LL-Refiner, from researchers at Wuhan University in China, is a two-stage machine learning system aimed at that problem. The goal is to brighten ultra-high-definition (UHD) low-light images without throwing away the small details that make a photo look like a photo. The research, reported by Tech Xplore, was published in the IEEE/CAA Journal of Automatica Sinica on July 3, 2026.

The problem grows with resolution. UHD images carry an enormous amount of information, so AI has to raise brightness while also preserving color, lighting, contours, texture, and the structure of the whole scene at once.

LL-Refiner splits the job in two. First, a transformer-based neural network handles a downscaled version of the photo. Instead of processing every pixel directly, it roughly adjusts only global properties like lighting, color distribution, and the scene's overall layout.

blocks.cap: The higher the resolution, the harder dark scenes are to process.

blocks.x: A second, adaptive refinement network then takes over that result. Using cross-attention modules, it gradually restores contours, texture, and detail across multiple scales, bringing the image back up to its original resolution. The payoff of this structure is that it eases the computational load of brightening a huge image while preserving information that would otherwise vanish in the dark.

The researchers pitted it against leading existing correction techniques using real low-light photos, including smartphone photos shot under conditions different from training. LL-Refiner consistently came out ahead, with the gap widening especially in preserving sharpness in textured areas together with the fine structure of patterns.

They didn't stop at whether it looked better. They fed the corrected images into a separate computer vision task, depth estimation, since cameras increasingly hand visual information to robots and self-driving technology. Images processed through LL-Refiner produced more accurate depth predictions, and Professor Jiayi Ma said it was the only method that estimated background depth reasonably accurately under these conditions.

This doesn't mean a software update will change night photography right away. For now it's closer to a demonstration of a new correction approach than a feature in a commercial camera. But the direction is clear: adding more pixels alone won't solve low light, and future phones will lean more on AI to redraw difficult scenes, while staying within the line of not fabricating a photo that never existed.

blocks.cap: Photo Mattias Inghe

blocks.x: The LG UltraGear Evo AI GM9, model number 27GM950B-B, is LG's new premium 27-inch desktop monitor. Its sturdy metal stand adjusts for height, swivel, tilt and pivot. The chassis is matte black plastic, and it looks solidly built and good-looking from any angle, front or back.

UltraGear is a gaming brand. You can turn on RGB lighting on the back, and the settings menu opens first to two player profiles and game genre presets. Still, it's not gaming-only. You can pick separate sRGB and P3 profiles to keep color accuracy, plus a reading mode with reduced blue light, an HDR video mode, and two more profiles you calibrate yourself.

The panel covers brightness, color, resolution and speed all at once. A quantum-dot LCD delivers DCI-P3-level color out of the factory calibration, and a Mini LED backlight behind it, with 2,304 dimming zones, produces brightness above 1,200 cd/m² along with deep black at the same time. It's certified for HDR10 and VESA Display HDR 1000. Play an HDR movie and it's among the best displays I've seen; even in SDR, it's brighter than most monitors' HDR.

blocks.cap: At 5K resolution, a single screen fits in a lot.

blocks.x: It has weaknesses too. Small bright highlights can't wake the backlight and come out dim, and a white mouse cursor on a black background turns noticeably darker. You can find a workaround by adjusting the dimming intensity or turning it off entirely. OLED does better here, but no OLED can match this screen's combined brightness and dynamic range.

At 5K, the refresh rate is 165Hz, rising to 330Hz if you drop to 1440p or below. When there's no 5K source, AI upscaling makes 1080p and 1440p video noticeably sharper. Upscaling the Nintendo Switch's 1080p output to 5K showed no noticeable lag. Turning the feature off brings response time down to 1 millisecond.

blocks.cap: If the lighting strip on the back bothers you, you can just turn it off.

blocks.x: For connections, it uses a downward-facing DisplayPort 1.4 and HDMI 2.1 on the back, plus USB-C DP Alt mode for laptop docking. Connecting via USB-C opens a small hub with two USB-A ports, but since there's only one input, there's no KVM function. It also has speaker and headphone jacks. The sound is decent for a monitor, but calling it good would be an overstatement.

The menu button is hidden very small on the lower back, making it awkward to find by feel. The menu structure you navigate with the 4-way control is well designed, though. LG was criticized this summer for using a Windows update to auto-install the LG app installer and bundle in bloatware, but nothing installed automatically when I plugged in this monitor.

blocks.cap: There aren't many ports, but the selection is well chosen.

blocks.x: The price is $1,200. From the feel of the controls to color, refresh rate and dynamic range, it delivers an experience that matches the price. Compared with a good OLED, it's a trade-off, but in brightness alone, it's hard to beat in either SDR or HDR. If you can't fully control room lighting, or sit somewhere with a lot of sunlight, the wide dynamic range and matte anti-glare finish matter even more.

blocks.cap: The One UI 9 splash screen on a Galaxy S26 Ultra.

blocks.x: Samsung released One UI 9 beta 6 for the Galaxy S26 series earlier this week. Since Samsung usually leaves a few weeks between betas, expectations were for a stable update to follow, but there were signs another beta was in the works. That turned out to be true. Samsung has started rolling out One UI 9 beta 7 for the Galaxy S26 series.

The seventh One UI 9 update has arrived on a Galaxy S26 Ultra used in the U.K. It's based on Android 17, carries the firmware suffix ZZHK, includes the August 5, 2026 security patch, and weighs in at 1,234MB.

blocks.cap: One UI 9 beta 7 arriving on a Galaxy S26 Ultra.

blocks.x: The changelog only says 'new AI features' without specifying what they are. It lists three items: added new AI features, improved an issue where the device would intermittently reboot in certain situations, and improved usability of Do Not Disturb mode.
Tarun Vats noted on X that this update brings over AI features from the Fold 8: a new Finder with Google Search built in, My Fan Cam, and customized cards for Now Nudge.

The rollout covers South Korea, India, the U.K., Poland and Germany, with the U.S. left out. It's expected to reach U.S. users enrolled in the beta program soon. We'll follow up if more new features or major changes turn up.

It's a surprise that the Galaxy S26's One UI 9 beta has gone as far as a seventh round. The Galaxy S26 FE, which launched just yesterday, already shipped with the stable version of One UI 9. It's good that Samsung is taking its time to polish things, but it's easy to understand the impatience of Galaxy S26 flagship users watching a cheaper, later device get the stable version first. Here's hoping software updates aren't being held back purely as a card to sell more phones.

blocks.cap: Image credit Viture

blocks.x: Viture has teamed up with S-Game, the studio behind Phantom Blade Zero. The Phantom Beast XR glasses the two made together carry over the game's edgy mood intact.

This is Viture's first collaboration with a Chinese game studio, and its second overall after Cyberpunk 2077 Lumacyber. The Viture x Phantom Blade Zero Phantom Beast XR glasses can be preordered for $599 at viture.com and the IGN store, with a release date of October 29. The red and black XR lenses carry colors that blend traditional wuxia with punk fantasy.

According to Viture, the glasses carry 'dedicated artwork, engravings and iconography drawn from the game's sword-centered visual identity,' all applied on top of Viture's existing Beast product. The temples have a story too — they're modeled after Soul's sword, frozen mid-draw. The neck lanyard carries traditional wuxia patterns, paired with a pad drawn from martial arts.

blocks.cap: Image credit Viture

blocks.x: The collector's package that comes with a preorder is also packed with content. The packaging itself is designed to double as a display stand, engraved with artwork and Soul, the game's character, reaching to draw a sword. Inside the box are a '12.5cm Mo Shengquan sword miniature, a game art card brick, a sticker sheet, and a lens cloth.' Preorder or buy before November 5 and you get a scroll-style collector's map.

The case resembles a sword sheath. In the press release's own words, it's 'a triangular metal drawer wrapped in textured black leather that slides open rather than flipping, like a blade in the game.' The inside is crimson, with a texture meant to evoke a blade catching sunlight.

blocks.cap: Image credit Viture

blocks.x: I've never been this drawn to a pair of XR glasses. I'd had my eye on the game since before the PlayStation State of Play. I like the traditional design language S-Game brought, and red is already my favorite color. Add black and white on top of that, and there's no resisting it.

As noted earlier, Phantom Beast is a special edition built on Viture's base Beast XR glasses. It uses a Sony micro-OLED panel to project a 174-inch virtual screen from 4m away, with a smooth 120Hz refresh rate. On top of that come VisionPair 3DoF spatial tracking and Harman AudioEFX spatial sound. There's one more difference: the OSD menu has been redesigned to match Phantom Blade Zero's in-game UI.

Out of the box, you pick from five screen modes, including a 32:9 panoramic aspect ratio for PC gaming. Connect via USB-C and it works right away with Windows, macOS, iOS, Android and Steam Deck. To play Phantom Blade Zero on PlayStation, you'll need Viture's Pro Mobile Dock, which also supports PS5, PS4, Switch, Switch 2, Xbox Series X|S and Xbox One, plus other HDMI devices. The Mobile Dock Mini connects to Switch and Switch 2. Viture is the only XR glasses maker that supports Switch 2.

blocks.cap: Edited from a Weibo post by Lei Jun. Xiaomi's CEO checked out the AI Cube prototype with three Xring chips on board.

blocks.x: Xiaomi has unveiled a prototype mini PC, AI Cube, that runs AI models locally. It showed the device at its Xring chip technology conference on August 24.

AI Cube uses three chips together for local AI work: Xring O3, O100 and D100. Xiaomi says this three-chip setup delivers sustained performance of up to 150W. For comparison, the GMKtec EVO-X2 we reviewed, which uses the AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395, hits 140W briefly and tops out at 120W under sustained load. Unlike the Ryzen AI Max+ 395 lineup, Xiaomi keeps compute chips and AI chips separate.

Xring O3 is the main processor and first appears in the Xiaomi 18 Fold. It has a 10-core CPU, a 16-core G2-Ultra NX GPU, and a 200 TOPS NPU for AI tasks. Xiaomi says this chip supports its on-device model, MiMo.

O100 handles AI work where bandwidth matters most. Xiaomi says it uses 6nm 3D wafer-level stacking packaging with 28,672 effective data lines and near-memory compute bandwidth of up to 1.22 TB/s. D100, built for high-performance AI and intelligent driving, uses a 3nm process with a 20-core CPU and a 16-core NPU. It supports up to 160GB of unified memory and can deploy models with around 200 billion parameters locally.

blocks.cap: Lei Jun's Weibo. The Xiaomi AI Cube prototype with Xring O3, O100 and D100 on board (machine translation).

blocks.x: Small AI machines like the Nvidia DGX Spark or the Asus Ascent GX10 also support 200-billion-parameter models with 128GB of unified memory. Xiaomi chose a different path, packing three of its own Xring chips into a single box.

The chassis is unusual too: an aerospace-grade aluminum unibody with 33,874 precision CNC-drilled holes. For local AI use, it's described as running both a 120B and a 3B large model, switching between a fast system and a slow one.

blocks.cap: The Xiaomi AI Cube prototype, announced directly by Lei Jun (machine translation).

blocks.x: According to event materials, O100 and D100 are targeting commercial launch in 2027. Pricing and a launch timeline for AI Cube itself have not been announced.

I've always been torn on smart glasses and mixed-reality headsets. I get what Meta Quest is good for in gaming, but Apple Vision Pro never pulled me in. Then, before Xreal released its first Android XR glasses, I used the Xreal One Pro for a while, and two things became clear. This is the hardware that will make Android XR work, and Xreal is about to benefit hugely from Android XR too.

It wouldn't be strange if you don't know Xreal well. I knew the company's name, but glasses that float a screen in front of your face never seemed especially worth it. Then, once I heard Xreal was adopting Android XR, I figured I should try it at least once.

These days I plug the One Pro into a Galaxy Z Fold 7, a MacBook, or a RedMagic Astra 2 tablet. The setup couldn't be simpler. Whatever I'm doing, plugging a cable into the glasses brings up a 157-inch screen in front of my eyes. The size is adjustable. At first I wondered how useful this could really be, and one use case showed up right away: flying.

A huge screen that follows when you turn your head fits that situation perfectly. There's no comparison to a seatback screen, and it stays reasonably comfortable even after hours of use. That would have been unthinkable with a full headset — too big, and too strange-looking to others. The One Pro doesn't exactly look 'normal' either. It sticks out a bit from your face, and the cable hanging down makes it obvious what you're doing. Still, it takes up little space in a bag.

blocks.cap: It's far easier to carry around than a VR headset.

blocks.x: Image quality is pretty good. Like any screen in front of your eyes, it takes a moment to dial in the settings, but once you do, movies look great. Mirroring a MacBook screen turns it into a sizable work canvas that doesn't care if the person in front reclines their seat. It's not perfect. Xreal's 3DoF tracking, excellent on the ground, drifts a bit in flight, especially in turbulence.

It's also a problem that not everything works. When plugged into the RedMagic tablet, video apps like Fandango at Home and Google TV had issues. Google TV worked fine when switched from the Fold to DeX. 3D conversion mode didn't work at all on the RedMagic tablet, but it was quite good on the Fold.

That's also where Xreal's Aura, which runs Android XR, is meant to 'complete' this experience. The One Pro only magnifies whatever it's fed; its own controls and software are limited, so it can't do anything without an accessory device. There's a gesture-control accessory, and Xreal also sells its own Android phone that puts a UI on the glasses, but the missing piece is Android XR. Xreal seems to agree, and it's been vocal about pointing its future direction at Android XR. That doesn't mean the plug-in approach is going away — Aura will keep supporting it too.

There's clearly a place for the current form factor. Just having a big screen for watching movies or for a laptop on the move while traveling is good enough on its own. But the price matters. I wouldn't spend $600 on the Xreal One Pro just to get a bigger screen, but I would pay $299 for the A01+. The $450 Xreal 1S I tried at CES was barely different from the One Pro for the uses described here. Aura is coming later this year, while the One Pro, 1S and A01+ are already on sale.
Google is working on a new privacy dashboard that tracks AI agents installed and running on the phone.
It looks like Android 17 will let users check not just agents built with Spark but also agents that use third-party services.
This appears to be part of Android's next privacy dashboard work, which covers AI activity.
Agentic workflows are the next phase of AI. Users hand off complex tasks to assistants like Gemini, ChatGPT, and Claude, without having to step in at every stage.

Google has been talking about automation for months. The picture is everything handled on the Android device itself, from simple tasks like ordering food online to going beyond trip planning and finishing the booking too.

Gemini can hardly be the only app able to build agents and run them in the background. So it looks like Google is building a dedicated dashboard into Android 17 QPR2 Beta 4 to watch what agents are doing, especially what they're doing behind the scenes.

blocks.cap: The new 'Agents' entry in Android 17 QPR2 Beta 4's privacy controls

blocks.x: A new entry called 'Agents' has appeared under Security & Privacy > Privacy Controls in the latest Android 17 QPR2 beta. No agents show up in the list yet, but the description says this page is where you'll see “agents that can access information or perform tasks within apps.” It also prompts you to install an agent to have it show up here.

blocks.cap: The empty agent list, with no agents installed

blocks.x: Judging by the description, this section won't be tied only to AI agents built with Gemini Spark. There's room for other dedicated apps with agentic features to show up here too.

This change strongly looks like groundwork for Android Halo. Like the indicator lights already attached to the camera and microphone, it's a status indicator that signals when an agent is working in the background. Unveiled at Google I/O 2026, the indicator takes the shape of a compass rose (aka the sparkle), and was promised to arrive “later this year.”

Alongside the indicator, Google also briefly showed off a reworked privacy dashboard that tracks AI activity. That hasn't shipped either, but it has taken its first step by logging data that leaves the Private Compute Core, which handles on-device AI processing.
As early as next year, Apple will launch its first AI smart glasses. It's a device that carries Visual Intelligence and pulls Siri out into physical space. Here's everything reported so far.

blocks.cap: Apple smart glasses concept image

blocks.x: One thing first: these glasses are AI glasses, not AR glasses. With no display, voice and the camera become the main way to interact with them.

Thanks to the camera, Siri sees the same reality the user is looking at. It answers questions, fills in context, and translates signs. A feature first revealed in the macOS 26.7 leak — saving something as a photo and asking Siri to bring it up again later — is also likely to make it in.
A speaker is included too. It plays music and audio, so it's fair to think of it as open-ear headphones.

On the other hand, the ability to take ordinary photos and videos may be left out. That's according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman. Meta's Ray-Ban glasses recently became a focal point of privacy controversy, and Apple appears to want to avoid that path.
Unlike Meta, Apple isn't teaming up with an existing eyewear maker. According to Bloomberg, it's handling the design in-house and running several styles at once.

There are four directions: a large square frame resembling the Ray-Ban Wayfarer, a thin square design similar to the glasses Apple CEO Tim Cook wears, a bigger oval or round frame, and a small, refined oval or round option.
The material is reportedly acetate, sturdier and more premium than plastic. A few finishes are planned, including black, ocean blue, and light brown.

There's word that for the next generation, Apple is also considering pushing this product as a health device — adding a heart-rate sensor like the AirPods Pro 3, or layering on software features like the Apple Watch's Workout Buddy.
Beyond that, what more Apple might do on the health side is still fuzzy. Just don't expect any of that in the first generation.

Putting recent reports together, Apple will unveil the glasses at WWDC 2027 to give developers time to prepare, then ship them later that same year. That effectively means a September debut, sharing the stage with the 20th-anniversary all-glass iPhone.

Framework has released more information about the 192GB version of its small desktop PC. The model carries AMD's Ryzen AI 400 Gorgon Halo chip, and a dedicated product page laying out the specs has also gone live.

blocks.cap: The Framework Desktop, about to switch to a new version

blocks.x: The core of the new configuration is the increased memory bandwidth. It opens room for this single machine to handle AI workloads that would normally need several high-performance discrete GPUs. Up to 160GB of the total memory can be allocated to the integrated GPU.
The chip onboard is the AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 495 Pro. Memory bandwidth is 273GB/s, 6.6% higher than the Ryzen AI Max+ 395.

Faster LPDDR5X-8533 memory makes the difference. The Strix Halo-based SKU paired a 256-bit interface with LPDDR5X-8000, yielding roughly 256GB/s. The new Ryzen AI Max+ Pro 495 keeps the interface width at 256-bit but raises the theoretical bandwidth with faster LPDDR5X modules.
The chip itself hasn't changed much from the previous generation. The 16-core, 32-thread Zen 5 CPU configuration stays the same, and only the max boost clock rose, to 5.2GHz.
The integrated Radeon 8065S GPU also keeps its 40 RDNA 3.5 compute units, with the max clock rising slightly from 2.9GHz to 3.0GHz. The XDNA 2 NPU is listed at up to 55 TOPS.

blocks.cap: Framework Gorgon Halo teaser

blocks.x: The timing of the announcement is worth noting too. GMKtec recently let slip that it will show an Evo X5 Pro mini PC using the Ryzen AI Max+ Pro 495 at IFA 2026 in September. There was also mention that more details on Gorgon Halo could come around September 5, timed to IFA Berlin.
If so, it wouldn't be a stretch to expect Framework and several other makers to roll out Gorgon Halo SKUs around the same time.
For now, Framework has also listed its 192GB desktop as “coming soon.” Pricing isn't out yet. But with this much soldered LPDDR5X capacity, the top-tier configuration is bound to be expensive.
Meta has released Meta XR Operator, an experimental tool that lets AI coding agents build, test, debug, and even visually verify VR apps on their own.

blocks.cap: Meta Quest 3 (Image credit: Meta)

blocks.x: Bringing in AI agents has let developers read and write code faster, and hand off running tests or fixing bugs too. But the step of confirming that it actually works has always been missing.
The XR Operator Meta announced is an OpenXR API layer aimed at that gap. It ships as an experimental component in the Meta XR SDK (v205).

With XR Operator, an AI agent that supports the Model Context Protocol (MCP) can see, move through, and manipulate a VR app running in the Meta XR Simulator. According to Meta, it can build a Unity scene directly, run it, take screenshots, spot problems, fix them, and even verify on its own that the fix is correct.

Beyond quick iteration and debugging, natural-language testing is included too. A developer describes a test scenario in words, and the agent carries it out, attaching screenshots as evidence and reporting a pass or fail.

Meta said it ran early tests with teams developing on the Meta XR SDK, including Beat Games, maker of Beat Saber. One early example was building an interactive tic-tac-toe app in VR. The agent wrote the game logic, aimed a virtual controller at a square, pressed “A” to place a piece, and finished a full round until a win or loss was decided.

Of course, it's not a 'finished' verification tool yet. Several significant limitations remain. Operator XR can't hear sound, can't properly evaluate animation or movement, can't track individual fingers, and can't reliably catch subtle visual defects. Dynamic interaction is also hard. It's too slow to keep up in real time, so Meta itself says it works best with “static, deterministic scenarios.”

Its scope of operation is also still limited to the Meta XR Core SDK for Unity. But Meta added that for other engines using OpenXR, like Godot or Unreal Engine, you can download a standalone package and hook it up yourself.

I dislike the idea of AI flooding most of the creative space with cheap mass-produced output, but this still isn't the era of 'one prompt, one full game.' When that era arrives, it will bring a flood of volume that buries even the Gorilla Tag clones already cluttering the Horizon Store. World models like Google's Genie 3, built by DeepMind, already generate game scenes, if only in a limited way.

Right now, Meta is focused on AI tools that automate the mechanical parts of development — making a better shovel rather than digging for gold itself. The era of buying up VR studios and throwing multimillion-dollar budgets at exclusive content started with the Rift in 2016 and ended with the Quest earlier this year.

The picture it's drawing is this: small developers use these tools to make something fast, cheap, and still very good, filling the Horizon Store with exactly the kind of content Meta didn't want to fund directly. Meta Connect 2026, starting September 22, will be packed with sessions on AI-related game development, so expect to hear more there.

What most wearables do with heart rate or step counts, Atlas 1.0 wants to do with brain activity. The $499 device, made by a startup called Atlas, gathers data through a small EEG patch worn behind the ear and processes it in a smartphone app to tell you how you've been thinking and feeling throughout the day.

blocks.cap: Atlas 1.0, worn behind the ear

blocks.x: It looks like a small round black or white puck that sits on an adhesive pad, and it's rechargeable. Besides recording brain activity via EEG, it also tracks electrodermal activity, head movement, and what the company calls "vocalization activity" — voice patterns, not the content of speech. Unlike traditional EEG equipment, which requires the user to stay still for an accurate reading, the company says this device is designed to tolerate movement. The goal, it says, is to create "a longitudinal record of how your brain responds to real life, far more meaningful than a single test or an isolated brain scan."

Atlas turns this information into three real-time metrics you can follow in the app throughout the day: Presence, Stress and Energy Burn. Presence shows whether your attention is turned inward or outward — whether you were really present in a conversation with a friend, for instance. Stress is your current level of psychological stress, and Energy Burn shows where your "mental resources" are being spent.

blocks.cap: Atlas 1.0's charging case

blocks.x: You get a notification when a metric swings sharply. But to get a sharper picture, you also have to pitch in: syncing your calendar and workout logs, or tagging the times when a metric changed. Atlas claims that combining this information reveals the habits and conditions under which you think and feel best. Software features and adhesive-pad refills come with a separate $30-a-month membership.

How accurate those insights really are remains to be seen. Atlas is explicit that the $499 Atlas 1.0 Pioneer Edition is a "limited first batch" "made for people ready to understand, at the source, what moves their own mind." At the very least, its way of measuring is different. Wearables that claim to read stress through heart-rate sensors already exist, but that's essentially an educated guess, and it mainly captures physical stress. Atlas 1.0 has its own limits, relying only on brain activity. Even so, it can give a clearer picture of how you're feeling right now.

blocks.cap: Pixel Watch 5 gains several new features in the September update.

blocks.x: Google has released the first major Wear OS 7 update for the Pixel Watch 5, a watch priced at $399 on Amazon. Google said it will take a few more weeks before all users can download it. A notification appears on the watch screen once the rollout reaches a device.

The September update puts most of its weight on Google Gemini. After the update, the voice assistant works offline for tasks like turning on a timer or starting a workout. Google also fixed the assistant so it appears more reliably when the watch is raised near the mouth. Gemini now reaches deeper into personal data such as the calendar and email to make its answers more accurate. It can also suggest information proactively. If a message asks about a planned meal time, for example, Gemini finds it in the calendar and shows it right away.

Google Health now shows GPS-recorded routes from runs or rides more precisely. The 「double pinch」 gesture, made by quickly touching the thumb and index finger together twice on the hand wearing the Pixel Watch 5, also gained more uses.

Going forward, this gesture opens notifications, scrolls through Gemini answers, switches weather maps, scans workout results, and changes Google Maps screens. Rotating the wrist outward now works as 「back」 anywhere. One-handed operation becomes considerably simpler.

blocks.cap: Mac mini and Mac Studio. Image courtesy of MacRumors

blocks.x: The Information reports that Apple's unusually timed announcement of new Mac mini and Mac Studio models this week was driven by unexpected corporate demand for AI hardware.

Apple usually releases new Macs in the fall, closer to October or November. That's why this week's announcement, coming just ahead of new iPhones, stands out as especially early. The Information attributes the early launch to an AI boom that has been driving Mac Studio and Mac mini sales.
Apple prominently highlighted the ability to cluster multiple Mac Studios together to run large frontier AI models, a feature aimed more at companies and developers than everyday consumers.

There were signs of this shift toward corporate buyers back in June too. At the “Business at the Park” event, attended by executives from Ford, Disney, and Anthropic, Apple put the Mac mini and Mac Studio front and center, and the Mac mini was reportedly the “darling” of the day.

Even so, the corporate demand that poured in for high-performance desktop Macs caught Apple off guard. According to the report, Apple had no engineering team dedicated to enterprise customers, no staff handling developer relations, and no enterprise AI strategy.

Companies that came looking to buy private cloud compute infrastructure were turned down. Apple instead relies on partners like WebAI and Mount Thor, which provide AI tools and runtime environments on top of its hardware.

The surge in demand for Macs to run AI models has coincided with a global memory supply shortage. Several configurations of the Mac mini and Mac Studio have been out of stock for months. As Apple's high-end configurations become harder to find, some corporate customers are shifting to other hardware, such as Nvidia's DGX Spark, a small AI desktop similar in size to the Mac mini that debuted late last year.

blocks.cap: Relay Q. Image courtesy of Relay

blocks.x: How much do you hate typing? With the rise of large language models, speech-to-text technology has advanced quickly. Whisper Flow, which joins meetings to summarize discussions, and Google's on-device dictation on the latest Pixel both go beyond simple transcription. They filter out filler words, clean up unstructured thoughts, and even mediate conversations that mix multiple languages.

A new startup has jumped in. Unlike competitors focused on software, Relay builds a portable, dedicated microphone for high-quality voice input anywhere. Based in London, the company was founded by two Nothing alumni: Cookie Shi, former head of AI and services, and Raymond Zhu, former hardware product manager. The software launched today, and the hardware, called Relay Q, arrives in early 2027.

Zhu says he “typed” most of his work messages using Whisper Flow during his time at Nothing. It helped him work through his thoughts, but speaking out loud in the office was a problem. “In the office, I could never find the right volume for input. Whisper too quietly and the Mac can't understand you; speak loudly and the person next to you hears everything.” During a video call, he added, holding an earbud up to his mouth: “This is a situation that needs dedicated hardware.”

blocks.cap: Image courtesy of Relay

blocks.x: Relay launches as macOS-only. Windows, iOS, and Android are planned, since the company sees desktop dictation as the most complex case. During setup, you pick a shortcut key, with Fn as the default. Hold that key down and speak in any text field with the cursor active, and Relay transcribes it. The speech recognition engine is a Google Gemini model.

It also performs context-aware actions it calls skills. Tell it to send a Slack message to a colleague, and it opens the app, finds the recipient, and drafts the message. In the author's testing, the Slack skill often got stuck, while creating a Google Calendar event worked well. In exchange, it needs broad permissions. The microphone is a given, and the skills only work if you let Relay take a screenshot every time it turns on. Data is stored on the user's device, where it can be edited or deleted directly; during processing, it passes through Relay's servers to Google's servers, but Relay doesn't keep it. Giving an AI model eyes onto the operating system comes with privacy and security trade-offs, much like Microsoft Recall.

Transcription quality isn't as impressive as the Rambler feature on the Pixel 11 series. It doesn't catch every word, and punctuation is sometimes off. If you misspeak and correct yourself, it does trim out the unnecessary part. It adds emoji too, but inconsistently: asking for a heart emoji works correctly, but asking it to add one at the end of a sentence made it spell out “heart emoji” in text instead.

blocks.cap: Image courtesy of Relay

blocks.x: Relay Q is a cylindrical device with a microphone on one end. Press and hold the top while speaking, and Relay activates on your computer or phone; you can also detach the button from the cylinder and clip it to your shirt. Seen from above, the microphone looks like the letter Q, which is where the name comes from. Double-tapping sends a message, and Zhu says it can pick up even a very quiet whisper. “Throughout building this product, one question stayed in my head: how much of a day can you get through without touching the keyboard?”

The idea of wearing a dedicated microphone for voice input isn't new on its own. Last year, Sandbar unveiled the Stream Ring, and a few months later, Pebble showed the Index 01. Both are whisper-into rings that are just now starting to ship to early buyers. Relay also considered a ring but dropped the idea, reasoning that there are already plenty of smart rings. It's priced at $150, which includes a year of software access; after that, it's $15 a month.

When Google launched Google Pics last May, it described it as a rival to services like Canva. The app handles image generation and design together, but until now only a small group of testers could use it. There's good news for anyone who's been waiting.

blocks.cap: Google Pics, as unveiled by Google

blocks.x: Google says Google Pics has moved past limited access and is now open to everyone. That includes subscribers to Google AI Pro and Ultra, Google AI Pro for Education users, and Workspace users on the Business Standard, Business Plus, Enterprise Standard and Enterprise Plus plans.

For anyone encountering it for the first time: Google Pics lets you create designs from a blank page or edit images you already have. Using image segmentation, you can select, move and resize a specific person or object within a photo. It also lets you edit or translate just the text inside an image while leaving the design and fonts untouched.

You can share what you make with others, so a friend or colleague can edit the same image with you at the same time. Pics is also built into Google Docs and Slides, letting you refine images right inside a document. Drive integration is coming "within a few weeks," according to the company.

This announcement comes well after competing service Canva was integrated into Gemini and Google's AI Mode search. For anyone who wants a smart image design tool within the Google ecosystem, there's now one more option.

Meta has released its first real-time audio model, Muse Voice Transcribe. The company says it handles dictation and transcription for more than 20 speakers and smoothly captures multiple languages mixed together at once.

blocks.cap: Muse Voice Transcribe, as unveiled by Meta Superintelligence Lab

blocks.x: Mark Zuckerberg, back on X for the first time in three years, posted a demo handling multiple speakers and multiple languages at once. In the video, the transcription automatically distinguishes who's speaking and follows along when the language changes. It even catches "code-switching," where the language shifts within a single sentence.

"Muse Voice Transcribe is MSL's first real-time audio perception model, and it's rolling out starting today. It's SOTA in streaming speech recognition, and it handles speaker separation and endpoint detection within a single model."

"The model decides on its own when to listen. It waits a bit longer on difficult words and commits quickly on easy ones. Adaptive latency predicts tokens one at a time to improve accuracy," Zuckerberg explained. "It holds up on messy, real-world audio. It was trained on more than 70 languages and validated on 25 at launch. It handles code-switching mid-sentence, and it can handle sessions with more than 20 speakers talking for over an hour."

This announcement comes less than a week after Google Gemini 3.5 Transcribe, which touted similar capabilities. Google is building its own audio model into Android, and later into Chrome as well. It's not yet known whether Meta plans to put Muse Voice Transcribe into its flagship services.

For now, the new model can be tried in the recently released Meta AI Mac app. Because that Mac app also runs the voice features for other apps, Muse Voice Transcribe handles dictation for other services too. Developers can call it as Muse Code or through the Meta Model API, priced at $3 per 1,000 minutes of audio. A demo version is also up on Meta's research blog.

Muse Voice Transcribe is the latest release from Meta Superintelligence Lab (MSI), which has been churning out new models and tools one after another. In the past few weeks alone, the team has also put out its first dedicated coding agent, an open-weight model, and the Meta AI Mac app mentioned above.

Along with new soundbars and headphones, Sonos has also announced an app update and a major change to the OS that runs across its entire product line. It's the biggest software news from the company since the 2024 app-update disaster, when Sonos rushed out an app to match new Ace headphone features, leaving out major functionality and shipping it full of bugs. The fallout cost Patrick Spence his job as CEO, and 2025 passed without a single new product.

blocks.cap: Sonos 27, as unveiled by Sonos

blocks.x: The OS now gets a version number every year, and this one is named Sonos 27. The biggest, and also most anticipated, new feature is letting AI handle control of the Sonos system. Sonos 27 lets you connect ChatGPT and, really, "any outside AI assistant or agent." That means you can have the AI you're already using take over system operations without having to stop what you're doing.

Sonos says it runs its own public MCP (model context protocol) server that any AI can find and connect to. Once connected, you can mostly make it do what you'd expect — play a specific song, move audio between speakers or groups, adjust volume. It's fair to see this as an extension of the decision, a few years back, to put Alexa and the Google Assistant on its speakers.

Sonos also previewed Sonos Custom Agents, a feature that lets users build agents with a "model, persona and voice" of their own choosing. A Sonos 27 voice assistant was also mentioned, described as "a proprietary assistant built for music and mood curation," but honestly, it's not yet clear how that differs from the bare-bones Sonos voice assistant that already exists.

There's more to see beyond the AI story. 'Sonos Fabric' is a new feature where products "sense" other devices in the same system and configure themselves accordingly. In practice, a speaker's role changes depending on where it's placed. Put two Move 2 or Play speakers behind your couch, for instance, and they'll automatically become the surround speakers for your soundbar. It uses high-frequency tones to locate the speakers and switch their roles, with no input needed from the user.

Another feature under Fabric is for the just-announced Ace Ultra headphones. Headphone linking connects the Ace Ultra to a Sonos system almost like another speaker, handing off audio that had been coming from the speakers to the headphones instead. It will be offered as early access when the Ace Ultra launches on September 29.

The app has also been redesigned. Home, system and search tabs stay persistently visible, and you can pin the speakers you use most. These are features that have been in testing all summer, but they'll become the default once the September 8 update rolls out. iOS lock-screen controls are also included. There are now presets too, letting you save a group of speakers along with content and volume settings and turn them all on at once.

For Apple users, there's a virtual volume knob you control by twisting two fingers on the screen to adjust system volume. The iPad app has been rebuilt for the bigger screen, and it now works with the Shortcuts app, so you can trigger automations with Siri. Sonos 27 is rolling out to every piece of hardware currently running the S2 platform. The new app navigation, early-access MCP features and portable surround feature all go live on September 8.
Acer unveiled the Aspire G 3D 16 laptop at IFA 2026 in Berlin. It offers gamers, 3D artists, architects, and video editors glasses-free stereoscopic images and video.

blocks.cap: The Acer Aspire G 3D 16 displays games, movies, and photos in true 3D on its 3,840 x 2,400 120Hz IPS screen.

blocks.x: It pairs a 16-core, 32-thread AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395 with up to 128GB of LPDDR5x-8000 memory and up to 2TB of M.2 PCIe Gen 4 SSD storage. The 3,840 x 2,400 120Hz IPS display reaches 450 nits of brightness and covers 100% of the DCI-P3 color space, driven by the integrated AMD Radeon 8060S GPU.
When displaying 3D images and video in games and other compatible apps, the resolution switches to 1,920 x 2,400. The pre-installed SpatialLabs 3D Hub handles that switch.

Running Windows 11 Home, this laptop can also run large local AI models like OpenAI's gpt-oss-120b or OpenClaw, thanks to its large maximum RAM capacity and a processor that delivers up to 126 TOPS of AI compute. The NPU alone provides 50 TOPS.

It includes a 5MP IR eye-tracking webcam and two 2-watt speakers. Ports consist of two USB4 Type-C, one USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-A, two USB 3.2 Gen 1 Type-A, one HDMI 2.1, plus an SD-4.0 card reader, an audio jack, and an RJ-45 jack. Wireless is handled by Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 5.4.
A 99.9Wh battery sits inside the 355 × 264.9 × 19.3mm chassis, which weighs 1.8kg.
Pricing and release date for the Aspire G 3D 16 (AG3D16-81M) will be announced later.
After first unveiling the Oryon CPU that will power its next flagship Snapdragon chip, Qualcomm has now revealed its next-generation Adreno Neural Fusion GPU.

This SoC is the first chipset to place dedicated AI GPU cores inside the graphics pipeline. Blocks called 'Matrix Cores' each take up residence in one of the new Adreno GPU's three 1.45GHz slices. Qualcomm describes these cores as dedicated local hardware for “running advanced AI models directly within the graphics pipeline.”

The Adreno GPU also gets an 18MB HPM (High Performance Memory) cache. Modest in size alone, but Qualcomm says this memory “attaches large, low-latency memory directly to the GPU, keeping tile-based rendering, frame buffers, and compute workloads inside the graphics subsystem.”

The two components together make up the Adreno Neural Fusion GPU. For users, turning this technology on improves power efficiency by 40%. Keeping AI computation close to the GPU reduces latency and raises efficiency, according to the press release.

The trick lies in keeping the work close to the silicon. Adreno Matrix Cores process AI models right where the graphics are happening, while the 18MB Adreno High Performance Memory holds heavy data like tiles, frame buffers, and compute workloads on-chip. Fewer round trips to system memory mean lower latency and better efficiency — and longer gaming sessions as a result.
For now, Unity and Unreal Engine have already integrated Qualcomm's Neural Fusion stack.

The result shows up in graphics quality. In Qualcomm's words, it's “AI rendering embedded directly in the Snapdragon graphics pipeline for upscaled imagery, stable frame rates, and improved efficiency.”
Snapdragon Summit runs from September 22 to 24. More details about the new chip's NPU are expected there.

blocks.cap: Image credit: Camera Intelligence

blocks.x: AI camera startup Camera Intelligence announced it is adding Generative Video Editing to its Micro Four Thirds mirrorless camera, Caira. It says it's the first company to put a video generation model into a mirrorless camera system.

The feature runs in the Caira app and works only on video shot with Caira — it can't generate new AI video from scratch. A private beta opens first for existing customers, and it will later join the paid Caira Studio software package in fall 2026. Pricing hasn't been announced yet.

“Last year we were the first mirrorless camera to edit photos with generative AI, and we learned a lot from the conversations that followed,” said Camera Intelligence CEO and co-founder Vishal Kumar. “After shipping Caira this year, the majority of backers who responded to our survey said generative video editing would be useful. That was a clear signal to actually build this idea.”

The feature is built on Google's Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash and Runway's Aleph 2.0. Camera Intelligence is the first company to embed a video generation model directly into a mirrorless camera system. In the Caira app, users apply templates to already-shot video and give natural-language instructions to add on-screen effects and camera movements on the spot.
We reviewed Caira last year. It was an odd but impressive object that paired proper Micro Four Thirds hardware with a smartphone's simplicity. It attaches to an iPhone via MagSafe.

Inside is a Micro Four Thirds sensor, driven by Qualcomm and Google silicon. Its real party trick is Google's 'Nano Banana,' an on-device editor sitting behind a $7-a-month paywall that also unlocks smart voice control. Editing is fast and the results are good enough that there's no need to open a laptop.

Video editing runs on a curated template library. It can color-correct or mimic drone-like sweeps and complex camera paths. At launch, there are four templates: Relight, Reframe, Camera Motion, and Set Extension. Conversational editing refines things further. Output comes in 720p or 1080p, and generation takes 1 to 3 minutes depending on resolution.

Since there's no text-to-video capability, every edit starts from video shot with Caira. The generated video is saved as a separate file from the original and carries Google's SynthID watermark, revealing it as AI-generated.

This Generative Video Editing feature is part of the Caira Studio app, arriving in fall 2026. The app will bundle it with existing image-editing features and one more feature that hasn't been revealed yet. The private beta opens today, and existing Caira customers can sign up to take part.

Camera Intelligence seems to be reassuring filmmakers that while it's bringing generative AI right up next to the act of shooting, it has no intention of eliminating the shooting itself. That condition keeps Caira tethered to photography. Whatever AI layers on afterward, it still starts with a person behind the camera deciding what to shoot.

blocks.cap: Phil Nickinson / Digital Trends

blocks.x: Smart glasses started out a decade ago as an awkward picture of wearable computing that Google pushed out too hastily, but more recently they've rolled into becoming a public nuisance. Norway wants to rein that in. According to AFP, the country's Digitalization Minister Karianne Tung said the government is weighing stricter regulation of smart glasses from companies like Meta and Snap.

Tung pointed to a clear trend of AI, cameras, and microphones being bundled into everyday objects, including glasses and headphones. The goal is to stop people from being filmed in public without consent using that gear. The rules under review could even include banning facial recognition features that identify people in public spaces. There's talk that some wearable makers are putting that capability into their next devices.

blocks.cap: Andy Boxall / Digital Trends

blocks.x: Civil society groups have raised similar concerns. Unlike smartphones, camera-equipped wearables blur the boundaries of consent, because the signal that recording is happening isn't easy to notice. It isn't a new worry. Google once told Glass Explorers not to become a 'Glasshole,' a term it coined itself to describe wearers who film others without asking. The recent popularity of Meta's Ray-Ban smart glasses has simply pushed the issue into the mainstream.
Tung said she would assemble a panel of experts to advise on stronger privacy protections. No formal legislative timeline has been announced yet.

Norway's crackdown isn't happening in a vacuum. Local bans aimed at filling the gaps manufacturers have left are already spreading. Meta built in a software safeguard that stops recording if the small LED indicator light is covered, but users bypass it with simple tricks like electrical tape or physical modifications.

So private venues have moved first. Several nightclubs, performance venues, and fitness chains across Europe and the U.S. now ban camera-equipped wearables. Schools have also sounded the alarm after reports that students secretly filmed friends and teachers with smart glasses.

The core of the problem lies beyond the hardware. It's a product of the industry tilting quickly toward always-on AI recording. The multimodal visual analysis that today's wearables tout only works by continuously processing real-time data about their surroundings. Add facial recognition on top, and these devices become tools for constant surveillance of public spaces.

That's why I welcome Norway's approach. We left social media platforms unregulated for years before even attempting oversight, and we're still dealing with the fallout. Tech companies have treated public anonymity as acceptable collateral damage in their race for new hardware and features. If companies won't build proper safeguards themselves, regulators need to draw the line instead.
Google Photos has been added to the list of in-house apps that Gemini Spark controls. Google says its personal agent can handle “complex, multi-step tasks” on a user's photo library.

blocks.cap: Gemini Spark

blocks.x: Here's what it can do: find photos and videos by subject, place, date, or event, and ask it to pick the best shots or filter out duplicates. It can touch up image quality, apply simple corrections, and make collages or stylized images. Edits are always saved to Google Photos as a new copy.

Albums work the same way. It can create a new album, shared or private, and fill it with chosen photos. Links to the album it creates get sent through connected apps like Gmail, Google Docs, and Messages. You can also schedule recurring tasks, like making a monthly highlights album or gathering receipt photos separately, and it can pull text out of images too.

Combined with Spark's existing features, like scheduling and background cleanup, this kind of instruction becomes possible: “Every weekend, pick the best food photos, make a collage, and put it in a new album called 'What My Camera Ate This Week.'”
It can also hand off information found in photos to other connected apps like Gmail or Workspace: “Match my local summer concert photos against my Google Calendar schedule. Which night can I go?”

Google also gave examples of chaining several actions together: pick the 15 best photos from last week's Hawaii trip, touch up the beach shots, put them in a shared album called 'Aloha 2026,' and draft an email with the link; or gather recent block-party photos and videos into a 'Summer Block Party' album and prepare an email to send to the neighborhood group.
Safeguards are built in too. A copy is made before any edit, and new albums default to private. Spark asks for permission before sharing an album or sending an email.
It is rolling out gradually over several weeks to Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in the United States.

Lenovo is a company that brings concept laptops to IFA in Berlin. The two it brought this year focused on productivity and portability, and looked closer to something you could actually buy than past concepts have.

blocks.cap: Lenovo Project Swan (Photo: Tom's Hardware)

blocks.x: First, Project AeroBlade is a 14-inch laptop. In the press release's words, it “redesigned every component around mobility.” It drops the fan for Frore Systems' AirJet solid-state cooling, in which a piezoelectric membrane vibrates at an ultrasonic frequency inaudible to human ears. Four AirJet Mini modules are packed in here, three more than the single one in the Intel Wildcat Lake reference design seen at Computex this year.

blocks.cap: Lenovo Project AeroBlade (Photo: Tom's Hardware)

blocks.x: Frore Systems' latest AirJet Mini pulls out 7.5 watts per module, so AeroBlade actively cools 30 watts in total. That matches well with the Intel Lunar Lake chip Lenovo put in this concept, which has a TDP of 17 to 30 watts.

Thanks to a small motherboard and a magnesium-aluminum frame, thickness came down to 0.39 inches (10mm) and weight to under 1.83 pounds (830 grams). Being this thin means the only ports are USB-C/Thunderbolt 4, but there are three of them, along with an OLED screen and Wi-Fi 7.

blocks.cap: AeroBlade, cooled fanlessly by four AirJet Mini units (Photo: Tom's Hardware)

blocks.x: The other machine is Project Swan, Lenovo's return to rollable screens, this time more restrained and realistic than before. It sits inside what looks like an ordinary 14-inch ThinkBook chassis, and pressing a button unfurls the screen to 17 inches at 16:9, with a resolution of 2850 x 1672.

blocks.cap: Project Swan unfurling to 17 inches at the press of a button (Photo: Tom's Hardware)

blocks.x: It's obviously not a light, thin 14-inch machine. It weighs 3.53 pounds (1.6kg) and measures 0.7 inches (17.9mm) thick. That added bulk is concentrated in the lid, which houses the rolling mechanism and bezels that spread out to the sides. The motor noise was loud enough that it would be hard to overlook in a finished product. On the other hand, it never jammed through repeated opening and closing, which is unusual for a concept like this.

If the screen mechanism could shrink just a bit more, this looks ready to cross over into an actual product. Even if the bulk isn't appealing, the idea of carrying around a 14-inch machine and unfurling it to 17 inches when you need it is quite tempting.

If you're always short on AI tokens, and you have a few PCs at home sitting on idle GPUs, this will catch your ear. Nvidia's pitch is to put those idle cycles to work, saving on cloud token costs while keeping the workload inside the house.

The tool, unveiled at IFA 2026, is called the Personal AI Router, or PAIR for short. It takes subtasks split off by the agent on your main PC and distributes them to systems with spare GPU capacity on your home network.

blocks.cap: Personal AI Router (PAIR) (Image: Nvidia)

blocks.x: Here's Nvidia's explanation: give a local agent one goal, and a central agent breaks that goal into several subtasks. If all of those tasks pile onto the same GPU, they compete for space and the whole thing slows down, much more than if each sub-agent had its own dedicated compute node.

PAIR scatters that work across the home network instead. In a house with plenty of spare GPUs, each participating system takes on one subtask and sends the result back to the main node, which creates room for a large job to finish faster.

Of course, other PCs aren't always idle. Their owners game, do creative work, or use the GPU for their own AI tasks. If someone reclaims their GPU, PAIR is designed to absorb that change smoothly. It doesn't reserve other people's PC capacity in advance; instead, it's built to expand and shrink to match whatever resources happen to be free at the moment.

Because there's no telling when spare cycles will show up, the quality of a PAIR cluster isn't guaranteed. But for a long job without a tight deadline, it still beats cramming an entire agent swarm onto a single node.

Setup is fairly simple. You set up a proxy that an AI front end like LM Studio or Ollama connects to, and PAIR distributes work across the network's nodes and returns results to that original app. Each participating node also needs PAIR installed alongside Ollama or LM Studio. Node discovery uses mDNS, falling back to IP addresses if that fails. Nvidia says participating nodes don't need to have the same model loaded.

Requirements are a DGX Spark (or other GB10) box, or a GeForce RTX 20-series or newer graphics card. For inference, Macs with M4-series chips or later are also supported. Clients are available for Windows, macOS, and Linux.

Three months ago, Nvidia unveiled the RTX Spark “superchip” along with a handful of laptops built to use it. Even with plenty of questions left unanswered, it looked like a moment that would mark a turning point in PC history.

At IFA 2026 in Berlin, I got my first hands-on look at one of those laptops. Mini desktop PCs built around the RTX Spark were also announced there. Demand for running agent workflows like OpenClaw on a personal computer keeps growing, and these new PCs are built squarely for that demand.

blocks.cap: An RTX Spark-based AI PC unveiled at IFA 2026

blocks.x: The one shown in person was the Lenovo Yoga 9n 2-in-1. It's a 16-inch laptop with a 360-degree hinge, and its finish makes clear it's aimed squarely at the MacBook Pro. The OLED touch display runs at 2880 x 1800 resolution and 120Hz, with six-speaker sound and a 9.2-megapixel webcam on top.

blocks.cap: Lenovo Yoga 9n 2-in-1 (Photo: Les Shu)

blocks.x: It's 0.69 inches thick, only 0.03 inches more than the 16-inch MacBook Pro. What makes that possible is Nvidia's Arm-based chip, which combines up to a 20-core Grace CPU and up to a 6,144-core Blackwell RTX GPU with shared memory into a single SoC. Going by core count alone, the built-in GPU's performance falls somewhere between today's laptop RTX 5070 Ti and RTX 5080.

Lenovo also prepared a 15-inch Yoga Pro 9n. Its display is 2560 x 1600, and its thinnest point is 0.66 inches. A unique feature of this model is a force pad touchpad you can write and draw on directly with a stylus. Memory tops out at 64GB on the 9n 2-in-1 and 128GB on the Pro.

Lenovo isn't the only one with RTX Spark laptops coming this fall. The Dell XPS 16, Asus ProArt P16, and Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra are all lined up. In the 14-inch category, the HP OmniBook X 14 is still the only one.

blocks.cap: Acer SFF RTX Spark (Photo: Acer)

blocks.x: On the mini PC side, Acer has released the SFF RTX Spark. It packs “petaflops of AI performance” and up to 128GB of memory into a body about the size of a Mac mini, and it uses the same superchip as the Asus ProArt Mini PC unveiled earlier in the summer.

blocks.cap: Asus ProArt Mini PC (Photo: Asus)

blocks.x: There's also the Lenovo ThinkCentre X Ultra, which uses AMD, with a Ryzen Max+ Pro 495 and 128GB of memory, starting at $3,699. What's left in the end is price. RAM has never been this expensive and this necessary at once. Considering that a 128GB MacBook Pro now costs $6,139, this isn't likely to come cheap either.

Medical device maker Stryker announced this week that its Apple Vision Pro app was used in what could be seen as a milestone surgery. The headset software, SportSuite Vision, was used in a hip arthroscopy at Duke Health—its first use in an actual clinical setting. The FDA granted De Novo approval on July 17.

blocks.cap: An Apple Vision Pro used in the operating room

blocks.x: Ever since Apple introduced its mixed-reality headset, the question of who it's actually for has lingered. The first model wasn't built for a mass audience, and neither was the more powerful M5 version we tried last year. Still, Vision Pro seemed to point toward an interesting future at home, waiting for the right situation to arrive.

Complex surgery is close to that situation. In mixed reality, clinicians can interact directly with the patient in front of them while also viewing data and tools in digital space. In this first SportSuite Vision surgery, the surgeon kept Stryker's orthopedic surgical planning tools, arthroscopic footage, and CT images on hand throughout the hip arthroscopy.

“Spatial computing let me arrange key clinical information to fit my workflow and check it right there within the sterile field,” said Chad Mather III, the orthopedic surgeon at Duke Health who performed the surgery with Vision Pro. “The OR setup became more comfortable and streamlined, and the information I needed stayed in view.”

Given the cost of the headset and how demanding the software development is, it'll be a while before your local doctor is wearing one during a checkup. Apple's reported cuts to much of the Vision Pro team last month aren't a good sign for mainstream adoption, either. Still, when it comes to judging what mixed-reality headsets are good for, this kind of application is exactly what could put Vision Pro in its rightful place.

At IFA 2026, Anker unveiled a new smart home hub. Its name, grandly enough, is MindBase. It looks like a tower, similar to a common Wi-Fi router. The company built on AnkaAI, the voice assistant previously limited to its Soundcore devices, expanding it significantly, marking Anker's first head-on attempt to compete in the smart home market dominated by Apple, Google, and Amazon.

MindBase doesn't stop at being a smart home controller. It includes expandable NAS-style local storage and on-device AI that processes security camera footage directly on the unit. Alongside the launch, Anker shared other news: it will retire its sub-brands Eufy and Soundcore, folding everything under the Anker name soon.

MindBase is a Matter 1.5 controller, meaning it can single-handedly act as the brain for Matter-compatible devices. Connect smart bulbs, garage door openers, robot vacuums, and various sensors, then give commands to AnkaAI by voice. It also ties into Apple Home, Google Home, Amazon Alexa, and Home Assistant. Brett White, Anker's PR manager, who spoke at the IFA booth, explained that in this role MindBase behaves like a Hue Bridge or SwitchBot Hub, handing off already-connected Matter devices to whichever platform the user chooses.

blocks.cap: MindBase with the top removed (Photo: Wes Davis / Gizmodo)

blocks.x: What stood out most was the smart home assistant side. Anker said it initially designed MindBase as a security-focused device, similar to its own HomeBase. For example, if it notices you come home around the same time every day, it proactively suggests turning off camera alerts. From there the scope widened, and now it can connect to any Matter device and control it either through the Anker app or by voice.

As a security camera hub, it's essentially a souped-up version of the Eufy HomeBase. It accepts 16 wireless security cameras, and connecting an external PoE switch adds four more wired cameras. Anyone coming from a HomeBase S380 can migrate their stored footage over to MindBase.

blocks.cap: The removable AI processing chip (Photo: Wes Davis / Gizmodo)

blocks.x: The on-device security AI runs Anker's own LLM on a 26 TOPS chip. For reference, Microsoft's Copilot PC requirement is at least 40 TOPS. Anker says this AI agent “evaluates events in real time to assess risk, and responds with observation, lighting, voice warnings, and active deterrence.” The company also plans to follow up with agents for home energy management and for managing cleaning devices and appliances. The AI processing chip sits near the hard drive slot on top of the device and can be easily pulled out, so it could be swapped later.

blocks.cap: Ports on the back of MindBase (Photo: Wes Davis / Gizmodo)

blocks.x: Last is the NAS. White said it's a proper NAS that not only stores files but also runs apps. Built-in flash storage is 64GB, and you can add up to 48TB more using 2.5-inch or 3.5-inch hard drives or SSDs. According to the company, you can search stored photos, recordings, and documents using natural language, and personal data never leaves the device for the cloud. There's no subscription fee either.

Anker also sells a MindBase security kit. It pairs the newly unveiled Eufy TrackLight Cam S1 and Video Doorbell S4 with entry and motion sensors and the Smart Security Shield. The Shield is a sensor that Anker says “detects strangers up to 15 meters away, and recognizes family members up to 30 meters away using DSKey digital credentials.” Here, “family” refers to members who have installed the Anker app and registered themselves to the home.
Pricing and availability haven't been announced yet.
The Gemini overlay on Android now has a multitasking option. Minimizing it leaves behind a floating bubble shortcut.

blocks.cap: The Gemini overlay on the Pixel 11 Pro

blocks.x: A “Minimize” button has been added to the top of the overlay. Right after you enter a prompt, it sits in the center; once an answer appears, it moves to the right side of the pill-shaped container.

blocks.cap: The minimize button that appears after entering a prompt

blocks.x: Tapping it collapses the overlay into a bubble bearing the spark logo. Google describes it this way: “Use Gemini even while multitasking. Tap to expand. Drag to move it or close it.”

blocks.cap: The Gemini bubble that remains on screen after collapsing

blocks.x: That said, the bubble locks into one of six fixed positions rather than landing anywhere you like. There's also a bug where the bubble snaps back to the bottom right every time you minimize it.

blocks.cap: The bubble floating over another app

blocks.x: Once the full answer has appeared, tapping outside the sheet sends it back into a bubble. Using the system's back gesture closes the whole overlay, and you can also drag it closed.

It's clearly faster than opening the Gemini app, going into the side panel, and returning to the conversation. People use it to fire off a question, minimize it, and do something else instead of waiting idle for the answer. For a richer experience, you can also apply Android 17's system bubbles feature to the Gemini app.
The minimize button and the Gemini bubble are rolling out broadly to Android today.

The Ringverse iKairos is a modular AI wearable that comes in the form of a desktop robot companion. You can also detach it from the body and wear it as an AI pendant around your neck. Its purpose is to gather contextual data and surface suggestions that are actually useful to the user.
Neither AI pendants nor desktop AI robots are new. But at IFA 2026, the Singapore-based company Ringverse brought out a modular wearable that can sit on a desk and also hang around your neck.

The product is named iKairos. Thanks to its modular design, it learns about the user's life from multiple angles. On the desk, it observes and responds like any other desktop AI robot. When you head out, you simply pop it out of the robot body and clip it onto a necklace.

blocks.cap: iKairos shown at IFA 2026 (Photo: Adamya Sharma / Android Authority)

blocks.x: That's how iKairos gathers contextual data about the user across multiple environments. The collected data feeds into Ringverse's AI operating system, LifeOS, which then picks out suggestions that are relevant and, hopefully, useful.
Here's the example Ringverse gave: if iKairos notices that sailing keeps coming up in conversation but never turns into action, it suggests taking a sailing lesson over the weekend.

blocks.cap: Detached as a necklace module (Photo: Adamya Sharma / Android Authority)

blocks.x: Privacy is also emphasized. According to the company, iKairos combines both software and hardware protections. It has a physical camera shutter, a privacy indicator light, and a manual mute button. Data is encrypted both in transit and at rest, it isn't used to train AI models, and retention periods are set by the user.

blocks.cap: The physical shutter and privacy indicator light (Photo: Adamya Sharma / Android Authority)

blocks.x: Ringverse's bigger vision is for iKairos to build a detailed, nuanced understanding of a user's habits, work, friends, and conversations. The plan is to transplant that accumulated understanding into robot bodies or accessories, eventually powering home robots.
Pricing and launch timing haven't been set. Anyone interested can join the waitlist on Ringverse's website.

After recently adding a conversational AI storytime feature, improved alarms, more accurate song recognition, and easier message broadcasting to the Google Home app, Google is rolling out a new update that takes Gemini for Home a step further.

blocks.cap: The Gemini logo on an Android phone.

blocks.x: This Google Home app update has already begun rolling out, bundling small improvements that widen Gemini for Home's voice control range and make automation management easier.

The biggest change is that Gemini now understands a much wider range of voice commands spanning both media and home device control. Media commands can now be combined with other kinds of commands in a single request, so you can issue two actions at once, such as 「turn off the lights and turn off the music too.」

Compared to the previous Google Assistant, Gemini for Home was already far more capable and conversational, so its inability to combine media and smart home commands was actually puzzling. Now that these commands can be chained together, requests like 「skip this song and turn on the backyard lights」 or 「turn off the music and turn off the living room lights」 no longer confuse it or trigger errors.

There is also good news for Google Home users who have recently had trouble setting alarms or adding items to a Google Keep list. Google confirmed that this update fixes both bugs and that the commands now work properly.

Finally, this update also makes managing Google Home automations much easier. The lists of starters and actions inside the automation editor are now automatically sorted alphabetically, making it faster to find the device feature you want. Also, for users who manage automations through third-party apps, Google Home now respects the visibility settings configured in that app, meaning third-party routines kept private will no longer clutter the Google Home automation list.

Govee is once again doubling down on smart home mood lighting at IFA 2026. The new AI lighting products it unveiled automatically adjust mood lighting, support fine-grained color transitions, and offer custom settings tailored to indoor and outdoor spaces alike.

The Sky Ceiling Light is built around managing how you feel throughout the day. Govee's new AI Lighting Bot 2.0 adjusts lighting to match your schedule or mood, and emits a sky-blue light at a 478nm wavelength to help maintain alertness during hours with little sunlight. It outputs up to 7,000 lumens of white light at a CRI of 95, with a color temperature range spanning 1,000K to 10,000K. It has earned TÜV Rheinland certification for flicker-free operation and low blue light, and it supports Matter. It goes on sale in the U.S. from September 4 for $399, and in Europe for €399.

blocks.cap: The Govee Sky Ceiling Light.

blocks.x: The COB Strip Light 2 Pro, intended for indoor accent lighting, produces seamless, smooth mood lighting. It also contains AI Lighting Bot 2.0, letting you create lighting scenes suited to gaming, watching movies, reading, and other situations using only text or voice commands. It arranges 1,344 LEDs and 16 ICs per meter in a triple-groove structure for seamless light diffusion, and raises color accuracy with RGBWWIC technology, a CRI of 92, and a color temperature range of 1,000K to 10,000K. The 5-meter model arrives September 4 at $169.99 (€179.99 in Europe), and the 2-meter model arrives in late September at $99.99 (€89.99 in Europe).

blocks.cap: The Govee COB Strip Light 2 Pro.

blocks.x: Last in the lineup is the Permanent Outdoor Lights 2 Pro, for exterior house lighting. The standout hardware upgrade is a dual-layer light-emitting structure, with each light head containing two independently controlled IC chips that let the upper and lower sections display different colors or effects at the same time. Govee's LuminBlend+ color management system handles complex color transitions across an entire roofline, and like the rest of the new lineup, it connects to AI Lighting Bot 2.0, letting users create holiday themes or everyday outdoor moods from simple prompts alone. It goes on sale in the U.S. starting September 7, priced at $499.99 for 100 feet and $799.99 for 200 feet.

blocks.cap: The Govee Permanent Outdoor Lights 2 Pro.
