Ugreen, known for chargers and cables, has entered the smart home business. Its new HomeAgent is a local AI hub that manages its ecosystem devices, designed to process all data on the device itself rather than on cloud servers.

blocks.cap: The Ugreen HomeAgent.

blocks.x: Ugreen released two models together, the HA100 and HA100 Pro. The core feature of this local AI hub, which operates on the home network, is summarizing events detected around the house. Similar to Google Home's premium feature, it analyzes camera footage without an external server to generate descriptions that distinguish between people, pets, and vehicles.

The hub also picks highlight images from an accessible photo library on its own and displays them on Ugreen's smart photo frame. According to the manufacturer, both HomeAgent models support Matter, allowing them to tie together other connected devices on the network within a broader smart home ecosystem and control them locally.

blocks.cap: The SinKare camera lineup unveiled alongside HomeAgent.

blocks.x: Ugreen also introduced devices that work right away with HomeAgent. The lineup includes three cameras aimed at both indoor and outdoor surveillance needs. The indoor model, SinKare, has pan-and-tilt functionality, 4K resolution, and Wi-Fi 6 connectivity, along with a physical shutter for privacy.

For outdoor use, Ugreen released SinKare PoE and battery versions. Both combine a fixed bullet camera with a pan-and-tilt module to capture three video feeds at once with up to 9x hybrid zoom. The biggest difference between the two models is their power source: one connects via Ethernet, while the other runs on a solar-charged battery, a difference that affects response speed and installation flexibility.
The entire HomeAgent ecosystem, including both hub models and the SinKare cameras, began taking pre-orders the same day it was unveiled.
Anthropic has added CarPlay integration to the Claude iOS app. Claude users can now talk to Claude through their car's infotainment screen.
Apple opened the door for this. iOS 26.4 added third-party chatbot support to CarPlay.
There are conditions, though. Any chatbot app that wants into CarPlay must support a voice-control screen, use the CarPlay templates Apple specifies, and receive an entitlement from Apple.
Claude answers spoken questions hands-free, but it cannot control functions of the car or the iPhone.
There's no wake word either. Third-party wake words aren't supported, so the driver has to open the Claude app directly from the CarPlay interface.
The Claude app on CarPlay opens to a “Start a hands-free conversation” screen. From there, you can start a new conversation or jump into a recent one.
Inside the app there are controls for muting and unmuting, and for ending or resuming a conversation. A visual indicator also shows whether Claude is currently listening or speaking.
CarPlay has accepted third-party apps for a long time, but Apple has kept what it allows narrow to avoid distracting drivers. OpenAI added CarPlay support to the ChatGPT app earlier this year.
The article carries an update note, revised to reflect that Claude's CarPlay integration is indeed live.

blocks.cap: Image credit: Tom's Hardware

blocks.x: Microsoft has released another version of Windows 11 aimed at developers. It's called Project Zenith, a version meant to let you start writing code the moment you open the box.
According to the Windows blog, the operating system has been tuned for developer workflows and is launching first on AMD Ryzen AI Halo. It's Team Red's direct answer to Nvidia's DGX Spark.
Microsoft said it will soon expand to devices from its own OEMs and other silicon partners.

Redmond describes Zenith as “a Windows experience where you can start coding immediately without friction, on developer-class devices with 64GB or more of unified memory and 250GB/s or more of memory bandwidth.” Developers can “dive right in.”

The tools come preinstalled: Visual Studio Code, GitHub Copilot, PowerToys, WinAppCLI, Windows Dev Skills, Intelligent Terminal, PowerShell 7, Git, GitHub CLI, AzureCLI, Core Utils, Oh My Posh, Python 3.14+, uv, NVM, Node 24+, WSL 2+ Ubuntu and .NET 10.
Settings are also preconfigured. Microsoft says this means you don't need to dig through each app's settings menu to tailor it to your own environment.

blocks.cap: Image credit: SK Hynix

blocks.x: The target audience is, above all, AI developers. The devices this OS runs on are designed to run models with more than 30 billion parameters locally, without metered usage. The environment for building and running agents has also been reworked, with OS-enforced identity verification, isolation through Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC), and enterprise-grade agent management features.

Behind this is an AI token crisis. Agents consume 1,000 times more tokens than typical AI, and costs have spiraled out of control. The calculation is to keep frontier models in the cloud while running everything else locally on devices like this — a calculation that's especially urgent for small organizations or people experimenting at home.

The price is the trade-off. At least for now, it only runs on expensive devices. An AMD Ryzen AI Halo with a Ryzen AI Max+ 395 processor, 128GB of LPDDR5x-8000, a 2TB SSD and Radeon 8060S integrated graphics costs $3,999.99 at Micro Center.

Even if Zenith is later sold separately so it can be installed on other mini PCs, the requirement of 64GB or more of unified memory remains a major obstacle — all the more so now that the AI boom has sent RAM prices soaring.

blocks.cap: StethO Sense combines BeamO's recordings with AI heart and lung sound analysis. Withings/CNET

blocks.x: I've spent a few weeks with the Withings BeamO since it launched last November. It's an FDA-cleared device that combines a stethoscope, an ECG and a thermometer in one. It was great at taking a temperature and listening to heart and lung sounds, but reading those values still required a doctor in the end. That part is about to change.

At IFA 2026 on Friday, Withings announced StethO Sense. The service opens up to Withings+ users starting October 1, with third-party AI analysis software reading BeamO's heart and lung recordings. According to the materials, detecting abnormal heart murmurs is handled by eMurmur Heart AI, and interpreting breath sounds is handled by StethoMe.

“StethO Sense lets families record heart sounds at home in seconds, as often as they want, and bring that record to their doctor,” said Livia Robic, BeamO product manager. “It doesn't replace a medical visit. It gives you one more piece of health data to bring to that visit.”

eMurmur is a medical AI company that built eMurmur Heart AI, an FDA-cleared algorithm for heart sound analysis. Withings' press release states that the algorithm has been validated through peer-reviewed clinical studies in both children and adults.

blocks.cap: Both BeamO and its StethO Sense service can be used on children and adults. Withings

blocks.x: It analyzes a heart sound recording taken at one of four points within seconds, sorting results into no murmur, abnormal murmur or innocent murmur. A confidence score comes with each reading.
StethoMe, which handles lung sounds, splits its protocol by age. It records lung sounds at six points for children and eight points for adults.
The result comes as a respiratory index from 0 to 100, looking at breath quality and sound, respiratory rate along with breathing rhythm and heart rate, to help detect changes in breathing patterns.
StethoMe, though, is meant for general lung sound tracking. It's not built for people already diagnosed with respiratory conditions such as asthma, COPD or bronchitis.

StethO Sense lives inside the Withings app, but it requires a Withings+ premium membership, which costs $10 a month or $100 a year. Choosing a heart or lung recording under the StethO Sense section of the app and sending it for analysis returns a result within seconds.

blocks.cap: Its one-button design and anatomical diagrams make BeamO simple to use. Cole Kan/Anna Gragert/CNET/Getty Images

blocks.x: The idea behind the design is to complement Withings+'s Cardio Checkup, a service that sends an ECG recording of the heart's electrical signals to a cardiologist for review within 24 hours, usable four times a year.
StethO Sense itself has no limit on how many times it can be used. In exchange, the results aren't a diagnosis. Every recording and analysis can be exported and shared with a doctor.

Starting October 1, Withings+ subscribers will be able to use this feature. Existing users who bought BeamO before that date get a one-month free trial of Withings+, as do those who buy the $250 BeamO after October 1.

I've heard about XREAL's Project Aura for a long time. It's a completely new approach for Android, and like any early-stage technology, I was skeptical about how mature it would actually be. Now that I've tried it myself, I'm counting down to launch day.

XREAL has been hinting at a fall launch for months, but these days it speaks more plainly: before 2026 ends, at a price under $1,500. The people I met at IFA were careful about that number — they said “under $1,500” doesn't necessarily mean $1,499.

The real challenge in XR was never showing off the technology. Impressive AR and VR have been coming out for years. The hard part is making it feel natural enough that you'd want to use it every day, and from my brief hands-on, XREAL has come pretty close.

If you're new to Android XR, think of it this way: instead of looking down at a rectangle in your hand, apps, screens and digital objects float in the space around you. You watch YouTube on a giant virtual display, or move around a city in Google Maps.

The demo started with an introduction to basic hand gestures: pinch, tap, drag, scroll. At first I had to think consciously about what I was doing, but after about 10 minutes I forgot about the controls and was just using it. XREAL said a longer gesture-learning process is planned for actual first-time wearers.

More important is how familiar the software feels. If you've used an Android phone for a while, there's no new operating system to learn. The apps, the navigation concepts and the basic interactions all sit on an ecosystem you already know.

The hardware is more complicated than it looks. Aura is a collaboration between XREAL, Google and Qualcomm. Google contributed the Android XR platform and ecosystem, Qualcomm contributed Snapdragon computing, and XREAL contributed optics and spatial computing experience. The main platform is Snapdragon Reality Elite, and XREAL separately built its own X1S spatial co-processor.

The display is a Sony micro-OLED at 1,920×1,200 per eye, up to 120Hz, with a 70-degree field of view. XREAL's own X Prism optics squeeze this into a glasses form factor. It also supports prescription inserts for people who need corrective lenses.

The most impressive part was Google Maps. The clarity while zooming in and out and spinning around cities and landmarks felt almost magical. Where immersive experiences are supported, you can even go inside buildings — I saw a New York restaurant's table layout, floor plan and soft lighting rendered as if it were real.

Aura uses electrochromic dimming. The lenses darken when you're focused on digital content, but look down and you can still see reality. Not many people want glasses that cut them off completely from their surroundings.

I also watched YouTube. The dedicated app crashed from a bug, so I watched it the old-fashioned way through Chrome, but scaling the virtual screen up as much as you want feels closer to a projector than a phone or tablet. I heard the battery is a 4,455mAh cell in the external compute unit, good for four to five hours of streaming.

The remaining question mark is apps. Since the Google Play Store is available, there's no need to build an ecosystem from scratch. Still, the success of an XR platform depends on apps designed specifically for this form factor, and XREAL only said it would share more at launch.
Sleep, exercise, and stress are now tracked pretty accurately, hands-free, by fitness trackers, smartwatches, and smart rings. Logging meals, though, remains a persistent headache.
There are plenty of ways to enter calories and nutrition by hand, like Garmin Connect or the Oura app. The problem has been that there's no easier path than that.

That's the spot the Odyss N1 AI necklace is aiming for. It's still a concept, but I tried it myself at IFA 2026 in Berlin, and while I'm split on how well it performs, I was drawn to the possibilities this device opens up.

The Odyss N1 is a small triangular pendant with a camera and an accelerometer built in. It tracks what you eat, when you eat, and how much you eat, all with this one piece. The necklace cord is actually a cable, connecting the pendant to a battery module at the back of the neck. That power module also contains haptics for notifications.

The pendant is metal and comes in black, silver, and gold. The finish is quite nice, closer to jewelry than a gadget. There's a single physical button on top; pressing it turns off meal-logging entirely. Not storing the original image data at all is also part of the privacy design.

Logging works by feeding visual and motion data into an AI algorithm. It also weighs prior context to estimate what you're eating and even how the food was prepared. You can correct the log at any time, and the Odyss N1 learns from those corrections. Because it gets more accurate the longer you wear it and the more you refine the log, the company says you need to wear it for at least two weeks to finish calibration before it performs at its best.

The accumulated meal data goes to a companion app, which organizes your overall nutrition flow and suggests diet improvements. Beyond nutrition, it also produces analysis reports centered on three metrics: quality, energy, and rhythm.

It's still a concept, but the plans are clear. Meal-logging data will be opened up so it can be viewed in other widely used health-tracking apps, and conversely, the Odyss app will pull in health data from other wearables to feed into its nutrition advice.

The weaknesses are clear too. For meal tracking to work properly, you essentially have to wear it all day. Battery life also appears capped at a day or two, meaning it has to come off and get charged often.

The Roomba Duo, which iRobot unveiled at IFA 2026, is one of the standout robot vacuum ideas I've seen this year. It's not just the Star Wars droid-like looks. The large cylindrical body steam-mops the floor and sets down a small robot, which had been riding in a compartment up top, into tight spots.

It's not a finished product. There's a chance it never reaches the market at all. An iRobot product manager I met on the show floor said, 'Roomba Duo is a concept we built to see how the market reacts, and it's the future of floor-cleaning robots as we see it.'

He described the large body as heavy-duty equipment meant to replace a stick vacuum or a wet/dry vacuum. It's about 2 feet tall and roughly 66 pounds, made heavy on purpose to pack in more power and a bigger water tank.

The demo started by spilling spaghetti on a carpet — closer to one coated in oil and herbs than red sauce. The body passed over it, sucked it up, and steam-cleaned right behind, leaving only a faint oily-looking stain where it had been.

What comes next is the whole point of this machine. When the Roomba Duo lifted its head and set itself down on the floor, a disc-shaped robot tucked inside popped out, Matryoshka-doll style. The product manager said this companion robot is essentially the same as the Roomba Plus 575, a small suction-and-mop robot the company showed earlier this year. Watching it sweep under a low stand with legs set close together made clear what the robot-inside-a-robot idea is actually for.

If it ships, it will likely look quite different from what I saw that day. Since it's still at the concept stage, the product manager wouldn't say much about price. But he didn't push back on the guess that it would cost more than a pricey all-in-one like the $1,700 Dreame X60 Max Ultra Complete reviewed this year.

Steam-cleaning performance is still an open question. It remains to be seen whether it can handle stubborn messes like old stains or grease. Still, if it can clean up a big accident that you'd never dare send a robot vacuum after — a whole dropped plate of food, say — it will have earned its keep.

Translation today mostly happens in software, but Timekettle has been doing real-time interpretation through earbuds. The W4 Plus, launched for IFA 2026, continues that line, with one condition attached.
Like last year's W4 and W4 Pro, it supports 52 languages, 106 accents, and 13 offline language pairs. What's changed is the software. Babel OS 3.0 is said to deliver faster, more natural translation.

There are also new field-specific profiles. Pick one of General, Tech & Internet, Manufacturing & Industry, New Energy & Green Tech, or Biotech & Pharma, and it reads the nature of the conversation to adjust the translation. The company says mistranslations drop when dealing with technical detail in a specific field.

More AI means more features. Conversation Memory 'maintains context' across long discussions with many back-and-forths, and Live Summary distills past conversation down to 'just the essentials, concisely.' An AI speaking coach helps you practice against simulated real-life scenarios, though for now it only works in English, Chinese, and Spanish. Registering terms, phrases, or names in a personal glossary makes them easier to recognize mid-conversation, and the tone and style of translation also adapt to the situation.

Noise handling got work too. The new noise-reduction algorithm is said to pick up quiet voices 32-47% better than the existing W4. Bone-conduction technology and dual microphones work together to preserve the user's voice while stripping out ambient sound. Online and offline translation switch instantly, so it holds up even with frequent movement. One earbud weighs 5.7g, and 116.5g with the case.
Battery life, if anything, got shorter. It's just over 3 hours of continuous interpretation, 12 hours with the case, and up to 18 hours of music playback.

Colors are Space Black, Midnight Blue, and Sandy Gold. The base model is $299, and some key AI features unlock with a $14.99-a-month subscription. Even on the base model, unlimited 1:1 translation, Listen & Play, AI Language Tutor, and offline translation work as-is. To get every feature without a subscription, there's a $379 version. In the US, it goes on sale September 6 on the Timekettle website and Amazon.

Apple's S-series chips rarely see a meaningful generational leap. The number tends to change every year, but actual CPU improvements have been rare, and last year the company skipped the S11 and kept the S10 as-is.

This year is said to be different. The Apple Watch Series 12 is expected to get an upgraded S-series chip. The name is likely S12 or S11, and it will be faster while becoming the first watch chip for the AI era.
watchOS 27's headline feature is Siri AI. It's expected to run best on the new chip, and the rest of the everyday features benefit too.

Talk of expanded health features has been around for a while too. The FDA reviewed an upgrade to hypertension notifications, reportedly set to be announced next week. There's also a specific rumor that the heart rate sensor will get always-on measurement, a method competing products like WHOOP already offer.
According to Mark Gurman, the new sensor in the Series 12 can 'collect data continuously throughout the day rather than only when it detects intense activity or at arbitrary intervals.'

On top of new bands and case options, there's speculation that a ceramic case is returning for the first time since the Series 5 in 2019, in white and dark gray. Bloomberg reported that 'Apple tested both white and dark gray configurations for the Series 12 ceramic case.' How much ceramic will raise the price is still unknown. The last time it was offered, it started at $1,299, far more expensive than today's Apple Watch Ultra.
Google is rolling out its September 2026 Android drop. It carries several substantial features.

Find Hub and Gemini can now help you find items without a tracking tag. The idea is to have Gemini remember where you put something important. You can say something like, “Hey Google, remember in Find Hub that I put my passport in the bedroom drawer,” and attach a photo too.
Saved locations pile up in a new “Remembered” tab in the Find Hub app. Ask by voice where something is, and Gemini answers. It works on Android 16 and up.

blocks.cap: The new “Remembered” tab in Find Hub. (Photo: 9to5Google)

blocks.x: Motion Assist eases motion sickness on Android 17 and up. It floats a faint bubble on screen that sways with the vehicle's movement. Google describes it as a device meant “to bridge the gap between what your eyes see and what your body feels in motion.” You can change the bubble's color, shape, and transparency, or let it change automatically every few seconds. Android turns it on by itself when it detects motion in a car, bus, or train. You can also turn it on and off yourself with a Quick Settings tile.

Gemini Live gains Guided Vision, which describes out loud what's in front of the camera. It's used for reading fine print on food labels, picking a menu in a dimly lit restaurant, or finding things around the house. It talks you through readjusting the camera, scanning a space, or moving an object to the center of the frame. It opens from accessibility shortcuts or the TalkBack menu, and is coming “soon” to Android 9 and up devices in countries where Gemini is available.

blocks.cap: A Keep list made right inside a Google Messages conversation. (Photo: 9to5Google)

blocks.x: Google Keep is coming to Google Messages, following the chat-theme update. “Share and edit a shopping list or travel notes right inside the conversation.” Tapping a “create a list” suggestion or a menu shortcut opens a sheet, and once you're done, it attaches to the conversation as a shared note. The rollout started right away.

Circular unveiled two smart rings at IFA 2026: the Circular Ring 3 Pro and the Circular Ring 3 Slim. Both let you make contactless payments with your finger and receive haptic alerts, including silent wake-ups, and health reminders.

The Ring 3 Pro packs an FDA-cleared ECG that detects atrial fibrillation, haptic vibration, and NFC contactless payments. The Slim is a scaled-down version of the Pro, so it drops the ECG, but keeps payments and basic health tracking.
To learn more about both rings, we spoke with Circular co-founder and CEO Amaury Cosman.

blocks.cap: Circular Ring 3 (Photo: Circular)

blocks.x: Vibration is a feature that was once dropped from the Circular Ring 2. Cosman said it was brought back based on user feedback. “At the time, we didn't have the know-how to fit the new ECG sensing and vibration together. We managed it with the Ring 3 Pro.”

Payments were a wall every major ring maker wanted to get over. Cosman said, “We're very pleased to have packed payments and health tracking into one ring. As far as we know, this is the world's first smart ring to support both payments and health together.”
Both rings work without a subscription. However, the newly added blood pressure and blood glucose measurements require opting into a subscription to unlock.

The Slim is 5.9mm wide and 2.35mm thick, weighing 1.9 to 3 grams depending on size — roughly the same class as the Oura Ring 5, which is 6.09mm wide and 2.28mm thick. Since the Oura Ring 5 launched earlier this year, smart ring brands have been competing over looking more like jewelry than a fitness tracker. The Pro is 6.8mm wide and 2.78mm thick, similar to the Ring 2. Battery life runs up to 12 days on the Pro and up to 10 days on the Slim, up from the Ring 2's 7 days.
Both products are slated to launch in 2027. Exact dates and pricing haven't been announced yet.

IFA, held annually in Berlin, is where big tech companies first unveil new products. TechRadar called this year's lineup one of the strongest it's seen in quite a while, ranging from next-generation AR glasses to self-driving personal mobility devices, kitchen appliances of uncertain purpose, and a row of humanoids. From the Best in Show contenders, it picked 25 based on how novel they are, how well they fill a need, and how much they'll shake up their market.

The Anker Soundcore Sleep A20 Pro earbuds measure heart rate with an in-ear PPG optical sensor. The ear canal has plenty of capillaries and doesn't shift position, making the reading more accurate than other optical methods. The data goes to a Sleep Hub charging case with a smart display, so it can be checked without a phone. 30dB active noise cancellation works alongside passive isolation, and the case detects snoring and masks it with built-in sound. Despite the added components, the body is thinner than the previous generation, which is more comfortable for side sleepers.

blocks.cap: The Agibot A3 doing a backflip. (Photo: Agibot)

blocks.x: The Agibot A3 is an adult-sized humanoid weighing 55kg. A power-to-weight ratio of 0.218kW/kg, peaking at 12kW, lets it do backflips. The battery lasts up to 10 hours and swaps out in seconds. Beyond voice and app control, it's the first in the industry to add tactile sensing, enabling hands-on manipulation. The standout feature is swarm control: using UWB positioning, up to 100 units can perform in formation, and the same principle lets multiple units divide up work in a factory or warehouse.

The Hypershell X Ultra S is what brought exoskeleton pricing down. Performance that once cost more than $100,000 now comes in under $2,000, at under 2kg. An AI model converts raw sensor signals directly into motor torque, making the response fast and the motion smooth. It has 12 modes, including walking, cycling, and running, plus a newly added Gentle Assist mode aimed at older users with shorter strides. The exoskeleton helped climber Adriana Brownlee at minus 30 degrees on Everest, and accompanied Aurélien Fontenoy, who was recovering from an injury, on his 4,037km trek along Route 66.

The EcoFlow Stream 5000 and Stream AC 5000 split home solar generation and storage into modules. Designed with renters and apartment dwellers in mind, they work as soon as you plug them in. You can add battery storage and power management onto an existing solar setup, or build a new one from scratch.

There's nothing that folds laundry, but one model with wheels that extend like legs stands out: the Saros Rover, first shown at CES this year. It extends its wheels to climb small ledges and even stairs. Other new models in the same lineup are the Saros 20 Flow Complete and the Saros 20 Neo. Both combine suction and mopping, with technology that makes it easier to cross double thresholds.

blocks.cap: The Roborock Saros Rover extends its wheels to climb a ledge (Photo: Engadget)

blocks.x: The F25 Ultra Steam 2nd generation was also announced. As the name suggests, it's a steam cleaner. It automatically adjusts when the floor material changes, with no input from the user. The F25 Pro Turbo Combo has a detachable drive module and multiple brush head types.

Preorders open Saturday, September 12 at 5 a.m. Pacific time, with in-store sales and shipping starting Friday, September 18.

When Apple unveiled Live Rewind at its “Surprise and Shine” event, worries that it could become a tool for secretly recording other people's words followed immediately. That's because pressing an Apple Watch button once plays back whatever sound it caught in the previous 15 seconds.

Reactions on social media were split. Some called it “creepy and rude,” while others pointed out it could be highly useful for deaf or autistic people. Whether the Apple Watch really turns into “mass surveillance equipment” is something you can only judge by examining how the feature actually works.

blocks.cap: The Live Rewind screen (Image credit: Apple)

blocks.x: Here's how Apple describes it: if an Apple Watch Series 12 or Apple Watch Ultra 4 user double-presses the Digital Crown, whatever was said in the previous 15 seconds appears as text. Apple cited missing something important, not hearing well, and recalling information a friend mentioned as use cases.

At the event, Apple stated plainly that the feature doesn't record or save audio, doesn't identify whose voice it is, and that no one, including Apple itself, can access the audio. The company published further detail separately in its Audio Intelligence Privacy Overview document.

Audio is processed only inside the Secure Enclave within the S11 chip. This area is cut off from the rest of the device, so neither the operating system, Apple's own apps, third-party apps, nor Apple headquarters can touch the original audio. Incoming audio disappears as it's continuously overwritten by new audio.

When the feature is turned on, the watch sends the previous 15 seconds of audio to the iPhone. If the iPhone is out of wireless range, that audio is discarded immediately. If the transfer succeeds, the iPhone converts it to text, deletes the audio, and sends only the text back to the watch's Secure Enclave.

The text remains for up to 30 seconds after the screen dims, then disappears. If it's saved separately in the Siri app, end-to-end encryption applies. That's the only case in which anything from the Live Rewind process is kept, and even that text contains no speaker information.

blocks.cap: The watch screen that signals the feature is working (Image credit: Apple)

blocks.x: Using it without people nearby noticing isn't easy, either. Double-pressing the Digital Crown triggers an alert sound even in silent mode or while wearing headphones, and the screen shows a full animation along with a microphone icon.

Live Rewind is off by default, and users have to turn it on themselves. It's toggled on or off either when setting up a new device or in the Siri settings on the watch and iPhone. There's no way to force someone to ask for consent beforehand, but there's also no way to save or extract the audio, or to identify the speaker. All that's left in hand is a single block of text.

blocks.x: Frontier AI models have made big gains in security capability over the past few months. They find zero-days in massive codebases and scan a computer's vulnerabilities in no time. There have even been cases of security agents colluding with each other to break into outside systems.

Wanting a closer look, I turned one loose on my home network. Over a few days, this unruly agent found vulnerabilities in household devices, broke into one PC, and confirmed that the projects I'd made through vibe coding were riddled with bugs. My wife rolled her eyes every time I bragged about a new vulnerability I'd found.

Handing your home network over to an all-powerful security agent is insane, right? That's a fair point. Still, you can't really grasp the security hellscape in front of you without going there yourself. The result was, unexpectedly, somewhat reassuring in places. The best defense against AI hacking might be having your own AI hacker.

The experiment started with Abliteration AI, a startup that sells powerful models with their guardrails removed. If you find and tweak the internal parameters of an open-weight model that lead to refusals, the restrictions disappear. This process is called abliteration.

Removing guardrails isn't rare. Academics use misaligned models to dig into how AI works, and security firms use them to probe systems. Abliteration AI's top model is a variant of Z.ai's latest agentic coding model, GLM 5.3. For the price of a pizza, you get capability on par with Anthropic's Mythos or OpenAI's Astra.

CEO Devon believes pushing these models out widely is actually the smarter defense. "From airlines to banks, critical infrastructure companies are adopting agents like crazy. How do you make sure bad actors can't use those agents for harm?"

I created an account and installed a harness called CyberStrike. When I told the misaligned GLM-5.3 to look at my local network, it found about a dozen pieces of hardware and pulled up a list of vulnerabilities within minutes. The printer was misconfigured so that anyone on the network could log in. The Wiim stereo leaked information freely; it even figured out that the last song played was Rein Me In by Sam Fender and Olivia Dean.

An unleashed agent would be useful to a hacker, but it left me with some solid advice too. Beyond updating firmware and locking down the printer, it recommended moving IoT devices like smart speakers onto a guest network. Not bad for a model with no morals at all. In my vibe-coding folders, it caught dozens of issues, including unprotected API credentials.

There was a scary part too. When I told it to try logging into a Linux machine, it inferred a valid username based on the names of other systems. When it said it would write a brute-force script, I told it to stop. It then found a cryptographic key, logged in without a password, and started digging for passwords to gain root access. Watching it rifle through directories sent a chill down my spine.

Shaanan Cohney of Tufts University thinks a day of reckoning is coming. "Attackers tend to be early adopters. To defend a castle, you need zero holes in the wall, not even one loose brick. To take the castle, you only need to find that one loose brick." Aleksander Mądry, an MIT professor currently on leave working at OpenAI, says we need to help people use these capabilities. But he added that the real issue is making sure the people running power plants or financial markets end up with AI stronger than the average script kiddie's.

blocks.cap: The Unitree Go2 Pro I brought to the office

blocks.x: On a clear June morning, I walked to work with the four-legged robot beside me. I had never drawn so many stares. People took photos, asked if I had built it myself, and pressed me about whether it was for surveillance. Real dogs kept their distance and growled.

It's two miles from my home in Mount Pleasant, Washington DC, to my office near the White House. The route is downhill, so the battery held up fine. The trip home was the problem. Going uphill as the temperature climbed to 87°F (30°C), its steps grew noticeably heavier. With my house in sight, the battery hit 5% and the internal temperature hit 84°C (183°F), and it simply sat down. It didn't power off gracefully either—it flipped over with its legs still raised.

blocks.cap: The robot dog collapsed a few steps from home

blocks.x: Plenty of people asked what it's actually good for, and honestly, not much. Wheeled robots are faster for deliveries, drones are better for surveying, and without arms it can't do housework. What it has instead is a startlingly low price: $4,017 including tariffs and shipping.

George Mason University roboticist Xuesu Xiao put it this way: “Ten years ago, only a handful of groups were working on quadruped locomotion, because they were the only ones who knew how to build the hardware themselves. Unitree coming in democratized quadruped research across the board.” The quadruped robots in his lab cost $15,000 apiece, while Boston Dynamics's Spot, long considered the industry leader, starts at $75,000.

blocks.cap: Professor Xuesu Xiao standing in front of a Unitree quadruped robot in his lab

blocks.x: Founder Wang Xingxing built a crude quadruped called XDog as his master's thesis at Shanghai University. “Boston Dynamics's Marc Raibert is my idol,” he said in a March 2016 interview with IEEE Spectrum. Unitree, which he founded that May, went on to release Laikago (2017) and AlienGo (2019), then Go1 for $2,700 in 2021, and Go2 for $1,600 (Air) and $2,800 (Pro) in 2023.

Why is it so cheap? When Simplexity tore down a Go2, they found three motors per leg—12 in total—all the same spec. “They use the same motor everywhere. It cuts both cost and part count, and the design ends up sturdier for it,” said mechanical engineer Luis Elenes. A leg can be swapped out in under a minute. Jakub Bartoszek of MAB Robotics credits much of the savings to the use of lower-quality components. Chinese government tax credits and bulk purchases by public institutions also pushed costs down.

The choice of reducer is also different. Spot's leg motors pair with a 51:1 reducer, which is precise but expensive and stiff. Unitree instead pairs a larger motor with just a 6.33:1 gearbox. The cost comes down and the movement becomes more agile.

The quadrupeds were a stepping stone. H1 came in 2023, followed by G1 the next year. The research-grade EDU runs around $50,000, while the consumer version starts at $13,500. Go2 runs on 12 motors, while the cheapest G1 uses 23. According to August listing documents, quadruped revenue rose from 230 million yuan ($34 million) in 2024 to 697 million yuan ($104 million) in 2025, while humanoid revenue jumped from 107 million yuan ($16 million) to 867 million yuan ($129 million).

On its first day trading in Shanghai on August 19, the stock price rose more than fivefold, and the company's valuation stood at $34 billion as of Monday's close. SemiAnalysis compares Unitree to DJI. The US, meanwhile, is leaning toward shutting the door: a bipartisan House bill in June named Unitree specifically in proposing restrictions on importing Chinese robots, and in July the FCC imposed rules on foreign-made robots. The lockout could end up pushing the US to the margins of robotics instead.

blocks.x: Nvidia is introducing a 64GB version of its DGX Spark, meant to be more affordable for local AI users who don't need 128GB of RAM.
The AI field moves fast: dense models like Qwen 3.8 27B can now fit within 32GB of RAM, and skyrocketing RAM prices make a chip permanently paired with costly LPDDR5X more of a barrier than an asset.

64GB GB10 systems from Acer, Asus, Dell, Gigabyte, HP, and MSI are slated to start at $4999 when they launch on October 23 — though memory prices may not let them stay there. 128GB GB10 systems, if you can find one, run roughly $7000 to $9000.
Otherwise the 64GB Sparks are unchanged: the same ConnectX 7 RDMA NIC for clustering, the same 20-core Arm CPU, and the same 273 GB/s of shared memory bandwidth.

Nvidia is also adding the Sync Cluster Assistant to automate joining Sparks together, plus a Model Launcher that downloads and starts models across one or more systems and links them to the OpenCode coding agent. The 128GB Spark remains available for larger models and fine-tuning.
At the start of September, the Google Assistant deprecation on mobile got underway. It now looks to be widely rolling out.

Google has been moving Assistant users to Gemini over the past few weeks. This deprecation was originally set for 2025 and later extended to 2026. In early August, Google announced the final timeline.
From various user reports today, this migration appears to be fully underway. Google Assistant is gone on all devices/accounts we checked in the US and Europe.
Notably, the Gemini app has removed the “Switch to Google Assistant” setting. This shortcut no longer appears at the bottom of the account menu with Google app 17.60 stable and 17.62 beta.
As such, you can no longer “use or switch back to Google Assistant on your phone, tablet, or paired devices.” The latter grouping includes Wear OS, headphones, and Android Auto.
There are no changes to Assistant just yet on “Google Nest and Google Home smart speakers, displays, or other Google Assistant-enabled speakers and displays.”
Gemini is now the “voice assistant experience on Android” when you long-press the power button or swipe from the corners.

Reliable Apple insider Mark Gurman revealed that Apple's long-awaited home hub could arrive later in October, and on his new Power On podcast he predicted that a security camera may follow — one that won't actually record video. He also claims Apple will launch more powerful versions of the HomePod mini and Apple TV.

According to Gurman, the camera is a companion to Apple's unannounced smart home display, internally called J490. The small cylindrical cameras, resembling chapstick, will have a very low frame rate and won't offer video recording.

Mindful of concerns about over-surveillance, Apple will reportedly have the sensor use AI to analyze movement in your home instead. It will be able to do facial recognition: if it identifies someone walking into a room, it can tell you whether you know that person, but you'll only receive text descriptions.

Gurman added that the camera will use “a very similar technology to what they're going to be using for the AirPods with cameras,” which reportedly take extremely low resolution still images analyzed by Visual Intelligence.

blocks.cap: The iPad 11 (2025)

blocks.x: Leaked code reveals that the upcoming iPad 12 will feature notable hardware upgrades designed specifically to support Apple Intelligence. The entry-level tablet is expected to include the A19 chip and 8GB of RAM.

References to the 12th-generation model, uncovered in Apple's code by MacRumors contributor Aaron Perris, also list the company's in-house C1X cellular modem and N1 wireless networking chip. The A19 replaces the A16 chip in the current iPad 11, which launched in March 2025.

The chip change brings Apple Intelligence to the entry-level iPad for the first time. The A16 does not support the platform, leaving iPad 11 owners without Apple's generative AI tools and the Siri features built on them. Memory rises from 6GB to 8GB, the minimum Apple requires to run Apple Intelligence.

The C1X supports sub-6GHz 5G networks and is more power efficient, while the N1 adds Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, and Thread support. The iPad 11 now starts at $449 following a June 2026 price increase, and its successor is expected to launch at the same price. The findings do not include a release date, and the iPad 12 is not expected before spring 2027.

blocks.cap: A new hand for Atlas.

blocks.x: Boston Dynamics' Atlas is getting new hands. The robotics company showed the new hand design, which should now be able to operate a drill or move two golf balls in one hand. According to Boston Dynamics, this increases the number of degrees of freedom to 13.

Boston Dynamics has presented a new hand for its high-end robot, Atlas. A new video showcases its new abilities, including handling a drill. Although this demo was conducted with the help of a remote operator, it should demonstrate what will be possible in the near future. Currently, Boston Dynamics is also researching how it can get Atlas to actually learn by itself rather than be trained.

Atlas can already use the new hands fully autonomously. Boston Dynamics demonstrates this with Atlas handling two golf balls in one hand. Atlas can do this without a pinky. According to the company, another finger is not worth the extra complexity it would add. It would also increase power consumption. It's just a thumb and three additional fingers.

The complexity already reaches a level that is close to a separate mini-robot. Atlas' improved hands now offer 13 degrees of freedom, says Boston Dynamics' mechanical engineer Dylan Thrush. Previously, Atlas was limited to 7 degrees of freedom. As the company is planning to use Atlas in car assembly, these additional degrees of freedom will probably come in handy. The new hand is both a bit larger and stronger than a typical human hand.
Boston Dynamics also hopes that the new hand is better at avoiding movements that could damage its mechanical parts because of the extra flexibility.

blocks.cap: Image credit: Insta360

blocks.x: Insta360 has launched Spatial Capture, a free feature that turns 360 video into a detailed 3D model of a real space that you can move around in. It's still in beta, available now for the Insta360 X6 and any of the company's 360 cameras that can shoot 5.7K video at 30fps or above, including the X4 Air and X5.

Spatial Capture is built on 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS): software works out where the camera was at each moment, then rebuilds the scene from millions of tiny, semi-transparent blobs. The result is a photorealistic 3D scene viewable from angles the camera never occupied.

Cloud platform Splatica starts at $49.95 a month; Spatial Capture gives you four free generations a month. Insta360 says Splatica produces higher-quality results for professionals, while Spatial Capture is meant for casual users and renders a two-minute video in one to two hours versus around eight.

You record a clip of two minutes or less, and processing happens in the cloud. Insta360 recommends well-lit indoor spaces up to 100 square meters, so it looks designed for rooms rather than landscapes. Scenes can be shared via a browser link, but can't yet be exported as files.

blocks.cap: Image credit: Insta360

blocks.x: The reviewer's own X6 test clip failed to upload twice — the kind of teething problem you'd expect from a beta — but it's a welcome freebie that adds value to a pricey camera.

blocks.x: Microsoft has started rolling out Windows 11 version 26H2, also called the Windows 11 2026 Update. The release began on September 29, 2026, and arrives as a small enablement package for devices already running version 24H2 or 25H2.

Most features already reached PCs through monthly updates; the package activates them with a single restart in most cases. It also resets the support clock: 24 months for Home and Pro, 36 months for Enterprise and Education.

File Explorer gets AI actions that let users edit supported images or summarize documents. Summarize works on files in OneDrive and SharePoint and requires a Microsoft 365 subscription and a Copilot license. Work or school accounts also see Open File Location and Ask Copilot when hovering over files in File Explorer Home.
Explorer adds support for uu, cpio, xar and nupkg archives and voice-typing renames, and the taskbar can now sit on any screen edge.
On security, Sysmon is built in, Administrator protection arrives (both off by default), and Windows adds API support for post-quantum algorithms ML-KEM and ML-DSA.

Apple's latest tvOS 27.2 beta adds weight to rumors that the next Apple TV will have Siri AI and Apple Intelligence support. Code suggests Apple is adding an Improve Siri & Apple Intelligence toggle to the tvOS Settings app.
“Help improve foundation models and Siri by allowing Apple to collect and use your text and audio interactions with Siri, Dictation, and Translate,” the text reads.

Other Apple devices with Apple Intelligence have similarly labeled privacy disclosures and data-sharing opt-ins. On devices that don't support Apple Intelligence, the setting is labeled “Improve Siri & Dictation.” The new code is included alongside the existing code for Siri data sharing, so it's likely only Apple Intelligence-capable hardware will see it.

tvOS 27.2 also has a new Siri Messages UI framework, indicating message content could be displayed on the Apple TV in the future. Siri may be able to read messages sent to a linked iPhone and show smart reply options on the Apple TV. The current version of Siri on Apple TV doesn't support sending or reading messages, so the framework is likely linked to Siri AI.

Apple is working on a version of the Apple TV with 8GB or 12GB of RAM and an A19 or A19 Pro chip, hardware that could support on-device Siri AI features. Apple appears to be laying the groundwork for the new Apple TV with tvOS 27.2. We could get a new Apple TV as soon as October 13.

Big tech firms want you to believe cloud-based AI needs GPU horsepower more than your home PC. The WiCi One proposes an alternative to yet another cloud subscription: essentially an eGPU that beams graphics processing power to a lower-end PC over a Wi-Fi 7 connection, turning “personal computing” into “communal computing.”

blocks.cap: Is it a toaster or a speaker? You decide. © Kyle Barr / Gizmodo

blocks.x: Wi-Fi 7 tops out around 11.5Gbps, versus 32Gbps for Thunderbolt 4. Co-founder and CEO Zill Meng says WiCi designed its own protocols and firmware to minimize interference and data transmission.

blocks.cap: There’s literally a whole desktop PC worth of parts in this thing. © Kyle Barr / Gizmodo

blocks.x: Two models are planned: $2,600 with an RTX 5060 Ti and $10,000 with an RTX 5090. Meng showed the RTX 5090 version running the DeepSeek-V3 AI model. Cyberpunk 2077 played from about seven feet away swung between 100 and 200 fps with frame generation, and dropped closer to 10 fps with path tracing.
Meng himself said gaming may not be the best use; a Thunderbolt 4 port is included. The WiCi One still needs work before its planned December launch.

blocks.cap: Pixel launcher search bar

blocks.x: The new Pixel Search app preloaded on the Pixel 11 series lets users search photos, emails, contacts and more from the app drawer. Now Google appears to be prepping a Gemini-powered upgrade, while also giving users more control over call log and message data.
The latest version (1.0.983036833) adds a "Privacy & Permissions" section in settings with three toggles: "Help improve Pixel Search," "Call Logs" and "SMS."

blocks.cap: Pixel Search Privacy & Permissions settings (AssembleDebug / Android Authority)
Pixel Search privacy toggles (AssembleDebug / Android Authority)

blocks.x: Turning off "Help improve Pixel Search" stops data being aggregated for usage insights; the "Call Logs" and "SMS" toggles stop Google using that history to improve contact suggestions. Disabling them doesn't hide calls or messages from results, though — for that, revoke the app's Call logs and SMS permissions.

blocks.cap: Pixel Search app permissions (AssembleDebug / Android Authority)

blocks.x: Android Authority also found code for an upcoming "Gemini-powered suggestions" feature. Strings read "Show Gemini-powered suggestions" and "See relevant info and Gemini-suggested actions to help you finish a task faster."

Gemini-powered suggestions aren't live yet and could arrive in a future update, but the privacy section is already available. Pixel 11 owners can update via the Play Store; older Pixels can sideload the app on Android 17 QPR2 Beta 5 or newer.
Ray-Ban Meta Audio drops the camera for a lighter and sleeker design that's likely to be more socially acceptable amid the public privacy backlash.

Announced at Meta Connect 2026, Ray-Ban Meta Audio are Meta's first smart glasses without a camera. Otherwise, they have the same functionality, offering Meta AI queries, listening to music, audiobooks, and podcasts, and taking calls.

Ray-Ban Meta Audio is available in two styles, Burbank and Clubmaster. Burbank looks a lot like the typical Wayfarer Ray-Ban Meta glasses but without the camera and LED, while Clubmaster is unlike any of Meta's other smart glasses.
The Clubmaster Ray-Ban Meta Audio is Meta's lightest smart glasses offering yet, at 43 grams for the standard size, while the Burbank takes second place at 47 grams.

The device comes after a widespread public backlash to the idea of smart glasses with a camera. Meta has been releasing firmware updates to make tampering with the recording LED more difficult. Still, the growing association with wrongdoing will put some potential buyers off smart glasses with a camera entirely, and Ray-Ban Meta Audio can target this market.
Despite this, Meta told UploadVR that Ray-Ban Meta Audio has been in development for years, and that its development wasn't driven by the public backlash.
Ray-Ban Meta Audio is available to preorder for $349, and ships from October 13.

Google today announced EmbeddingGemma 2, a model that can "organize, search, and connect information directly on consumer hardware." To show off its potential, Google created an AI Edge Foresight Mac app for "intelligent notetaking."

The 740 million parameter model is built on the Gemma 4 architecture under an Apache 2.0 license. With quantization, on a Pixel 11 Pro it needs as little as ~191MB active RAM for text-only weights and ~567MB for the full multimodal model.

During meetings, Foresight listens in the background so you can "scribble shorthand bullets," which it "enriches into polished notes using the meeting transcript instantly." Transcript and audio are processed entirely on your device.

You can also point it at project folders, diagrams, and your calendar, local or Google Drive, then ask questions. Chat offers retrieval and summary, and Live Assistance will "listen and automatically answer questions." It joins AI Edge Gallery and AI Edge Eloquent on Mac.

blocks.cap: Google Fitbit Edge (Android Headlines)

blocks.x: Google may be preparing to give the Fitbit Charge line the upgrade it’s been waiting for. A new leak has revealed a huge amount of information about the rumored Fitbit Edge, an upcoming fitness tracker that appears designed to sit somewhere between the minimalist Fitbit Air and Google’s much more capable Pixel Watch 5.

The Fitbit Edge will reportedly feature a 1.34-inch AMOLED display with an always-on mode, built-in GPS, Bluetooth 5.4, and support for both Android and iPhone. But Gemini could be the Edge’s biggest differentiator.

blocks.cap: Google Fitbit Edge (Android Headlines)

blocks.x: The tracker reportedly supports personalized fitness coaching powered by Gemini, including customized workout programs, an Ask Coach feature, and coaching directly from your wrist. Some of those smarter features may require a Google Health Premium subscription.

The tracker reportedly lasts up to seven days on a charge, although enabling the always-on display could drop that to around two days. Just five minutes of charging is said to provide roughly 24 hours of use.

blocks.cap: Google Fitbit Edge (Android Headlines)

blocks.x: Dealabs reportedly lists it at €179 (~ $201) in Europe and £159 (~ $211) in the UK. Google hasn’t officially announced the Fitbit Edge yet, but given how much has leaked, it probably won’t remain a secret much longer.

JBL is expanding its party speaker lineup with the $1,800 PartyBox Ultimate 2, which puts out 1,500W from six drivers: dual woofers, dual midrange drivers, and dual tweeters. It weighs 120 pounds and has no battery, so it must be plugged in.

JBL put its AI isolation features in the PartyBox Ultimate 2, so you can strip vocals out of tracks with the push of a button. On JBL's Bandbox Solo, the feature "works far better than you'd expect," and doing it with literally any song is "still pretty rad."

There's also AI Sound Boost, meant to maximize volume without distortion, and Smart EQ Mode, which uses AI to assess what you're listening to and adjust EQ in real time. It streams over Wi-Fi via AirPlay 2, Spotify Connect, and Chromecast, with USB-C lossless, optical, and XLR inputs.
The PartyBox Ultimate 2 is available for preorder now and ships starting Oct. 25.

blocks.cap: Image Credits: Sigil Wen

blocks.x: Now a Thiel Fellow, Wen on Monday launched an invite-only beta of Underdog, one of the most private AI assistants Silicon Valley has yet to offer. The model runs wholly on-device, meaning the user’s data remains on devices they already own, currently Macs and Windows PCs, with Linux, iPhone, and Android versions coming soon.

Underdog is powered by Husky, the inference engine Wen built to run AI models quickly on a user’s own hardware. Wen says it moves less data between a computer’s main chip and its graphics chip than rival on-device engines.

It currently uses a 27-billion parameter reasoning model fine-tuned from Qwen3.8-27B. Wen argues that this model compares favorably with Claude Opus 4.6 in some benchmarks, and can handle everyday tasks like shopping research or answering math homework questions.

The app will be free at first and never ad-supported. Since the AI runs on users’ machines, Underdog doesn’t have the giant overhead of paying a provider for inference. Instead, it will take a tiny percentage of payment transactions the assistant makes using Stripe’s payment rails, something like an interchange fee.
The startup behind Underdog is Conway Research, backed by Andreessen Horowitz, Khosla Ventures, Hummingbird, SV Angel, the Anthology Fund, and angels including Patrick Collison and Guillermo Rauch.
Meta's most recent updates for its Ray-Ban smart glasses deliver upgrades to audio playback as well as new turn-by-turn walking navigation.

System update version 129 brings two audio changes. Mono Audio combines the left and right channels so nothing gets missed on the side you can't hear, and Audio Balance shifts sound toward your left or right ear. Both apply to sounds the glasses make, like Meta AI responses and notifications.

Version 128, which first debuted earlier in September, is now broadly available. It adds Spatial Audio support, further anti-tampering tweaks that stop the camera from working if the privacy LED has been messed with, and new location features.

Chief among them is turn-by-turn pedestrian navigation: just say “Hey Meta, navigate to Times Square.” Directions pull your location from your phone, and you can share a place from your mapping app directly to Meta AI to start navigation on the glasses. For places further away, Meta sends driving directions to your phone.
The audio changes are still starting to roll out, while the navigation upgrades are broadly available as an update in the Meta AI app.

At today’s Windows and Surface event, Microsoft showed off an upgrade to its Copilot AI system that will give it access to local files on your PC and the ability to take actions across the OS. It’s part of an idea Microsoft is calling “Hybrid Intelligence,” where apps and tools rely on a mix of local and cloud AI models to accomplish tasks efficiently.

To show off how Hybrid Intelligence works, Jacob Andreou, Microsoft’s EVP of Copilot, walked through a video demo onstage asking Microsoft’s Autopilot tool to help with filing taxes. Andreou told the AI agent that he got an email from his accountant and asked Autopilot to get her what she needs. Autopilot then used Hybrid Intelligence to search across different folders to find the documents, rename the files, zip them into a folder, and draft an email to send to the accountant with the zip file attached.
Features powered by Hybrid Intelligence will be coming to Copilot over the “next couple months,” Andreou said.

Microsoft also showed off a new Windows search experience that lets you take quick actions from the search bar, like turning on dark mode, turning up your mic volume with an in-line slider, or even sending a text. The new experience will be available starting this fall on Windows 11 PCs, according to Windows and Surface boss Pavan Davuluri.

One UI 9 brings Android 17 and several new features to the Galaxy S26, S26+, and S26 Ultra, including more Galaxy AI tools and additional customization options. The S26 series launched with One UI 8.5, so some features were already available.
Call Brief displays relevant information on the call screen — for example, a caller's country and local time when calling overseas.

My FanCam takes an existing video and creates a cropped version that follows a person you select: open a video in Gallery, tap the Galaxy AI icon, choose the person, orientation, and aspect ratio, then tap Follow.
Now Brief gets custom cards: you can create up to three using weather, health, or video information and choose when they appear.

The rest of the update is non-AI: resizable Quick Panel controls, a Warranty and care section, Bixby home screen widgets in three sizes, split layouts for Dual Recording, Driving Report, and easier Samsung DeX desktop management.
Good Lock's Home Up adds multi-finger gestures, such as a pinch-out to launch AI Select. The biggest reasons to explore One UI 9 are the additional AI tools and smaller conveniences.

At the inaugural MIT Future Fest, Tony Fadell projected a slide of three discontinued AI devices: the Rabbit R1, the Humane Ai pin, and the Limitless pendant. “These were kind of the ‘Gen 1’ AI products, and because of my background, these companies called me and asked me to help them,” he said. “I didn’t.”

“You have to really understand what you’re trying to do, what pain you’re trying to solve,” he said. “In each of these cases, each one of them didn’t meet any kind of need — it was just interesting technology for geeks.”

“It’s less than 0.01% of the world population that has ever had a human [assistant] do anything,” Fadell said. “Trust and safety are going to be paramount with anything that we turn over to some kind of intelligence.” He sees Apple — maybe one other company — as able to do this, and predicts a successful agent will have to operate on-device only.

He theorizes that Meta and OpenAI are turning to gadgets because they lack access to the sensors on your phone. “Because it’s a startup, you get one shot,” he quipped. “It’s not like Apple with the Vision Pro.”
The current beta of iOS 27.2 includes a Siri AI “suggested actions” feature in the Messages app that some will consider useful and others find annoying.

Suggested Actions were present in the initial iOS 27 beta, but Apple later pulled the feature after complaints that some suggestions were rather random. It returned in the iOS 27.2 beta. Messages offers one-tap suggestions based on the context of conversations, such as Add to Reminders and Add to Notes, or a button that jumps to a search for requested photos.

Leaker pdfu found new controls in iOS 27.2 beta 3 code to selectively toggle off unwanted suggestions. They allow suggestions to be toggled off by category, or you can let Siri AI hide the categories you haven’t used in the last 30 days.
These options aren’t yet live in the beta, but we can likely expect to see them soon.

Startup Ghost's first product is Core, a PC for local AI agents that runs LLMs exclusively on-device. Ghost calls it "a personal AI computer that runs models entirely on device," one that connects to your apps, files, and devices and "builds context on your life over time." Founder and CEO Zain Javaid, whose company just raised $11 million, calls it a "brain in a box".

Core is built around an Nvidia RTX Pro 4000 (Blackwell) with 24GB of video RAM, plus 64GB of DDR5, rated at 770 TOPS. It ships with Qwen-3.8-Next, Qwen-3.8-27B, and Gemma-4-31B pre-installed, updates models over the air, and is controlled via a phone or laptop app, including by voice.

blocks.cap: Ghost Core AI PC case shown removed, with the components on display

blocks.x: Personal data is encrypted, even Ghost can't access it, and the device is designed to keep running if Ghost shut down, with no subscription fee. A firewall limits how agents use credentials and flags suspicious outgoing requests for user review.

Core costs $3,499 in the US; the first batch sold out on day one and ships at the end of this month. A top-spec Mac mini for AI runs $3,199, but lacks Core's dedicated local-AI software and privacy features.

Meet Interface, a new $99 smart ring from AI and hardware startup Natura that's designed for the era of AI agents. With a press of your finger, you can ask an AI agent to complete a task, capture thoughts, and get things done without reaching for your phone — and the ring doubles as a health tracker.

At launch it connects with agents and apps including Meta's Muse, Instinct, Grok Bot, Claude and ChatGPT, and users can pick which agent handles which task. Responses arrive via headphones, an iPhone Live Activity or the NatureOS app. Preorders open next month, shipping in December or January.

"Ultimately, the main interface between users and technology is going to be the ring," founder Carlo Edoardo Ferraris said. After a three- to six-month free period, Natura plans a $9 monthly subscription.
The ring tracks heart rate, HRV, sleep stages, steps and skin temperature, and lasts six to 12 days per charge.

Apple has announced its second event of the fall, teased with the phrase "Welcome home," for October 13 at 9AM ET in Tribeca, New York. Along with refreshed versions of the Apple TV and HomePod mini, Apple is said to unveil its long-expected HomePad.
Apple has long been rumored to be working on a smart display to rival Amazon's Echo Show, and Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reported that Apple delayed the device until Siri AI was ready.

The HomePad is said to have a seven-inch display, a new operating system dubbed homeOS and a StandBy-like dashboard. Rumors suggest it will use face and voice recognition to personalize content for whoever is using it, alongside smart home control, FaceTime, streaming and intercom.
The new Apple TV and HomePod mini are likely getting spec upgrades so they can support Siri AI.

blocks.cap: Agility Robotics' Digit humanoid robot uses Nvidia's Halos system to help safely work around people. Credit: Agility Robotics

blocks.x: Nvidia's Halos system launched in 2025 to help developers implement guardrails in self-driving cars, and in June 2026 the company extended it with Halos for Robotics — for warehouse robots, factory humanoids and even surgical robots. "A thing we thought is going to be the next bottleneck is safety," said Nvidia's Amit Goel.

The full stack spans the IGX Thor module with an independent safety processor, a Halos OS that monitors "every hardware block" and "every software library," the Holoscan Sensor Bridge, simulation and an inspection lab program. Because a robot vacuum and a warehouse forklift define safety differently, developers can program custom safety functions.

Agility Robotics was first to put Halos inside its Digit 5 humanoid, letting it work near people without external sensors. "Now the robot is literally unchained," Goel said. Boston Dynamics, KION Group and LG are also on board.

blocks.cap: Image credit: Cybopal/Kickstarter

blocks.x: The Kickstarter-funded CyboPal ONE bolts a 27-inch 4K, 160Hz display to a six-axis robotic arm that clamps to your desk, keeps an eye on where you are, and moves the screen to match. The $1,599 Super Early Bird price compares with a planned $2,499 retail price.

It carries its own computer: an eight-core Rockchip RK3588 with a 6 TOPS NPU, 8GB of RAM and 128GB of storage in a "Linux AI Compute Base" that handles face tracking, gesture recognition and 3D spatial sensing on the device. A binocular 3D sensor handles obstacle avoidance and path planning, and face tracking repositions the screen in under four seconds.

The Pauli voice agent runs in a desktop client, and you still need a laptop or desktop for actual compute. The campaign, closing November 21, 2026, sits at over 11,000% of its HK$80,000 goal — but TechRadar notes backers are betting on software that hasn't been independently tested.

Back in June, Nvidia announced agreements with Microsoft and other PC makers to develop AI- and agent-ready Windows PCs based on its RTX Spark chip. On Wednesday, at an event in San Francisco during Tech Week, Microsoft revealed the specs and price for its new Surface Laptop Ultra. It comes in two base models, starting at $2,600 and $3,700, with options up to $5,900. (Microsoft says the highest-end device is already out of stock.)

Microsoft also revealed the Surface RTX Spark Dev Box workstation, which starts at $6,000 and comes with VS Code, GitHub Copilot CLI, WSL, and PowerShell 7. Both are designed to run AI models on-device locally (and for free).

They run a revamped Windows 11 with a feature called “Execution Containers,” which makes it easier to sandbox AI agents; it will be available for all Windows 11 users, CEO Satya Nadella said. “You need to have this harnessed layer that is able to take multiple models plus context, plus memory, and the action space,” he said.

The devices are clearly aimed at developers: Microsoft is offering up to $1,000 off to people who trade in a MacBook Pro. Dell also detailed its Nvidia-RTX Spark XPS 16 Creator Edition, priced at $3,800.
